stories.Headline: States Don’t Have to Solve the AI Education Equation Alone. Tennessee Shows How
stories.Summary:
States across the country are taking different approaches to AI policy, with governors forming task forces, state education agencies issuing non-binding guidance, and legislatures requiring districts to adopt AI policies. A November 2025 survey found that 93% of 29 state education agency respondents had communicated or planned to communicate a vision for AI in K-12 education, but only 43% had assisted or planned to assist districts with implementation support. Among the 39 states and territories studied for a state early adopter database, just 11% had reached the "integrator" stage of moving past guidance into pilots, evaluation, procurement help, and implementation strategies. The authors, Bree Dusseault and Dana Harrison of the Center on Reinventing Public Education, argue that this gap leaves schools without the practical help they need. The authors say AI is a difficult policy area because both the technology and public opinion change quickly, so guidance and task forces alone fall short.

School and district leaders need state help with vetting products, generating evidence on what works, and building trust in how AI is used. States also need infrastructure that links policy to classroom practice and turns scattered local experiments into shared knowledge. The article notes that many state education agencies lack the funding or internal expertise to lead these efforts. Intermediary organizations, the authors write, can fill that role, and a majority of participants in their study reported pursuing partnerships for strategy development, implementation, or both.

The article uses Tennessee's State Collaborative on Reforming Education, known as SCORE, as its main example. SCORE is a statewide nonprofit without formal authority over district decisions, and its influence comes from long-standing relationships with state leaders, districts, colleges, funders, and technology providers. After Tennessee required districts to adopt AI policies covering safety, academic integrity, and risk mitigation, SCORE convened a working group that met regularly for roughly 18 months, and its recommendations were reflected in the state's Action Plan. SCORE also helps districts evaluate tools without endorsing products, and it helped fund a larger rollout of Coursemojo, an AI-enabled literacy tool, across seven districts, 20 schools, and more than 4,000 students in 2025-26.

The authors say participating leaders and teachers reported positive results, and districts later renewed the work, often with their own funds. The authors stress that the Tennessee model need not be copied exactly, since an intermediary could be a nonprofit, a university, a technical service provider, or a research group, as long as it has trust, staying power, and the ability to connect people who do not normally work together. They warn that without such coordinated support, better-resourced districts may experiment while smaller and higher-need systems struggle to evaluate tools, set safeguards, and provide training, which could widen existing inequities. They conclude that the next phase of state AI leadership will depend less on publishing guidance than on building infrastructure for continuous learning, so that policies set direction and partnerships provide the capacity to follow it.

stories.Headline: Researchers are getting tired of OpenAI gatekeeping its breakthroughs
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on Monday, October 26, 2026 three results in mathematics, computer science and physics, along with a stated new approach to sharing its findings. The announcement followed a turbulent few months in which the company released hundreds of AI-generated preprints on mathematicians at the start of October. This time, OpenAI said it would work with expert "shepherds" to decide how to share the work, and each result got a different release strategy. The mathematics output was released as AI-generated text, leaving researchers to organize their own explanations, the computer science finding will be explained by an outside group of researchers, and the physics result has not been released at all, with OpenAI deferring to outside experts on how to proceed.

The mathematics result claims to resolve the Kakeya conjecture in all dimensions, a question about how little space is needed to turn a needle in every direction. Brown University mathematician Brendan Hassett said the claim "looks well supported," though he had not yet checked the Lean formalization used to verify it computationally. The physics result concerns quantum chromodynamics and its link to Yang-Mills theory, but it does not address the unresolved mass gap in the related Millennium Prize problem. The computer science result claims to disprove the exponential time hypothesis, a widely held assumption that closely relates to the P versus NP question. Researchers described the results as huge, major and significant, though they noted the difficulty of checking them.

Researchers who spoke to The Verge said they were tired of OpenAI's conduct, and many objected to handpicking experts to review the work first. Constantin Kogler of the Institute for Advanced Study said it made no sense for only a few scientists to see the results first, while Andreas Karch of the University of Texas at Austin called the handpicked group a disaster and asked why the proof could not be released publicly now. The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence had warned a day earlier against this practice, recommending release on scholarly repositories with formal proofs and funding for independent work. After the announcement, that group urged OpenAI to publish the physics output without delay, arguing the Lean formalization was already complete. Xiaoyu He of Georgia Institute of Technology said the deeper concern is that fundamental results are arriving quickly without human contribution and are hard to read and verify, a problem that changes in release method cannot fix.

stories.Headline: [PRNewswire] Guidewire Delivers Core Platform for Agentic Insurance
stories.Summary:
Guidewire, the insurance software company listed on the NYSE as GWRE, launched a new platform approach to agentic insurance on October 28, 2026, at its Connections conference in Las Vegas. The company says the platform gives insurers an open, secure, and complete foundation for using AI across the insurance lifecycle. It brings together applications, data, workflows, and controls so that insurers can move from isolated AI experiments to governed agents that improve the speed and precision of decisions. Guidewire presents this as a practical model for doing so.

The platform places agents on the same system that runs the company's core applications, so they can work with an insurer's current data and workflows. Controls define what each agent can know and do, with consistent security and an audit trail that stays current through ongoing updates. Guidewire describes its growing portfolio across underwriting, claims, and technical infrastructure, including Advanced Product Designer, PricingCenter, Risk Accumulation App, UnderwritingCenter, ProNavigator, Concierge, and Kaleidoscope. Several features, marked as early access or roadmap items, are available only to certain customers, and the company notes that some release features may not be available in all regions.

Mike Rosenbaum, Guidewire's chief executive officer, said that insurance is a business of decisions made in context and that embedding agents in core operations gives them the context and controls they need. Diego Devalle, the company's chief product development officer, said the scalability and observability that support the core now support agents as well, which lets insurers put them to work on live claims and policies. Amy Mollin, vice president of product management, said agents built into ClaimCenter capture losses, summarize files, and flag risk so adjusters have more time for important conversations. Karlyn Carnahan of Celent said the next challenge for insurers is making these capabilities work within existing systems. Tatjana Lalkovic, chief technology officer at Definity, said Guidewire's Developer Assistants help her company's teams move from idea to implementation faster.

The announcement comes as insurers face pressure from competitors to become more agile with products and pricing, and as many have moved past early AI experiments. Guidewire says it is also using AI in its own professional services, where it reports materially shorter migration and implementation timelines. The company is demonstrating the platform at Connections, where more than 3,000 insurers and partners from 36 countries are gathered for its annual customer conference. Guidewire will continue to expand its portfolio of agents, though the announcement itself does not specify a timeline for further releases.

stories.Headline: UnitedHealthcare Is Rolling Out Its AI Agent To 21 Million Members
stories.Summary:
UnitedHealthcare is expanding access to Avery, its generative AI companion designed to support care coordination for members, to 21 million people. The tool was first unveiled earlier this year, when it was available to about 6.5 million members in employer plans and 160,000 people enrolled in Medicare Advantage. The expansion is growing the tool's reach faster than the insurer originally expected, according to the reporting. The company says Avery has resolved 90% of member interactions, and in the remaining 10% of cases it can hand off to a human advocate.

Avery is built on what the company calls ground truth systems, a data foundation that sits on top of the information available through UnitedHealthcare. Craig Kurtzweil, the company's chief data and analytics officer, said that foundation is what lets members get better answers. Avery can provide details on deductibles, out-of-pocket maximums, provider networks, pricing and claims processing. Kurtzweil said accuracy is central to members trusting the tool and using it effectively. He described making the tool as accurate as possible as a major part of earning consumers' trust.

Kurtzweil told Fierce Healthcare that the expansion makes sense given the early results and feedback from users. He said Avery fits into a broader push to put more information in members' hands, including plan designs like Surest, which offer variable copayments that let members choose providers and care. The team is also building an option for Avery to call providers and schedule appointments on a member's behalf. Kurtzweil said the company intends to keep widening access until all of its enrollees can use the tool. He added that more and more people will be affected as the company works to reduce friction and make things easier for consumers.

stories.Headline: Businesses increasingly adopt AI for cybersecurity while individuals expand privacy protections
stories.Summary:
Businesses across the OECD are turning to artificial intelligence to defend against cyber threats, while individuals are using privacy tools to take more control of their personal data, according to new OECD data released in late October 2026. In 2023, 17.7% of enterprises in the OECD experienced ICT security incidents, a rise of 28.2% from 2018. In 2025, 5.3% of enterprises used AI for ICT security, roughly one quarter of all enterprises using AI. Uses include machine learning systems that detect and prevent attacks and AI-based user authentication. Adoption in 2025 was 23.2% higher than in 2024, 68.6% higher than in 2023, and more than double the 2021 level.

Use of AI for security depends heavily on company size and sector. In 2025, 26.7% of large enterprises used AI for ICT security, compared with 9.6% of medium-sized enterprises and 3.7% of small ones. Among industries, 18.1% of firms in information and communication reported using it, well ahead of professional, scientific and technical activities at 8.9%. Adoption in the ICT sector was about nine times higher than in accommodation and food services, at 2.1%. The OECD suggests these tools spread most in information-intensive sectors, where cyber risks and reliance on digital systems are greatest.

Individuals are also acting more on their own data. Between 2020 and 2025, the share changing browser settings to limit cookies rose by 26.8%, while those refusing personal data use for advertising rose by 17.2% and those restricting access to their location rose by 14.0%. Smaller increases were seen for limiting social media profile access (11.3%) and using anti-tracking software (7.0%). The OECD links these trends to more privacy controls in browsers, operating systems and online platforms, and to greater awareness of data protection. By 2025, more than half of individuals had either restricted location access or refused personal data use for advertising, while the share reading privacy policies before sharing data fell by about 8.4%.

Concern about privacy is rarely the reason people avoid generative AI, with only 4.5% of OECD individuals citing it as their main reason in 2025. Older adults aged 55 to 74 were more likely than those aged 16 to 24 to avoid AI over such concerns, at 5.8% against 1.9%, and less likely to take active privacy steps. Younger people reported fewer worries about AI but frequently used privacy controls and anti-tracking tools. Education also shapes privacy behaviour: individuals with higher attainment were far more likely to refuse personal data use for advertising (68.1% against 39.5%) and to restrict location access (65.8% against 38.9%) than those with low attainment, although concern about generative AI was similar across both groups.

stories.Headline: Vera Health has secured $28.5M for clinical AI search platform
stories.Summary:
Vera Health, a company that offers an AI search platform for clinicians, announced on October 27, 2026 that it had secured $28.5 million in Series A funding, bringing its total raised to $32 million. Threshold Ventures led the round, with participation from Mantis VC and SV Angel, and existing investors Y Combinator and Gradient also put more money in. Fierce Healthcare reported that Optum Ventures took part as well. The platform is free for licensed clinicians and medical trainees, who can ask questions about diagnoses, medication dosing, guidelines and treatment and receive summaries linked to their sources.

The company plans to use the new capital to improve its platform, scale into more healthcare markets and expand partnerships with medical societies, publishers and health systems. It also intends to keep investing in locally relevant clinical guidance and in tools that let healthcare institutions add their own medical knowledge to the platform through its Vera Spaces offering. Fierce Healthcare reported that the platform scans more than 60 million peer-reviewed publications, clinical guidelines, consensus statements and drug labels, and that it is used by more than 800,000 clinicians in 190 countries, up from a few thousand a year earlier. The company also said it doubled its team from six to 12 people and is now hiring internationally.

Taieb Bennani, a cofounder of Vera Health, has described the company's focus on clinicians and its emphasis on evidence. He said clinicians make decisions in seconds and that the team, which includes clinicians or their relatives, builds the product around that need. Threshold Ventures co-founder and managing partner Emily Melton said in a statement that the platform starts with evidence rather than just an answer, which helps clinicians assess the research behind a decision. Bennani also told Fierce Healthcare that the company's approach rests on honesty, traceability, transparency and context, and that the tool searches for evidence before writing an answer.

The funding comes amid growing competition in clinical AI search. MobiHealthNews noted that OpenEvidence secured $250 million in Series D funding in January, doubling its valuation to $12 billion, and that Doximity recently partnered with Wolters Kluwer Health to bring UpToDate content into its Ask tool. Fierce Healthcare added that established reference companies such as Elsevier's ClinicalKey and Wolters Kluwer's UpToDate are competing with AI-native tools as well as consumer technology firms like OpenAI and Anthropic. The articles do not say what Vera Health will do next beyond the plans already described.

stories.Headline: Apple announces Siri AI will expand to these new languages soon
stories.Summary:
Apple released iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 on Monday, October 26, 2026, as the first major updates to the iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 systems that launched in September. The update expands Siri AI to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish, which were not supported before, and it adds several other features. Apple also said four more languages, Chinese (Traditional), Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese, will arrive by the end of the year. Siri AI was previously available only in English.

The Siri AI improvements in this release let the assistant recall earlier conversations, so a user can ask about a restaurant it suggested the week before. It can also draw on more sources, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, voicemails, and Safari history and Reading List. A new Excluded Apps setting lets users choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can reach from one place. Other additions include Messages suggestions that help with tasks like adding a dinner invite to Calendar, and support for SynthID watermarking in Photos and Image Playground. The update also brings Simple Profiles to the Apple TV app and lets FaceTime calls include a third-party sign language interpreter or live captioner.

Apple did not describe who was responsible for the changes beyond the company itself, and the articles give no statement from any individual. The release notes say Siri AI is not available in the European Union or mainland China. Bloomberg reporting cited in one article says Apple plans to bring some initial Apple Intelligence features to China with iOS 27.3, but Siri AI is not expected among them. The articles expect the new Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese support to arrive with iOS 27.3, which is expected in December, with its first beta possibly appearing the following week.

The release also comes alongside other Apple announcements, including a new Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini 2 with Siri AI announced on October 13. Users can get the update by going to Settings, then General, then Software Update. Apple also released iOS 26.7.2 with security fixes. Readers who have tried Siri AI in a language other than English have been invited to share their experiences in the comments.

stories.Headline: ‘If you’re hungry in the city, this building’s for you,’ Met Council says of new, $25 million, AI-powered Brooklyn warehouse
stories.Summary:
The Met Council, a Jewish anti-poverty organization, opened a new $25 million, AI-powered food distribution warehouse in Canarsie, Brooklyn, on Monday, October 26, 2026. The 22,000-square-foot facility lets people in need order groceries in advance for home delivery or pickup, instead of taking whatever is available at a pantry. Roughly 250 people attended the opening, which the organization called the largest capital project in its history. The warehouse was built to serve up to a million people a year, and the group hopes to eventually triple its current reach beyond the more than 350,000 New Yorkers it serves annually.

The facility uses advanced cold storage, automation and artificial intelligence to manage inventory and distribute food more efficiently. It supports the Met Council's network of more than 200 food pantry partners across the five boroughs, along with year-round kosher and halal distributions. It also helps the group provide medically tailored meals and groceries to eligible Medicaid recipients through New York's Social Care Network program. Officials described the project as a major step in expanding the group's ability to feed hungry New Yorkers. The building was reported to have taken about five years to develop.

David Greenfield, the Met Council's chief executive, said the organization was building infrastructure to fight poverty on a much larger scale, and he called the project a labor of love. He told attendees that anyone who is hungry in the city is welcome at the building, regardless of background or language. Joseph Allerhand, the group's co-president, said the facility shows its commitment to feeding those who need help most, including working-class and middle-class families. Speakers at the event, including New York City Comptroller Mark Levine and state Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli, praised the use of technology to reduce waste and serve more people.

The project sits within growing demand for food assistance across the city, and speakers linked the work to public safety and community strength. Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said his own family needed help to get by and that such support can strengthen neighborhoods. Greenfield closed by citing a Torah commandment to care for the widow, the orphan and the stranger, saying an open hand is open to everyone. The articles do not describe any further phases or timelines beyond the reach the organization hopes to reach over time.

stories.Headline: US Bishops Appoint Georgetown Leader on Catholic Social Thought to New AI Task Force
stories.Summary:
The United States Conference of Catholic Bishops announced on October 16, 2026, that it had appointed Kim Daniels, a Georgetown University figure, as a consultant to its new task force on artificial intelligence. The task force was inspired by Pope Leo XIV's first papal encyclical, "Magnifica Humanitas," and aims to help American Church leaders understand the opportunities and risks AI poses in areas such as education, governance and human welfare. Daniels directs Georgetown's Initiative on Catholic Social Thought and Public Life, previously served in the Vatican Dicastery for Communication, and took part in the Synod on Synodality, which concluded in 2024. Last month she moderated a Georgetown panel on AI, Catholic social teaching and the pope's invitation to dialogue with the world.

Daniels said she would help the task force stress that AI must serve human dignity and the common good, drawing on the encyclical's central message. She quoted the encyclical's call for a social, economic and political order that lets everyone, particularly the weakest, live a dignified life without anyone being left behind. As part of its broader mission, the task force plans to engage with AI labs, research groups and other institutions. Daniels said she was grateful to partner with the bishops on this work, and she looks forward to the effort.

Separately, Cleveland Clinic's cancer institute, which published its account on October 26, 2026, has formalized a strategic approach to evaluating AI technologies. The Cancer Institute Office of Technology and Digital Strategy, led by Dr. Paul Thambi and Dr. Louis Williams, vets proposals from AI companies for their effect on operations, care delivery and alignment with enterprise goals. The institute already uses AI to personalize radiation doses for lung cancer patients, cut note-taking time by up to 75 percent and streamline patient referrals. A separate enterprise AI Task Force, described as analogous to an institutional review board, evaluates non-research AI applications for safety, bias, data security and changes in performance over time.

The clinic's leaders said the goal is to adopt AI responsibly so that clinicians have more time for patients. Williams said AI will become fundamental to running the institute, from operations to scheduling to clinical decision-making, and that continuous re-evaluation of each tool is essential because models can drift or carry hidden bias. Thambi said the richness of the clinic's clinical data allows AI models to make accurate predictions and could lead to new discoveries. He added that the human element remains necessary for delivering a diagnosis and supporting patients, and that the tools are meant to keep clinicians more present with patients.

stories.Headline: AI and the quiet erosion of human judgment
stories.Summary:
Winnipeg Free Press columnist Rod Lastra, in an opinion piece posted on October 28, 2026, argues that the quiet loss of human judgment is a more pressing concern than the predictions surrounding artificial intelligence. He opens by recalling Paul Simon's 1986 song The Boy in the Bubble, using its image of a world more technologically capable but not necessarily wiser as a frame for the present. Lastra notes that predictions about AI have multiplied since ChatGPT's release in November 2022, and that tech leaders have talked up approaching superintelligence and futures ranging from flourishing to catastrophe. He says these predictions often carry more confidence than evidence.

The column's central concern is whether people can still understand, question and oversee AI outputs as systems grow more capable and take on more complex work. Lastra explains that AI is not a single technology, that fluency does not guarantee accuracy, and that agentic systems can carry out sequences of actions on people's behalf. He describes a paradox in which delegating work to gain efficiency can produce so much output that meaningful human review becomes difficult. He also points to Manitoba's Bill 51, the Public Sector Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity Governance Act, which recognizes human oversight as part of responsible AI governance, while asking whether that capacity could be lost anyway. Signing off on a result, he writes, is not the same as understanding it.

Lastra's thought experiment describes an organization in which one AI analyzes thousands of records, a second summarizes the findings, and a manager approves the recommendation, leaving the question of what was actually reviewed. He warns of oversight fatigue, in which approval becomes routine once recommendations arrive faster than people can examine them, and he cites automated financial trading as an earlier example of transactions outpacing human intervention. The more work is delegated, he argues, the fewer chances people have to practise the judgment needed to supervise it, so dependence can reinforce itself. He says the aim is not to reject AI but to adopt it deliberately, defining its purpose, testing it under real conditions, keeping the ability to intervene and allowing time for review. He adds that AI literacy must mean more than writing prompts.

A separate opinion piece on UPI.com, published October 27, 2026 by Carlos Cantero Ojeda, raises a parallel concern for Latin America. It notes that the fourth Latin American Artificial Intelligence Index, released October 20, 2026 by Chile's National Center for Artificial Intelligence and the U.N. Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, ranks 20 countries, with Chile first, followed by Brazil and Uruguay. Cantero Ojeda argues that technological readiness differs from human agency, which he describes as the capacity to act intentionally, reflect on choices and accept responsibility for them. He draws on the work of Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela to argue that AI systems are designed and sustained from outside themselves, so they cannot carry the ethical judgment and moral responsibility that people bear. He describes the weakening of attention and deliberation as "agency starvation," which he attributes partly to platform designs that narrow what people see and make reasoning harder to follow.

stories.Headline: Agentic AI Foundation expands with four new projects
stories.Summary:
The Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) has grown from three projects to ten in its first year, adding four new initiatives at the AGNTCon + MCPCon North America 2026 event in San Jose on October 22 and 23. Mazin Gilbert, the foundation's executive director, announced the new projects along with three new governance committees. Alibaba contributed OpenSandbox, a secure sandbox for running agents, while OpenAI contributed Open Responses, a specification for interoperable large language model interfaces. Anthropic added its Agent Skills standard, and Hugging Face contributed OpenEnv, a framework for reinforcement learning environments. The event itself shifted much of its focus toward protocol features, security, and identity.

Open Responses already has support from AWS Bedrock, Databricks, Ollama, Nvidia, and vLLM, according to coverage of the event. Anthropic's Model Context Protocol received a stateless server mode in its July 28 specification, and about 70 percent of traffic on some platforms already uses it. Anthropic also announced support for MCP tasks in Claude Code, which lets tool calls run for minutes, hours, or even days. On the security side, cumulative SDK downloads for the protocol have reached 4.17 billion, up from about 3 billion a month earlier. About a third of the 116 conformance scenarios now test security, and enterprise-managed authorization is live in Claude.

Manik Surtani, the foundation's CTO, said the organization launched a year ago with a belief that agentic AI needed a neutral home to thrive. He compared the situation to Kubernetes, which succeeded after Google moved it into a neutral foundation. Surtani argued that a license alone does not keep infrastructure open and said the remaining open problems sit in identity, attestation, audit, and payments. Some outside observers were more skeptical, with one publication noting that Anthropic still defines its own Messages API and Google its Interactions API. Another warned that the rapid embrace of AI agents may be too fast for some industries.

Other speakers addressed practical and security concerns. Dawn Song, a UC Berkeley professor, warned that frontier AI could help attackers more than defenders in the near term, citing a benchmark in which one model produced about 230 working exploits against 869 targets in two hours. Her proposed response was secure-by-construction systems supported by AI-generated proofs. Chrome's Sarah Drasner presented WebMCP, a proposed web standard in origin trial that lets websites expose tools directly to agents, which she said can make some actions 2.5 to 7.5 times faster and complements MCP rather than replacing it. Block also demonstrated Buzz, an open source workspace where people and agents share channels, with version 1.0 expected in mid-November.

stories.Headline: Risks & Rewards: How AI Is Redefining the CISO's Role
stories.Summary:
Mark Weatherford, Nvidia's head of cybersecurity policy and strategic engagement, spoke at the ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026 in Denver, where he described how the chief information security officer role is changing around artificial intelligence. Security leaders are now expected to help their businesses gain a competitive edge with AI while also using the technology to manage cyber risk. Weatherford's remarks were reported by Jai Vijayan of Dark Reading on October 26, 2026. He said keeping up with the pace of change is the biggest challenge, noting that penetration testing four times a year, once considered adequate, is no longer enough and that testing should now run around the clock.

Weatherford said many organizations are deploying AI out of a fear of missing out, often without sufficient business due diligence or a clear understanding of the value they will get. He also observed that CISOs tend to default to "no" whenever there is any element of risk. He pointed to the Navy concept of command by negation, in which subordinates act on their own toward a goal unless a superior tells them to stop, and suggested security leaders should accept more risk on their own, calibrated to their company's risk tolerance. He urged CISOs to stay curious, step outside their comfort zones, and keep finding ways to improve their role, suggesting that one way to get up to speed on AI is to take up one new topic each week.

Weatherford argued that it is the CISO's job to make sure the board understands the risks and knows who owns each one, especially when another executive's AI deployment creates the risk. He acknowledged that such frankness can be career-limiting, but said CISOs often get blamed for decisions that are not theirs and should push back. In his words, the people taking a risk need to be responsible for it. On talent, he favors paid internships that bring AI-native young people into the company, and he has suggested interview exercises in which candidates use AI to solve a live business problem with no single right answer. He also said organizations should maintain career paths and upward mobility, and that simply paying people more while keeping them in the same roles is not an effective way to retain them.

stories.Headline: Liquid AI Releases LFM3: 6 Open-Weight 2B-Class Multimodal Models
stories.Summary:
Liquid AI has released LFM3, a new generation of its Liquid Foundation Models, consisting of six open-weight models in the 2-billion-parameter class that share one backbone. The family covers text, vision, audio, omni, and decision tasks, and Liquid AI says every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU and then deployed on phones, laptops, private servers, or in the cloud. The two articles report the release on October 27, 2026, with the Hugging Face post presenting it as the starting point for specialized models. Both are written around the same family of models.

The family includes LFM3-1.7B, a text model with 1.73 billion parameters and a 256K context window that can run in about 1 GB of memory at 4-bit precision. LFM3-VL-2B is the first LFM vision model to accept video input, sampled at 2 frames per second, and LFM3-Audio-2B handles speech in and out across 18 languages with tool calling. LFM3-Omni-2B combines vision, audio, and language, and two decision models, d1-2B and d1-Omni-2B, answer many questions in one forward pass. According to Liquid AI's own evaluation, LFM3-1.7B averages 49.37 across 29 benchmarks, ahead of Qwen3.5-9B at 47.24, with strong results on IFEval and AutomationBench but weaker ones on Humanity's Last Exam without tools and RULER at 128K. Checkpoints in GGUF, MLX, ONNX, FP8, and NVFP4 formats ship with the release.

The architecture uses a tri-hybrid layer mix across 24 layers, made up of 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention layers with a 256-token window, and 6 global attention layers, with convolution kernels grown from 3 to 7. Liquid AI says it found this design through a hardware-in-the-loop architecture search covering 14 device and backend combinations, including a Raspberry Pi 5 and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU. Other changes include head-wise sigmoid gates, partial RoPE on global layers, and sandwich norm. The base model was trained on 22 trillion tokens, with the final 3.5 trillion focused on agent-heavy mid-training that extended context to 256K, and post-training ran in four stages.

Liquid AI reports that LFM3-1.7B beats its own LFM2.5-2.6B with 35% fewer parameters, and that it scores 38.42 on WebArena-Verified against 28.94 for Qwen3.5-9B. Its comparison table lists the LFM Open License v1.0, which carries a $10 million revenue threshold, while several rivals use Apache 2.0. The Hugging Face post, written by members of the Liquid AI team, presents LFM3 as a basis for fine-tuning on private data and deployment at the edge. Neither article describes further releases or timelines beyond the current family.

stories.Headline: AMD, Nvidia target substrate capacity amid 4x expansion constraints
stories.Summary:
AMD and Nvidia, two of the largest makers of graphics processing units used in artificial intelligence, have been compared as investments in an article published by The Motley Fool on October 27, 2026. The author, Keithen Drury, argues that the two companies are fundamentally different as stocks, especially on price. He notes that Nvidia's data center division posted revenue of $89 billion in the second quarter of its fiscal 2027, which ended July 26, while AMD's second quarter, ended June 30, brought in $6.7 billion from its data center division. Nvidia's total revenue for the period was $96.2 billion and AMD's was $11.5 billion, so the article treats the comparison as imperfect because the two companies' financial calendars are about one month apart.

The article points out that Nvidia grew its data center revenue by 117 percent in the quarter, compared with 107 percent for AMD, even though Nvidia is more than ten times larger in that segment. Drury describes the usual expectation that a smaller company grows faster as the law of large numbers, and says the data does not show that happening here. On valuation, he states that when measured by forward earnings, AMD trades at roughly three times the multiple of Nvidia. He calls this gap illogical and predicts that the two stocks will eventually trade at similar valuations, though he says it is uncertain whether that will come from an AMD sell-off or an Nvidia rise.

He is confident Nvidia will outperform AMD over the next few years. The article is an opinion piece from a financial publication that sells investment advice, and it includes promotional material for its Stock Advisor service, noting that Nvidia was not among its ten top picks. The author states that he holds a position in Nvidia, and the publisher discloses positions in both companies. The article does not describe any upcoming regulatory action, earnings release, or formal announcement, so the forecasts about future valuations and share performance remain the author's own views.

stories.Headline: ASMPT sales jump 49% on AI chip packaging as core equipment unit misses
stories.Summary:
ASMPT, the Hong Kong-listed chip equipment maker, reported third-quarter revenue of HK$5.25 billion, about $669 million, up 49% from a year earlier, according to a Bloomberg report published October 28, 2026. Its advanced packaging business drove nearly all of that growth, while its semiconductor solutions segment, which sells front-end manufacturing gear, came in just short of analyst expectations. The company guided fourth-quarter revenue to between $670 million and $730 million. The split result points to packaging, rather than front-end chipmaking tools, as the current bottleneck in AI hardware. Advanced packaging is now growing faster than the equipment that makes the chips themselves.

Thermo-compression bonding equipment, used to stack high-bandwidth memory onto AI accelerators, is the fastest-growing piece. ASMPT's advanced packaging unit posted record first-half revenue of $339 million in 2026, up 17% year over year. Thermo-compression bonding revenue grew 146% in the most recent period covered by the company's disclosures. The company has said the addressable market for its bonding tools alone could top $1.6 billion by 2028. ASMPT's legacy business trails well behind that growth.

The constraint now lies in packaging capacity rather than wafer output. TSMC's CoWoS capacity, the process that binds compute dies to memory stacks, is reportedly booked through 2027. Nvidia alone is expected to need about 1.2 million CoWoS wafers that year, while AMD's needs are projected to rise roughly 308%, from about 130,000 wafers in 2026 to 530,000 in 2027. AMD has reportedly routed about half its packaging orders to ASE, SPIL and Amkor. SK Hynix, which along with Samsung and Micron controls nearly all HBM supply, has committed roughly $12.85 billion to a new packaging facility in Cheongju, South Korea.

ASM International, a separate Dutch equipment maker often confused with ASMPT, reported its own record quarter the same day, with revenue of €1.159 billion, up 44% at constant currencies. It now expects to reach €5.7 billion in 2027 revenue, a target it had originally set for 2030. Similar AI-driven beats have come from SK Hynix and TSMC this year. Companies selling into advanced packaging and HBM are beating guidance, while those in legacy chipmaking equipment are relying on a recovery in the mainstream market.

stories.Headline: WRI STATEMENT: Antalya AI Pledge Must Turn Climate Ambition into Accountability
stories.Summary:
On October 27, 2026, the COP31 Presidency of Türkiye released the Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge and invited countries and organizations to sign it ahead of the next U.N. climate conference. The voluntary pledge aims to use AI to advance climate action while addressing the environmental strain of its growing energy and water demands. Türkiye released the text in Antalya, and the pledge is open for signature before the conference, which is set to be held next month. Two groups responded the same day, and both view the pledge as a useful first step that still falls short. Its purpose is to make AI work for climate goals while limiting the harm that large data centers can cause.

The pledge includes voluntary commitments to new reporting on environmental impacts and to the allocation of infrastructure costs, along with support for climate solutions in developing countries. Critics say it lacks meaningful accountability or enforcement, gives companies wide discretion over what they promise, and does not establish real participation by affected communities. World Resources Institute's Evan Tachovsky said the pledge sets the right direction but needs accountability mechanisms, real funding behind its finance commitments, and safeguards for water and air quality. He also called for clean energy for data centers, full disclosure of energy and water use, companies paying for their own grid upgrades, and local communities involved from the start. He suggested the pledge's first stocktake at COP32 could serve as the point to move toward real accountability.

Julie Cerqueira, Chief Program Officer at the Natural Resources Defense Council, said the pledge is an important start but is only that, and that more work is needed quickly because of the pace of industry growth. She said the pledge needs enforcement, tighter limits on company discretion, and meaningful participation by affected communities, and that broader impacts such as water supplies, air quality, and community effects must also be addressed. She described the challenge as larger in speed, scale, and scope than most previous ones, so the safeguards must match. Both organizations describe the pledge as a step in the right direction that would need stronger enforcement and wider protections to produce results. The next major test is the first stocktake at COP32, where supporters and critics alike will look for evidence that the commitments have become binding.

stories.Headline: Anthropic Unveils 335-Page Public Prospectus: Poised to Make History as the Largest-Ever IPO and the Most Loss-Making AI Company of All Time
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the parent company of Claude, has publicly filed its formal prospectus for a NASDAQ listing under the stock code "ANT." The 335-page document was posted on the SEC website on October 27, 2026, after the company confidentially submitted its S-1 draft on June 1. Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter, has reported that Anthropic plans to complete the IPO in mid-November. Because the SEC requires an S-1 to be public at least 15 days before a roadshow, the roadshow could begin as early as the second week of November.

The public version updates the computing power commitments in the earlier leaked draft. The commitment to Microsoft has risen from 31.4 billion dollars to 44.9 billion dollars, the commitment to Google stands at 114.5 billion dollars, and the largest contract with SpaceXAI is worth up to 120.5 billion dollars. Two new suppliers, Nscale and Lambda, are also disclosed. On finances, revenue reached 16.286 billion dollars in the first half of 2026, compared with 1.16 billion dollars a year earlier, while the net loss for the half was 80.748 billion dollars, against about 41.965 billion dollars for all of 2025. Roughly 72.4 billion dollars of that loss comes from fair value changes on convertible notes, derivative liabilities and other financing instruments, a book entry that does not mean the same amount was paid in cash.

Usage-based billing, including API calls, brought in about 13.06 billion dollars in the first half, or around 80.2 percent of revenue, while subscriptions contributed about 3.2 billion dollars, or 19.6 percent. As of September 30, 2026, more than 11,900 customers had trailing twelve-month revenue of at least 100,000 dollars, up from 950 a year earlier. The final version names Amazon and Google as the two largest customers, each at about 12 percent of revenue, rather than Cursor and Microsoft's Github Copilot as earlier rumored. At an investor day in mid-October, the company said third-quarter revenue hit 16.8 billion dollars, up 45 percent from the prior quarter, and that it reached profitability on an adjusted basis. The prospectus describes a single operating segment, with CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei as the top operating decision-makers, and says the company has chosen not to build image or video generation models so it can focus computing power on programming, agent capabilities and safety research.

The fundraising size and price are not yet final, but the earlier draft pointed to a maximum raise of about 1 trillion dollars at a valuation near 2 trillion dollars. That would top the 1.77 trillion dollar valuation of Elon Musk's SpaceX in its June offering and make this the largest IPO on record. Some investors, however, have cut their expectations to about 1.5 trillion dollars as the AI sector has come under pressure. Anthropic would be first past the post in the race with rival OpenAI, and the first pure frontier model developer to list on U.S. markets. Menlo Ventures data cited in the coverage gives Anthropic 42 percent of the 1.9 billion dollar code generation market, ahead of OpenAI at 21 percent.

stories.Headline: Lumion Highlights AI Agents for After-Hours Inquiries and Lead Follow-Up
stories.Summary:
Lumion, a technology company based in Salt Lake City, Utah, announced on October 27, 2026 that it is promoting AI agents built to handle customer inquiries, automated follow-up, and outreach to prospective customers. The platform combines AI-powered communication, workflow automation, and a unified inbox so organizations can manage calls, text messages, and website inquiries in one place. The company says the agents answer after-hours calls and other messages around the clock, and they can capture conversation details for employees to review later. The announcement targets a familiar problem, namely that inquiries often arrive when staff cannot respond, and delayed replies can cause prospects to move on.

The agents are meant to handle routine questions and record relevant context while leaving employees free to take over conversations that need more attention. A unified inbox gathers interactions from phone, email, and text so staff do not have to check several systems to see a customer's history. The platform also includes lead reactivation, which lets businesses reconnect with older prospects who never enrolled or completed a transaction. Lumion says businesses can start using the agents in as little as two weeks, configured around each organization's information and processes. Afterward, customers can extend the platform into application and onboarding workflows.

Lumion's chief statements come from Bilal Aslim, who is quoted in the announcement. He says a customer inquiry can arrive at any time, while a business team cannot always respond right away. According to Aslim, AI agents can help maintain continuity by responding to initial inquiries, capturing context, and supporting follow-up, so employees can concentrate on work that needs their judgment. The company presents the platform as a way to coordinate these tasks rather than to remove people from customer communication.

The announcement includes one customer example. At a career school, AI outreach to leads inactive for about two years produced two enrollments in the first week and 14 more over the following several weeks, with the first two generating a combined $10,000 in paid deposits. The articles stress that this reflects one customer's experience and that other organizations may see different results depending on lead quality and prospect responses. The company also says it has worked with more than 400 businesses and has managed and generated over $300 million in customer revenue through its platform. It further reports a $10.7 million seed round announced June 16, 2025, led by TTV Capital with participation from Tusk Venture Partners, intended to support market expansion and product innovation.

stories.Headline: Azerbaijan to establish Artificial Intelligence Observatory
stories.Summary:
On 27 October 2026, the Ministry of Economy of Azerbaijan and IE University of Spain signed a framework cooperation agreement to establish and develop an Artificial Intelligence Observatory focused on competitiveness and economic transformation. Deputy Minister of Economy Samad Bashirli announced the deal at the opening ceremony of IE University's Leadership and Innovation Center, which was set up with the backing of the Ministries of Economy and Science and Education. One report describes the agreement as part of the AI Hub initiative, and names the university partner as the University of Artificial Intelligence, which differs from the IE University named in the other report. The announcement came the same day as the ceremony, and the reports were published that afternoon and evening.

The observatory is meant to bring together academics, government bodies and business representatives to produce knowledge on Azerbaijan's economic development and to inform policy decisions. Its work will centre on applied research into economic diversification, productivity, competitiveness and international comparisons. The reports say the goal is to turn research findings into practical policy recommendations, and one adds that discussions will be held to support this. The articles do not give a budget, a timetable, staffing numbers or a launch date for the observatory.

Bashirli said the centre would help build human capital, strengthen the country's economic competitiveness and raise its innovation potential. He stated that the aim is to link international knowledge with national economic priorities and to turn investment in people into higher productivity and concrete economic results. He also said that Azerbaijani startups and entrepreneurs would be connected with international innovation networks, investors and experts, and that startups, investors, and technology park residents and operators would be able to benefit from tax incentives lasting up to 20 years, along with incentives for research and development, entrepreneurship investment and hiring international specialists. One report includes a letter from Mikayil Jabbarov that stresses developing human capital and modern technology as priorities.

The reports attribute the announcement to the government, with Bashirli speaking on its behalf, and the framework agreement is between the ministry and the university. The articles offer no comment from other parties or critics. They place the observatory within the country's wider push to diversify its economy and build innovation, and they note the support mechanisms already in place for startups. Beyond the stated plan to carry out the research and hold discussions, the articles do not say what will happen next.

stories.Headline: Cosm by Cielo™ introduces an AI-native operating model for the next era of talent acquisition
stories.Summary:
Cielo, a talent solutions firm based in Milwaukee, introduced Cosm by Cielo on October 27, 2026. The company describes it as an AI-native operating model meant to turn workforce demand into business outcomes faster than traditional recruiting models. It is powered by Cielo Lumis, which Cielo calls its system of action, and it links talent expertise, governance, AI-enabled workflows and real-time intelligence. The launch follows faster shifts in business priorities, skills demand and talent availability across employers.

Cielo cited its own Talent Benchmark research, which found that 87% of organizations increased talent acquisition technology investment over the past 12 months, yet many still struggle to turn that spending into greater hiring agility. It also referred to McKinsey research showing that organizations getting the most value from AI are redesigning how work gets done. Cosm starts with the business outcome and then determines the workflows, systems, decisions and human touchpoints needed to reach it. Rather than optimizing isolated hiring steps, it treats talent acquisition as a connected business capability.

Cielo says this moves hiring beyond faster task execution toward better decisions and quicker responses to shifting demand. Cielo reported results from early Cosm-enabled deployments, compared with prior performance: up to 5x higher candidate submissions, a 10% productivity improvement, a 15% lower cost per hire, and 20% fewer aged requisitions. Cielo's chief executive, Marissa Geist, said companies need a better way to turn work priorities into action rather than more disconnected recruiting tools. Cielo Lumis, the company says, connects workforce, talent and market signals to workflows and recruiter actions, and it works across applicant tracking and human capital management systems that organizations already use.

Cielo's chief operating officer, Molly Thiel, said the platform is meant to reduce friction so recruiters can spend more time advising the business and making accountable decisions. Cielo says Cosm operates within governed workflows and human oversight, with built-in transparency, accountability and clear limits on autonomous action. The company states that its AI governance framework is supported by ISO/IEC 42001 certification for AI management systems and ISO/IEC 27001 certification for information security management systems. The articles describe Cosm as a launch and do not report any further rollout timeline or next steps beyond that.

stories.Headline: Idris Elba's Akuna Group launches free Artificial Intelligence filmmaking programme for creators in five African countries
stories.Summary:
Akuna Learning, the education arm of The Akuna Group chaired by Sir Idris Elba, opened applications on 26 October 2026 for a free AI filmmaking programme called From Script to Screen with AI. The programme is open to aspiring creators in Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone and South Africa, and it is delivered in collaboration with Google. Google.org is supporting it with US$1 million, and the curriculum was developed by Curious Refuge. Applications close on 15 November 2026, and the programme is free both to apply for and to attend if selected. Over fifty weeks, selected creators will move through a twelve-week academy, then mentoring, pitching and production.

Everyone takes a foundational course in AI filmmaking before choosing one of five pathways: fiction, documentary, animation, advertising or screenwriting. The stages run from applications and selection between October 2026 and January 2027, to learning and certification from February to April 2027, then mentoring, a pitch round in June and July 2027, and film production through October 2027. Funded films will be showcased in October 2027, and creators keep control of their work, with no ownership claim by the programme or its partners. Applicants must be 18 or older, live in one of the five countries, and have a laptop, reliable internet and power for the full programme.

The Akuna Group is responsible for the programme, and Sir Idris Elba, its chairman, said the initiative is about education and giving creators across the continent access to courses that help them tell their own stories. He said selected projects will receive production funding and that he hopes the training leads to employment and helps shape how Africa is portrayed. Khaled Gad, the group's chief executive, said training alone does not build an industry, so the programme takes creators from their first application through to a finished, funded film. He also said that no film school background or prior AI experience is needed, only finished work that shows what the applicant can do.

The release notes that women are strongly encouraged to apply. The Akuna Group describes itself as a pan-African creative economy organisation that builds skills, capital and platforms for African creators. The articles do not say how many creators will be selected, how the funding will be divided among projects, or what the programme will cost Google beyond the stated US$1 million. stories.Headline: Why F1’s rule-makers are turning to AI to keep up with the teams and close loopholes
stories.Summary:
The Formula 1 governing body, the FIA, has chosen Amazon Web Services as its new partner for artificial intelligence, cloud computing, machine learning, and cloud infrastructure, an announcement made on Wednesday, October 28, 2026. The move follows the F1 organization's own work with AWS, which began in 2018, and comes as all 11 teams have already announced partnerships with AI firms. The FIA writes the final rulebook and polices how cars must look and perform aerodynamically, so the new deal is aimed at its own technical work. AWS already helped shape car design rules for the 2022 and 2026 regulation cycles.

The partnership gives the FIA more access to AWS capabilities, including newer and better hardware, while reducing costs. AWS's head of motorsport, Michael Aghataher, said the approach lets the FIA run thousands of simulations in parallel, turning a process that once took months into one that can finish in hours. The FIA is also looking at AI for policing track limits, with a road map to expand its use over the next couple of years. Under that plan, a human would still make each call, while AI pulls the needed data points and camera footage. Each F1 car carries 300 sensors that produce 1.1 million data points per second, or 24 million data points per race, which the FIA also hopes to process faster with AI.

The FIA's single-seater deputy technical director, Dominic Harlow, said AI is among the top interests for engineers right now and framed the effort as a way to keep pace with the teams. He said the teams are working hard to find loopholes in the rules, and that the FIA's technical department faces larger staff groups at each team. Aghataher described AWS as a supporting tool that optimizes human performance rather than a replacement for people. Harlow also said generative AI in car design regulation was something the FIA could imagine in the future, but that the work remains human-driven for now.

AI is now a regular agenda item at F1 Commission meetings, which set the rules and include the teams, the FIA and the F1 organization. Harlow said the sport is still in an exploration phase and has not yet made a large deployment or a real shift in how people work. The FIA plans to keep discussing the technology and monitor how it affects the areas that matter most to the sport. Given F1's long positioning at the leading edge of technology, all parties are watching closely how AI will be put into practice.

stories.Headline: AI Can Draw Any Building. But Can It Imagine One?
stories.Summary:
The first article, published by Sixth Tone in August 2026, describes architect Peter Guohua Fu's experiment with artificial intelligence. He had been prompted by a friend, Canadian composer Steve Barakatt, whose AI-generated design of a "piano café" surprised him. Fu then used AI to produce a two-hour film, "The Architect with Three Shades of Blue," recounting his career and the completion of "Music on the River" in Hengqin. The team was ten people, and the film cost under 200,000 yuan, or $29,650, and took less than two months to finish.

Fu's conclusion is that AI excels at execution but cannot originate ideas. He notes that the later stages of architectural design, such as detailed development and technical drawings, are where AI is most useful, and he cites a 2025 Royal Institute of British Architects report showing AI adoption among practices rose from 41% in 2024 to 59% in 2025. He estimates that large firms in China and Canada may already exceed 80%. Yet he argues that concept design remains beyond AI, since the tool can only recombine what already exists. He expects the profession to split toward two extremes: rare, original thinkers at one end and a growing number of people who can visualize their ideas at the other.

Fu also voices concern about education and development. He says that students at Tongji University and McGill's School of Architecture, where he has taught, have suddenly submitted work of remarkable quality, and he does not know whether they used AI but worries that they may not be building independent thinking skills. He describes this as a paradox, since excellent architects may need only a strong idea and the ability to direct AI, yet fewer people may gain the experience that produces such ideas. He also observes that the barrier to entry is falling, because anyone with aesthetic judgment can now generate a building image. Most such images will never be built, he concedes, and he recalls an abandoned underwater theater design that he later had his son recreate in a video game.

The second article, dated October 27, 2026 and reported by Jang Ji-seung for Seoul Economic Daily, covers a different AI development. Researchers led by Professor Baek Seung-ryeol at the Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology, working with the University of Aberdeen, created "FlexiAvatar," a system that builds 3D avatars from footage showing only part of a body. Existing methods assumed the whole body was visible, so upper-body or face-only video produced distorted results. The team combined a body model called SMPL-X with a rendering method known as 3D Gaussian splatting, and it used generative AI to supply unseen views such as the back of the head while weighting real footage more heavily. The work was presented at the European Conference on Computer Vision in Malmo, Sweden, in September 2026, and it was supported by South Korean government bodies including the National Research Foundation of Korea.

According to the report, FlexiAvatar outperformed comparison technologies on image quality measured in PSNR across all filming ranges. On the NeuMan full-body dataset it scored 35.77 dB against 34.80 dB for ExAvatar, and on real-world full-body footage it scored 30.98 dB against 28.65 dB for ToMiE. For face-focused footage the number of 3D components fell from 167,390 to 84,095, data size dropped 49.8% to 4.49 MB, and rendering speed rose about 34% to 39.15 frames per second. The report notes that total production time and graphics memory use did not fall by the same proportion, and the team plans further work on rendering loose clothing. Baek said the technology could serve video conferencing, virtual reality, films and games.

stories.Headline: SK Hynix profits soar amid roaring AI chip demand
stories.Summary:
South Korean chipmaker SK hynix said on Wednesday that its operating profit for the July to September quarter jumped 632 percent from a year earlier, driven largely by explosive demand from the artificial intelligence industry for its advanced memory chips. The company is a specialist supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips to Nvidia and a pillar of South Korea's tech-led economy. The global race to build AI data centres has transformed its fortunes, even though some people worry the sector may be overvalued. Demand is strong for DRAM chips and NAND storage components, which are used in everyday gadgets but are also needed to process the huge volumes of data handled by generative AI.

Operating profit for the quarter came to 83.33 trillion won, about $62.8 billion. Net profit rose 215.7 percent from last year to 39.77 trillion won, while sales reached 104.61 trillion won. The company said it has posted record revenue and operating profit for six straight quarters, going back to the second quarter of last year. Even so, the results fell short of market expectations, as analysts had on average forecast net profit of 59.67 trillion won, according to figures from the Yonhap news agency. On the same day, SK hynix announced a new plan to return 60 trillion won to shareholders, following the completion of an earlier 40 trillion won shareholder return programme.

In a statement, SK hynix said a virtuous cycle has taken hold, in which productivity gains and new revenue from AI in areas such as software development, customer service and search are leading to wider adoption of AI. Analysts say soaring DRAM prices during a global shortage, along with stronger sales of high-margin high-bandwidth memory, have lifted earnings, and the AI boom has also pushed up prices and shipments of conventional NAND chips. MS Hwang, an analyst at the research firm Counterpoint, said long-term agreements with major customers including Nvidia point to another round of price increases across DRAM, NAND and HBM. In his view, quarterly earnings have not yet peaked and the upward trend is likely to last at least through 2027. Kim Dae-jong, a business professor at Sejong University, said the shareholder return push matters because the stock has fallen nearly 60 percent from its June peak.

The share price has been under pressure since June, as investors largely shrugged off record earnings that had already been priced in, and as concerns grew about US tech firms' AI spending. Record profits have also fuelled calls from investors for more cash to be returned through dividends or buybacks. Hwang warned that for 2027, weaker AI spending, more competition and the company's own capacity expansion could all drive price volatility. He named the most severe threat as a repeat of 2018, when cloud service providers cut their orders at the same time. Kim added that the worry is that today's extraordinary earnings may not be sustainable in one or two years, and that this concern is already reflected in the share price.

stories.Headline: Acts of God Meet Acts of AI in Private Equity’s New Debt Play
stories.Summary:
Private equity firms are adding force majeure-style clauses to new buyout loans that would let borrowers pause the consequences of defaults they attribute to artificial intelligence disruption. H.I.G. Capital secured such language in a €470 million ($524 million) loan backing its majority stake in Terras Group, a German-headquartered provider of infrastructure engineering and construction services, according to people familiar with the deal. Several creditors said the language goes further than usual and has appeared in at least two leveraged buyout financings since September. One lender-side lawyer, Jeremy Duffy, a partner and chair of European leveraged finance at Cahill Gordon & Reindel LLP, said lenders and investors are closely reviewing such proposals.

Traditionally, force majeure clauses cover catastrophes such as hurricanes, earthquakes, the Covid pandemic or the 9/11 attacks. In the Terras deal, H.I.G. adapted that language so the clock stops on a default if AI disrupts the company, alongside other triggers including Covid-19 or another pandemic, a substantial rise in energy or resource prices, and war or terrorism. Lenders normally allow a grace period, typically 30 days, before a missed interest payment becomes a default that lets them demand repayment. The new provisions are framed as extending that grace period, but AI disruption has no clear end date the way a pandemic might. According to one person familiar with the deal, the clause would let Terras defer the consequences of unpaid interest for as long as it feels AI's impact, although the company still owes the interest.

Some creditors argue the provisions undermine the basic expectation that lenders will recover their money even when things go wrong. Lenders succeeded in having similar language struck from Bain Capital's €4.7 billion-equivalent ($5.3 billion) leveraged loan for its acquisition of a controlling stake in Volkswagen AG's heavy diesel-engine unit Everllence, according to the same people. The market's approach to investor protections has become split, with sponsors pressing for looser terms where they expect deals to perform well and reinserting covenants in troubled sectors like software. Software-as-a-service firms are seen as especially exposed to AI disruption, and buyout firms have large bets on them. H.I.G. was advised by Paul, Weiss lawyers including Neel Sachdev, while representatives at H.I.G. and Bain declined to comment and Sachdev did not reply to a request for comment.

stories.Headline: Otto Group and Sereact Bring NVIDIA-Powered Physical AI to Returns Processing
stories.Summary:
Otto Group and robotics software company Sereact announced on October 28, 2026 a two-phase program to test AI-controlled robots at Otto Group's logistics center in Poland. The robots will inspect and sort returned customer orders, a task that is hard to automate. Ten dual-arm systems will be deployed first, and 15 more robotic arms are planned for a second phase, bringing the total to 25. The companies are developing the technology together, and Otto Group will evaluate a wider rollout across its logistics network if the second phase succeeds.

The robots run on Cortex, Sereact's Physical AI model, which can handle items it has never seen before without product-specific training or a fixed catalog. Returns are difficult because items arrive folded, crumpled or repackaged, and the product mix of a multi-category retailer keeps changing. Cortex decides in real time how to grasp each item, assess its condition and route it. Sereact trains and validates the model with NVIDIA Isaac Sim, NVIDIA Isaac Lab and NVIDIA Cosmos, turning real picks into simulated variants so that fixes can reach the robots within days rather than weeks.

Sereact operates and maintains the systems under a Robotics-as-a-Service model. Employees will move away from repetitive grasping and lifting and toward supervision, handling exceptions and making final quality decisions. The robots will be introduced in stages, and each stage will produce operational feedback that the partners will use to improve the systems. The companies say this process will show whether the technology meets the reliability, flexibility and quality standards needed for broader use.

Martin Umland, Group Vice President Supply Chain Management at Otto Group, said the project will show at real scale how far Physical AI can go in making returns faster and the supply chain more flexible. Sereact CEO and co-founder Dr. Ralf Gulde said a robot that knows only yesterday's catalog is of little use in a returns center and that each handled return improves the model. The partnership is part of Otto Group's medium-term commitment to invest €350 million in technology and AI, and it follows the group's earlier robotics investments across its logistics operations. Sereact, founded in Stuttgart, raised a $116 million Series B in 2026 and counts Zalando, IKEA, DHL and BMW among its customers.

stories.Headline: UTA uses AI to uncover drivers of eye disease
stories.Summary:
The University of Texas at Arlington has received a $1.96 million grant from the National Eye Institute to build AI-powered computational tools that can identify the biological "control switches" that keep eyes healthy and reveal what causes eye disease. The four-year project was announced in an article posted on the UTA College of Science website, with the page dated October 8, 2026. The grant is meant to support the development of targeted therapies that could improve and preserve vision. The article does not say exactly when the work began.

The project will produce two separate computational tools. The first is a scalable tool designed to analyze large genomic datasets and identify regulators that matter for ocular health and disease. The second is a deconvoluting tool that separates mixed signals from whole eye tissue samples, which contain many cell types with different functions, so researchers can see how a regulator behaves in a specific cell type without running costly single-cell experiments for every regulator. Together, the tools are meant to let scientists study the eye both at the level of the overall tissue and at the level of individual cell types.

The researchers say this should help the field focus on the most promising targets and save time and resources. Xinlei (Sherry) Wang, the Jenkins Garrett Professor of statistics and data science in UTA's Department of Mathematics, leads the project in collaboration with Lin Xu, an assistant professor at UT Southwestern. Wang described the eye as containing many specialized tissues and cell types that work together to make vision possible, and she called understanding the relationship between tissue-specific transcriptional regulators and visual function a cornerstone of vision research. Morteza Khaledi, dean of the College of Science, called the grant an outstanding achievement that reflects the strength and growing impact of Wang's interdisciplinary research program.

The article also notes that Wang is co-leading a related project with Junzhou Huang, a professor in the UTA College of Engineering, on combining AI and Bayesian learning to speed drug design. The award builds on Wang's broader work using AI and advanced statistical methods to help scientists understand complex diseases, with a focus on finding patterns hidden in very large datasets. The article describes UTA's College of Science as a Carnegie R1 research institution. The article does not state what results the project is expected to produce or when, beyond the four-year timeline.

stories.Headline: Elon Drone Day to explore AI, emerging drone applications on Friday, Oct. 30

The free event is organized with the North Carolina chapter of the Association for Uncrewed Vehicle Systems International and is open to the public, though attendees must register. Recreational and commercial pilots, industry professionals, educators and students are expected to take part. This year's program puts particular emphasis on artificial intelligence and emerging drone applications. Last year's event drew a record 185 attendees, vendors and volunteers.

The keynote will be delivered by Sambit Bhattacharya, a professor at Fayetteville State University, under the title "Preflight Checks for Intelligent Machines: What Drones Can Teach Us About Trustworthy AI." His talk will argue that aviation's focus on safety, testing and accountability can guide the development of reliable AI systems. Drawing on research from Fayetteville State's Intelligent Systems Lab, he will examine how autonomous drones make decisions and the difficulties of deploying AI in real-world settings. Bhattacharya's research team was recently awarded a $10 million grant to expand its work on AI and unmanned aerial systems. Beyond the keynote, the program covers agriculture, disaster response, invasive species management and flight planning software.

Randy Piland, a teaching professor of visual communication who organizes the event, said the keynote reflects both the growing role of AI in drones and Elon's wider effort to broaden conversations about AI across its programs. He noted that many new autonomous drones depend on AI to function. Piland's stated aim is to give local drone enthusiasts and professionals a place to exchange knowledge, network and find solutions to their problems. The schedule opens with a drone soccer demonstration by Asheboro City Schools and a vendor showcase. Flight demonstrations take place in the afternoon in the parking area behind the Schar Center.

Elon Drone Day was established in 2021 and has grown into an annual gathering for people interested in the evolving drone industry. Its mission has stayed the same even as the technology has changed quickly. Organizers describe the event as a practical outlet for people working to improve their drone operations. The 2026 gathering will carry that purpose forward with its focus on AI and new applications. Registration is required for the free public event.

stories.Headline: Collaborative Collision: FSU researchers explore the future of artificial intelligence

Paul Marty, associate vice provost for academic innovation, said the conversations stressed keeping humanity at the center of the university's work on AI in society, health, education, science, and the workforce. Mike Wolfe, director of AI research solutions, said bringing different perspectives into one room was meant to encourage cross-domain discussions that could produce new project ideas. stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence use doubles in rural Nebraska, poll shows
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence use among rural Nebraskans has roughly doubled since 2024, according to the 2026 Nebraska Rural Poll. Fifty-five percent of those surveyed said they have used an AI tool, up from 27 percent in 2024. Use is concentrated among younger residents, with at least three-quarters of those ages 19 to 39 reporting use compared with 23 percent of those 65 and older. Respondents with higher education levels or household incomes, and women, were also more likely to have used the tools. The poll was conducted annually by Rural Prosperity Nebraska with funding from Nebraska Extension.

Even among those who use AI, most do not rely on it for learning about specific topics. Just over one in ten said they often or frequently use generative AI to learn about education and skill development (16 percent), topics affecting them or their family (14 percent), or science and technology (12 percent). When asked about their interest in learning more, respondents most often named protecting privacy when using generative AI (45 percent), evaluating response accuracy (36 percent), recognizing bias (33 percent) and using it ethically (28 percent). Many respondents also described some wariness about how reliable these tools are. The findings are drawn from questionnaires mailed in April and May to nearly 6,900 households, with 881 households from 86 of the state's 93 counties responding.

Heather Akin, an associate professor of agricultural and environmental sciences communication at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln, said the rapid growth shows AI is becoming part of everyday life for many rural residents. She said residents should have chances to explore AI's uses, understand its limits and decide when to use it. Mary Emery, director of Rural Prosperity Nebraska, said the interest in privacy, accuracy and bias shows residents want to use the technology responsibly. She said accessible learning opportunities could help Nebraskans build confidence and make informed choices about when and how AI can serve them.

The report will be highlighted in a Rural Poll webinar at noon Central time on November 18, and the full report is available on the Nebraska Rural Poll website. The 2026 poll marks the 31st year the survey has tracked rural Nebraskans' views on policy and quality of life. The poll carries a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. Organizers describe it as the largest and longest-running poll of its kind.
