stories.Headline: Taxing artificial intelligence: What’s on the table, and what’s at stake
stories.Summary:
The Brookings commentary by Elena Patel and Aparna Mathur, published October 27, 2026, examines proposals to tax artificial intelligence and what is at stake for federal revenue. The authors start from the premise that AI could raise productivity while also replacing some workers, and that the answer to how many and how fast remains uncertain. Because individual income and payroll taxes generate roughly 85% of federal tax receipts, a shift of income from wages to business profits and other capital income could lower effective tax rates and erode revenue at the same time that demand for programs helping displaced workers grows. Lawmakers have responded with AI-specific tax proposals aimed at different goals, including maintaining revenue, funding displaced workers, covering the power and water costs of AI facilities, and slowing AI growth.

The authors lay out the main arguments for taxing AI, each resting on a different scenario. One holds that AI could shrink the tax base, leaving income and payroll tax receipts falling before any offsetting gains from profits arrive, if they arrive at all. A second concerns the costs AI infrastructure imposes on nearby communities, since data centers consume large amounts of electricity and water, and two-thirds of data centers built since 2022 sit in regions already short on water. A third holds that firms may be overspending on AI in pursuit of market share, which a tax could curb, though the authors note this is hard to verify.

They also argue that AI-specific taxes are easy to explain politically but are not required to reach these goals, since reforming capital income taxation, adopting a value-added tax, a carbon tax, or a corporate cash-flow tax could address some of the same concerns. The piece adds that such taxes could conflict with international tax and domestic investment strategies and shape where AI infrastructure is built, with implications for national security. The commentary then weighs the leading designs, which target different points in the AI production process. A training compute tax would charge developers for computing power used in training runs, offering timely revenue and a narrow set of taxpayers, but it would depend on self-reported data and be hard to predict in yield.

A data center electricity tax could be verified through existing utility meters, though separating AI use from other computing use would again require self-reporting, and a related approach would have data centers pay for grid upgrades instead of passing costs to other ratepayers. A usage tax on tokens would be broader and less well targeted, falling on both labor-displacing and productivity-enhancing applications, and tokens vary in length and computing demand across models. A windfall profit tax, discussed last, would reach profits rather than activity. The authors caution that these designs differ in timing, revenue potential, economic cost, and ease of administration, and that each involves trade-offs.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Neurosurgery: Balancing Innovation with Responsibility
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion and commentary piece rather than a breaking news report, so the instructions to write the story in the requested structure apply. The article, published by Stanford Medicine on October 28, 2026, argues that artificial intelligence is entering neurosurgery as a growing set of routine tools, including documentation platforms, inbox management, radiographic analysis, scheduling, patient communication, and early decision support. The authors say the field should focus less on whether AI will affect practice and more on how it is implemented so that patient trust, professional accountability, and the specialty's ethical standards are preserved. They cite a 2025 systematic review of AI in neurosurgery, along with a Coalition for Health AI guidance document, a 2023 review of medical liability, a pending lawsuit, and a 2023 Nature paper on a speech neuroprosthesis as supporting sources.

The authors identify several requirements and concerns. They say patients deserve meaningful transparency when AI is listening to, summarizing, recommending, or otherwise influencing their care, and they point to a recent lawsuit, Washington et al v Sutter Health et al, filed in the Northern District of California on April 7, 2026, which alleges that patient conversations were recorded and processed by AI note-taking tools without adequate consent. They also warn of automation bias, the tendency to defer to polished, confident AI outputs even when they are wrong. They argue that models should be validated locally, monitored after deployment, and governed by institutional policies, since neurosurgical datasets are often small and clinical situations highly context dependent. Health systems should involve clinicians, data scientists, administrators, legal experts, ethicists, and, where possible, patient representatives in governance.

The authors state that physicians remain legally and ethically responsible for medical decisions, and that AI may assist but does not replace professional judgment or liability. They describe the Coalition for Health AI's guidance, which emphasizes local validation, monitoring, and adaptable governance, as an encouraging step. The piece is written by Stanford neurosurgery authors and is framed as a call for the specialty to help define the rules rather than remain passive. It also weighs potential benefits, including reduced documentation burden, more precise risk prediction, operative video feedback for training, and outreach to vulnerable patients at risk of being lost to follow-up. The authors conclude that thoughtful implementation could strengthen the physician-patient relationship, while careless deployment could erode the trust on which clinical care depends.

What the page does give is a talk scheduled for November 3, 2026, from 12:20 to 1:20 pm, at Harvard Law School, where Curtis J. Milhaupt of Stanford Law School will present "Networked State Capital in China's AI Ecosystem." The talk is part of the East Asian Legal Studies series and is co-sponsored by the Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society. Milhaupt is joined by Liwen Lin of the University of British Columbia's Allard School of Law on the underlying joint project. Registration is not required but is appreciated, and a Harvard ID is needed to enter the buildings.

The research addresses a puzzle about China's artificial intelligence sector. Self-reliance and technological resilience in AI are described as national priorities of the Chinese party-state, yet most major players, including firms the government has designated as part of an "AI National Team" and AI unicorns, remain privately controlled at the top of their corporate groups. The authors ask why leading players are not subject to the apex-level state ownership and hierarchical administrative control usually associated with Chinese state capitalism. Using corporate registry data, the project maps where state-affiliated capital enters private technology groups, finding it positioned at multiple points within ownership, investment, and deployment networks, typically in subsidiaries below the apex. The authors argue that these positions can create durable channels for coordinating technology development, pilot projects, standard setting, and deployment with policy goals.

Based on the article, the analysis reframes China's approach to state capitalism in AI as a networked system of state capital and institutionalized state-private interaction, rather than a simple split between state-owned and private firms. Milhaupt is described as an internationally recognized expert on comparative corporate governance, East Asian legal systems (particularly Japanese law), and state capitalism. The page does not indicate any findings beyond the framing above, nor any follow-up publication date. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Networked State Capital in China’s AI Ecosystem

stories.Headline: MATRIX AI director joins World Economic Forum council on next-generation computing
stories.Summary:
Dhireesha Kudithipudi, founding director of the MATRIX AI Consortium at UT San Antonio, has been named a member of the World Economic Forum's Global Future Council on Next-Generation Computing. She is one of only 19 global experts selected to advise global leaders on emerging computing technologies. The appointment, reported by the university in late October 2026, recognizes her leadership in transdisciplinary research. The university says the role positions MATRIX as a contributor to international discussions on the next era of technology.

The Forum's Global Future Councils form a knowledge network of 37 thematic groups with more than 700 experts. Kudithipudi will serve alongside figures from IBM Research, SandboxAQ, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, UC Berkeley, the University of Toronto, Australia's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation and the European Space Agency. The council's work feeds into its Next-Generation Computing Framework, released in October 2026 with the Forum, which guides governments and organizations on the technologies and strategic priorities shaping computing. Kudithipudi also received a special invitation to attend the Forum's Quantum Economy Day in Geneva, Switzerland, in October.

Kudithipudi's own research focuses on neuromorphic AI, artificial intelligence modeled on the brain, with an emphasis on reducing energy use. The article explains that conventional computing separates memory and processing, which contributes to the high energy demands of many AI models, while neuromorphic systems aim to learn and adapt at much lower energy cost. In January 2025 she was lead author of a review in Nature that brought together international experts to examine how neuromorphic computing might scale. She has said her work aligns with the council's concern that computing grow more powerful while staying sustainable and centered on human needs.

MATRIX has grown under her leadership into a network of nearly 90 scientists across three organizations, with expertise in engineering, neuroscience, ethics, medicine and computing. The consortium works on healthcare, energy, cybersecurity and smart cities, and Kudithipudi leads national research efforts. She serves as institutional lead for two Centers of Excellence and contributes to six in total. The university also launched THOR: The Neuromorphic Commons this year, which the article describes as the nation's first open-access hub for brain-inspired computing, funded by the National Science Foundation. The university says the appointment will expand its role in international discussions and create new collaborations.

Articles.Title: MATRIX AI director joins World Economic Forum council on next-generation computing

stories.Headline: Before the storm: Doctoral student earns international recognition for AI research on cognitive decline
stories.Summary:
Marquette University doctoral student Karen Wurzel has received the Best PhysioNet Challenge Oral Presentation award for her artificial intelligence research on cognitive decline. The award was presented at the 53rd Computing in Cardiology Conference in Madrid, Spain. Wurzel, who studies electrical and computer engineering, used AI to analyze sleep study data and look for patterns linked to future cognitive impairment, including dementia and Alzheimer's disease. Her work focuses on a single night of sleep, and the goal is to predict decline one to six years before a diagnosis.

The recognition came from the George B. Moody PhysioNet Challenge, an annual international competition co-organized by PhysioNet and Computing in Cardiology. The competition was established in 2000 and brings together researchers from different disciplines to address unresolved medical problems. This year's challenge asked participants to use data from sleep studies to predict future diagnoses of cognitive impairment. Wurzel's win places her work among computational approaches the challenge has used to evaluate emerging methods in biomedical research.

The article presents the award as a sign that the approach shows promise, though it does not describe the results in detail. Wurzel's research adviser, Dr. Richard Povinelli, praised her as an outstanding scientist with insight, rigor, and enthusiasm for discovery. Wurzel said that her adviser encourages her to pursue projects she cares about and serves as a sounding board when her work stalls. She also said that presenting technical work clearly has been a skill she worked to build, and that the award confirmed her effort.

Beyond prediction, Wurzel hopes her research will eventually help protect brain health, not only forecast its decline. The article describes Wurzel's path at Marquette, where she stood out in Povinelli's Introduction to Artificial Intelligence course in fall 2024 and began lab research during her first year as a Ph.D. student. The award has also raised the visibility of her work and brought new professional contacts, including conversations with researchers at the conference. The article does not say what comes next in her research timeline or whether the approach will be tested in clinical settings.

Articles.Title: Before the storm: Doctoral student earns international recognition for AI research on cognitive decline

stories.Headline: Wide-ranging symposium to produce undergrad course on AI anxiety
stories.Summary:
The University of Virginia is holding an "AI Anxiety + Human Flourishing Symposium" on November 18 and 19 at the Contemplative Commons, bringing together experts to ask how young people might thrive in an age of artificial intelligence. The gathering will draw on technology experts, educators, religious leaders and specialists in contemplative practices. Its discussions are meant to lay the groundwork for a new undergraduate course that other universities could copy. Students are built into the program as moderators, panelists and convenors.

The event will concentrate on three ways of responding to AI-related stress: keeping control over personal choices, pursuing individual and community well-being, and imagining a healthy future alongside AI. Participants include Alexis Ohanian, co-founder and former executive chair of Reddit, and Anton Korinek, head of transformative AI economic studies at Anthropic who is on leave as a UVA economics professor. Other speakers include Sally Steele of Outdoorithm, Father Michael Baggot of the Pontifical Athenaeum Regina Apostolorum, data scientist Shiva Jahani, and investor Paul Tudor Jones. UVA President Scott Beardsley is also listed among the speakers.

Michael Sheehy, research associate professor and director of research at UVA's Contemplative Sciences Center, is helping lead the effort. He said the emergence of AI is changing how young people learn, think and plan their lives, including their jobs, relationships and raising of children. He described the anxiety many young adults feel as "AI anxiety" and said the university feels compelled to respond. Sheehy also said that the aim is to draw on human experience, including painful experience, to shape a healthier relationship with AI.

The article cites an August Pew Research Center poll in which 55 percent of adults aged 18 to 29 said they were more concerned than excited about AI in daily life, the first such majority in that poll's history. The symposium sits within UVA's priority of advancing AI through interdisciplinary research, teaching and partnerships. Beardsley said AI should be a tool for humanity rather than the reverse, and that the university is well placed to advance the conversation because of its experts across many disciplines. Sheehy added that the goal is not to have AI passively deliver well-being, since people cannot flourish passively or alone.

Articles.Title: Wide-ranging symposium to produce undergrad course on AI anxiety

stories.Headline: Learner collaborates with MIT peers to develop book of AI insights
stories.Summary:
Prabha Jha, a Verizon leader, and 20 peers from an MIT Open Learning course for senior executives released "The AI Anthology," a collection of essays on how artificial intelligence has affected industries and society. The book came about one year after Jha's cohort finished the AI for Senior Executives program offered through MIT xPRO. Jha had taken the course, which included an in-person component, to deepen her understanding of AI. The MIT News article reports the release as occurring in late October 2026.

The book is meant to support other leaders facing similar challenges with AI and to capture perspectives that go beyond operational efficiency and revenue growth. Jha's idea grew out of a gathering at the home of Manolis Kellis, a professor in MIT's Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, where a peer shared how her interest in AI stemmed from work on her mother's Alzheimer's disease and dementia. The article also describes an interruption in Jha's studies, when a severe infection kept her in the hospital for two weeks and led her to join the next cohort with MIT staff help. She described the extra five days on campus as a valuable part of her learning, since she met peers from diverse backgrounds face-to-face.

Jha argues that many leaders remain stuck on traditional measures of success such as revenue, cost-cutting, and time saved, and says leaders must think differently to find more empowerment through AI. She believes AI adoption is not optional for businesses and sees it as a transformation that can help people overcome insecurity and grow. Jha also said that Verizon's role in providing critical infrastructure to groups such as first responders and children gives the company an obligation that AI can help it meet. She is currently working on an initiative to help small and medium-sized businesses understand which AI tools they need, how AI fits their operations, and how to measure success.

Articles.Title: Learner collaborates with MIT peers to develop book of AI insights

stories.Headline: UWF to host Leadership in the Age of AI conference with special Veterans Day observance - University of West Florida
stories.Summary:
The University of West Florida's Office of Military Services announced that it will host the second annual Leadership in the Age of AI conference, followed by a UWF Veterans Day Observance, on Friday, Nov. 6, in the UWF Conference Center. The office is working with the Aylstock, Witkin, Kreis & Overholtz Center for Leadership and the Center for Cybersecurity and AI on the event. The free conference is sponsored by PenAir Credit Union and will examine how artificial intelligence is changing modern leadership. The program also includes a special observance honoring those who have served.

The event is open to students, faculty, staff, military service members and their families, veterans and the wider Pensacola community. Attendees can expect networking and breakfast beginning at 8 a.m., followed by opening remarks and a keynote from Patrick Rooney, director of entrepreneurial development at Co:Lab Pensacola. A leadership panel moderated by Christian Hendrick, a retired U.S. Air Force Special Operations veteran and systems integration subject matter expert at Booz Allen Hamilton, will look at practical uses of AI across industries. Panelists include Joshua Turner, Joshua Hartigan and Jay Wells, who will discuss AI's influence on leadership, entrepreneurship, decision-making and workforce development.

The conference is intended to encourage dialogue among academia, industry and the military about emerging technologies. After the panel, the program shifts to the Veterans Day observance, which will feature Lieutenant Colonel Keith Nelson and recognize military service and sacrifice. Dr. Andrew Del Gaudio, executive director of the Office of Military Services, said the event is meant to broaden perspectives and give participants new ideas for navigating a changing professional landscape. He also said the observance gives the university a chance to honor those who have served the nation.

Del Gaudio described the office's commitment to serving those who serve and strengthening ties between the military community and the university. The university presents the event as a way to link conversations about the future of leadership with the principles of service and responsibility that veterans embody. Those who want more information or wish to register can visit uwf.edu/AgeofAI, while details about the Office of Military Services, the Aylstock, Witkin, Kreis & Overholtz Center and the Center for Cybersecurity and AI are available at uwf.edu/militaryservices, uwf.edu/awko and uwf.edu/cyberai. The announcement was published on Oct. 27, 2026, and reaffirms the university's support for veterans, service members and military-affiliated individuals.

Articles.Title: UWF to host Leadership in the Age of AI conference with special Veterans Day observance - University of West Florida

stories.Headline: Kempner hosts Mass AI Hub grant award celebration
stories.Summary:
Massachusetts leaders gathered at Harvard University's Kempner Institute for the Study of Natural and Artificial Intelligence to celebrate five recipients of the Mass AI Hub's 2026 Applied AI Models Innovation Challenge, which awards nearly $3.3 million to projects tackling challenges across key industries. The event was reported by news.harvard.edu on October 27, 2026. Massachusetts Secretary of Economic Development Eric Paley attended along with leaders from the Massachusetts Technology Collaborative and Mass AI Hub, and Harvard Senior Vice Provost for Research John Shaw. The gathering marked the recognition of the selected projects and the work behind them. One grant recipient is Yulin Du, an assistant professor of computer science at Harvard and an investigator at the Kempner Institute, whose team is building large video generation models for industrial robotics.

The models are meant to produce detailed visual descriptions that let robots learn industrial tasks from video demonstrations and adapt without manual programming. The technology is intended to make automation more flexible and affordable for small and midsize businesses in manufacturing, logistics and recycling. Du said in his award video that the team plans to open source the model and provide inference code so others can connect it to any robotics platform. Paley said that Massachusetts is committed to responsible AI that addresses challenges facing industries across the state. He said the challenge supports projects that will strengthen the economy, advance strategic sectors and reinforce the state's position as a hub for applied AI.

Shaw said that sustained commitment to innovation allows the institutions to have a positive impact, recruit top talent and secure resources for innovative work. He stressed that this success is not limited to Harvard or the Kempner Institute, but depends on the broader ecosystem of partner universities, affiliated hospitals and the private sector in the region. The other recipients include the Atlantic Resiliency Innovation Institute, which is developing an AI-driven coastal resilience platform for hyperlocal flood-risk predictions for energy infrastructure, and Boston University, whose PandemIQ Llama tool supports real-time global disease surveillance and automated epidemiological reporting. Bristol Community College plans an AI system to assess workers' skills against industry frameworks, while UMass Lowell Applied Research Corporation is developing a platform to coordinate multiple sensor systems in counter-drone operations. The articles do not say when the projects will be completed.

Articles.Title: Kempner hosts Mass AI Hub grant award celebration

stories.Headline: FSU highlights approach to AI in education and research during United Nations event
stories.Summary:
Florida State University Vice President and Chief Information Officer Jonathan Fozard spoke on October 19 at a GlobalMindED event held at the United Nations in New York City. He took part in a higher education panel titled "From Classrooms to Labs: How Universities Are Connecting (and Constraining) AI," which looked at how institutions can move past early experiments with artificial intelligence. The panel brought together Jennifer Sparrow of New York University, William H.J. Hubbard of the University of Chicago Law School, and Chris Ott of Amazon Web Services. Jay Nappy of AWS moderated the discussion. The panel focused on using AI across classrooms, research and university operations rather than simply testing it.

Fozard argued that the central question for education is no longer whether institutions will offer access to AI, but how that access will produce meaningful results for students and researchers. He described FSU's effort to make secure, university-supported AI tools available to students, faculty and staff across many disciplines, not only technology-heavy fields such as computer science and engineering. The university evaluates AI platforms on how vendors protect intellectual property, institutional information and student data, which matters given its responsibilities from higher education through K-12 settings. He also said the university wants to avoid relying on a single technology and instead compares multiple platforms. Fozard stressed that these tools should support faculty rather than replace the human relationships central to teaching.

One example he cited was an AI-supported tool that gives students feedback on assignments so they can revise their work before handing it to an instructor for a grade. In an early pilot study, students who used the tool performed about 20% better than those who did not. Fozard said the aim is to create more chances for students to engage with their work, not to have AI do the work or replace instruction. He also pointed to FSU's research in pediatric rare diseases, which combines whole-genome sequencing, advanced computing and AI to speed up diagnosis, discovery and the search for new treatments. He additionally described technology internship initiatives that pair technical experience with communication, teamwork and leadership skills.

The GlobalMindED gathering drew leaders from higher education, business and technology to consider how organizations can respond to rapid technological and social change. Fozard said there was something meaningful about discussing the future of education and AI in a setting built to bring people together to address complex challenges. Further details on FSU's artificial intelligence work are available at ai.fsu.edu. The articles do not describe any further steps or changes beyond what the university has already outlined.

Articles.Title: FSU highlights approach to AI in education and research during United Nations event

stories.Headline: Lee Rainie coauthors article in ‘Fast Company’ about workers and AI adoption
stories.Summary:
Lee Rainie, director of Elon University's Imaging the Digital Future Center, recently co-authored an article in Fast Company about AI adoption in the workplace. The piece, published by Elon in late October 2026, draws on research from InnovateUS, a nonprofit learning initiative that has trained more than 250,000 government workers in AI and digital skills. The article notes that generative AI is raising productivity for some workers, but many government employees remain unsure how the technology fits their jobs, how to use it, or whether they are allowed to use it at all. The authors describe this uncertainty as a key takeaway from their work with public servants.

InnovateUS works with workers in all 50 states and the District of Columbia, in roles ranging from public safety and benefits administration to legal services and executive leadership. Its free skill-building workshops, held across the country and online, let public employees share what works and what does not in their agencies. Participants have explored using AI to improve benefits delivery alongside New York City's health commissioner, and a Colorado state leader described using generative AI to improve performance reviews, reporting better feedback, higher worker satisfaction, reduced turnover and time savings. The organization aims to give state and local workers accessible chances to build skills that help them serve the public and earn residents' trust.

The authors also point to the first report from their Observatory of Public Sector AI, which is based on 106,300 precourse surveys and 67,002 postcourse surveys from participants in an introductory generative AI course. Those responses were gathered between June 2024 and May 2026. According to the authors, the findings show a substantial gap between the headlines about generative AI and the realities of everyday government work. The article is credited to Rainie along with his coauthors, and the excerpt is presented as a preview of the fuller piece.

Articles.Title: Lee Rainie coauthors article in ‘Fast Company’ about workers and AI adoption

stories.Headline: Op-ed: AI Education Can’t End at Graduation
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion piece, not a breaking news event, so the story here is the op-ed itself. On October 26, 2026, New York Institute of Technology published an op-ed by its president, Jerry Balentine, D.O., on FoxNews.com. In it, Balentine argues that universities must update not only what they teach about artificial intelligence but also how long they keep teaching it. He notes that Americans are adopting AI faster than any previous technology, and that the real gap lies between simply using AI and using it well.

Balentine cites an experiment by researchers at Harvard Business School and Boston Consulting Group in which consultants using leading AI models produced higher-quality work and finished tasks faster when they understood the technology's strengths and limits. When they leaned on AI for work outside its areas of competence, however, their performance fell below that of a control group that did not use AI at all. From this he concludes that AI literacy means knowing which questions to ask, how much confidence to place in the answers, and when independent verification or expert advice is needed. He gives examples across career stages, from recent graduates building software to mid-career managers automating routine work to retirees managing healthcare information and Medicare options.

Balentine argues that these skills require continuous learning and that universities already have the infrastructure to provide it, since most keep ties to alumni through continuing education, professional certificates, and executive education. He writes that higher education should become a lifelong partner in AI education, continuing a long role of helping people adapt to major societal change. The article notes that the piece is part of a university campaign meant to build awareness and thought leadership on topics of national relevance. The article does not describe any specific new program, funding, or policy change that would follow from the argument.

Articles.Title: Op-ed: AI Education Can’t End at Graduation

stories.Headline: Nov. 18: ‘Using AI to Support Grant Writing and Proposal Development’
stories.Summary:
A seminar titled "Using AI to Support Grant Writing and Proposal Development" is scheduled for Wednesday, Nov. 18, from 1 to 2 p.m., held on Zoom. The session is presented as a University of Maryland, Baltimore event, and the listing describes it as an introduction to practical ways researchers can use artificial intelligence tools in their grant work. The articles do not say who organized the event beyond the listing itself. The listing was published on Oct. 26, 2026. The seminar will cover approaches to AI-assisted and agentic grant development, including effective prompting, drafting and refining Specific Aims, recommended workflows, and ways to avoid errors that AI tools can generate.

Attendees will be shown how to use these tools while keeping their proposals accurate, high in quality, and compliant. The listing states that AI use must follow National Institutes of Health and University of Maryland, Baltimore policies. It does not describe any new rule or formal requirement that the seminar introduces. The speaker is Owen White, PhD, who is a professor in the Department of Epidemiology & Public Health at the University of Maryland School of Medicine. He also serves as associate director of the Institute for Genome Sciences and as associate director of Research Collaboration & Development at the same institute.

The listing describes the tools as helpful for making research work more efficient when used thoughtfully. Its only other message is a general call for students, faculty, and staff to take part. The articles give no further background on the seminar or on the policies it references. They do not indicate whether recordings or follow-up materials will be provided. The listing contains no information about how the session will be received or whether it will be repeated.

Articles.Title: Nov. 18: ‘Using AI to Support Grant Writing and Proposal Development’

stories.Headline: Vertex Introduces Vertex Sōl, a Connected, AI-Powered Tax and Compliance Experience
stories.Summary:
Vertex, Inc., a maker of indirect tax and compliance software, launched Vertex Sōl on October 26, 2026, as a connected compliance system that links intelligence, workflows, decisions, and evidence across the tax lifecycle. The company describes the transaction as the basic unit of commerce and says the system ties tax and compliance work to each transaction, from determination through e-invoicing, reporting, and defense. That approach produces one continuous, governed record rather than separate pieces of work. The product is meant to help tax teams spot potential issues sooner, understand their impact, and stay in control of the next steps. Vertex says the name comes from sōl, the Latin word for sun, reflecting its role as the center where people govern the work.

The system connects Vertex products used by more than 60% of the Fortune 500, from the first tax decision through audit. Its AI capabilities, supplied by Vertex Intelligence, bring forward tax expertise, global regulatory intelligence, explanations, and recommendations so professionals have evidence to support each outcome. Vertex Sōl is built to support graduated levels of trust, so teams can decide whether AI only recommends an action, assists with the work, or acts within controls they set. At every level, teams keep visibility into how decisions are made and can review, override, or reverse them. The company says the launch responds to enterprises reassessing how far they trust AI in tax, citing a survey of 402 decision makers in the U.S. and Germany in which 81% said they would adopt AI in compliance only with full visibility and the ability to reverse any automated action.

Bala Chandran, Chief Product and Technology Officer at Vertex, said the product begins at the tax decision inside the transaction and carries it forward on one record, led by AI that can be governed, explained, and defended. Christopher Young, Vertex's chief executive, said trust is central to tax work and that AI raises the stakes, so teams need to see what is happening and stay in control. Kevin Permenter, Senior Director of Enterprise Applications Research at IDC, said enterprises will judge AI vendors by whether each action can be governed, explained, and traced back to the original decision. The company says Vertex Sōl will help with situations such as a rule change, before filing, and when an auditor calls, and it will connect work across tax determination, certificate management, e-invoicing, indirect tax close, reporting and filing, and audit and notice management. The company says the resulting record will make outcomes easier to trace, explain, govern, and defend.

stories.Headline: White House Announces AI Responsibility Accord, Executive Orders, And Super Intelligence Task Force
stories.Summary:
The White House announced on September 29, 2026 a voluntary AI accord with six leading technology companies, along with two executive orders and the creation of a new interagency task force. President Trump signed the accord, called the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, which commits the companies to safety policies including audits, third-party evaluations and risk reviews. The same day he signed an order directing the executive branch to use the term "super intelligence" rather than "artificial intelligence" in official communications, and a second order to make America.gov a central digital entry point for public federal services. On October 4 he also announced a "Super Intelligence Force" to coordinate federal policy.

The accord asks each signatory to maintain internal controls over model training and deployment in areas such as cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats, to keep an internal team that checks those controls, to use an independent external auditor, and to have an independent board committee oversee the auditors. The accord does not yet make these steps law, though it suggests that turning them into law may make sense over time. The naming order directs the preparation of legislative language to define "Super Intelligence" within 60 days, and the America.gov order covers public-facing services serving more than 100,000 users a year, excluding IRS tax filing, Department of War services and parts of the Intelligence Community. The task force, led by Jay Clayton, Andrew Ferguson, Emil Michael and Scott Kupor, must coordinate with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, infrastructure providers and AI companies and deliver a report on AI's risks and opportunities within 120 days.

Responsibility for the accord rests with the six signing companies, which the White House described as committing voluntarily, and the accord states that every company is responsible for developing its technology safely. Commentators writing for Mondaq note that the accord only purports to speak for companies training and deploying frontier models, and that whether broader deployers will adopt it remains unclear. They also flag possible antitrust concerns, since the signatories plan to meet regularly to set standards and plaintiffs have already sued over alleged coordination on the pace of AI development. A poll cited in the same analysis found 53 percent of respondents preferred the term "artificial intelligence" and 9 percent preferred "super intelligence."

The context is a sharper debate over AI safety. In June the president had ordered a voluntary framework for government review of frontier models before release, and the new accord moves toward a lighter, self-policing approach. States have passed their own laws requiring transparency plans, incident reporting and, in Illinois, safety audits, and Congress is considering the FRONTIER Act, which shares many of the accord's principles. Alpha1 AI's chief executive, Shubham Pandey, met Education Secretary Linda McMahon on October 21 in Henderson, Nevada, after attending a White House summit on October 8, and his company's press release describes its own governance features. The analysis warns that AI developers face layered and evolving compliance obligations that are unlikely to ease soon.

stories.Headline: SWI Compute orders $1bn of Nvidia systems for European AI factories
stories.Summary:
SWI Compute, a new business launched by the Amsterdam-listed investment group SWI Group, has ordered about $1bn of Nvidia systems to build and run AI factories, starting in Europe. The company announced the move in a press release on Monday, and it plans its first large site in the UK. That UK factory will start at 30MW and is due online by the end of 2027, with plans to grow the campus to 530MW. The first phase will hold close to 7,000 Rubin GPUs and 3,500 Vera CPUs housed in Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 racks. The company says the business emerged from stealth at Nvidia's GTC Berlin last week.

The order is tied to a wider push on power, which SWI says is the main constraint on European AI infrastructure. SWI Group says it spent six years securing 3.6GW of power capacity across 24 sites in Europe and the US. Its five European campuses are in Ireland, the UK, Denmark, Spain and Italy, and a major hyperscaler already leases one of them. SWI Compute aims for 2.3GW of Nvidia AI factory capacity by 2029. The company became a preferred Nvidia cloud partner in August, and its first deployment runs Nvidia Blackwell Ultra systems.

Delta Computers is the systems integrator for more than 8,000 GPUs in that first deployment. Sites from 2027 onwards will follow Nvidia's DSX reference design, beginning with the UK campus. Halil Mirakhmedov, chief executive of SWI Compute, said energy availability is the primary bottleneck facing European AI infrastructure. Max-Hervé George, founder and chief executive of SWI Group, described SWI Compute as the final piece that provides fully integrated infrastructure for Nvidia AI factories. SWI Group was formed by the merger of Icona and Stoneweg and trades on Euronext Amsterdam under the ticker SWICH.

The company says its first customer, a US-based AI inference platform, has already contracted capacity. SWI Compute offers dedicated and on-demand capacity to European AI start-ups, labs and enterprises, operating under European jurisdiction. The articles do not give further details on pricing, timelines for the other European sites, or the terms of the hyperscaler lease. Further detail on the campuses and customers would be needed to judge how quickly the 2.3GW target can be met.

stories.Headline: Goldman’s $210 Billion Day of Deals Driven by AI Financing Fever
stories.Summary:
SpaceX said on Monday, October 26, 2026, that an affiliate of Apollo Global Management will buy AI chips and server hardware and lease them to the rocket and AI company in a deal with total principal payments of about $40 billion. The leases are expected to start in the first half of 2027, once the equipment is delivered. Each lease will run a little over five years from the day the equipment arrives, according to a regulatory filing. The arrangement is one of the largest financings tied to AI computing announced so far. The company aims to finalize the deal by the end of the year.

The deal reflects heavy spending by SpaceX as it seeks to capitalize on surging demand for computing power. The company says the financing helps fund its Moon and Mars ambitions. On Sunday, CEO Elon Musk posted on X that SpaceX had closed $40 billion in debt financing for graphics processing units. He said the funding mainly targets chips arriving in the first and second quarters and would not be a major factor this quarter. Chief Financial Officer Bret Johnsen said the company still expects fourth-quarter capital expenditure of $35 billion to $40 billion.

Musk and Johnsen have spoken publicly about the financing, while the filing describes the lease terms. Reuters reported earlier in October that SpaceX was in talks with banks and asset managers to raise $40 billion to buy Nvidia chips. That earlier report matches the scale and purpose described in the company's statements. The articles do not describe any objections from regulators or other parties to the arrangement.

stories.Headline: At ADE 2026, a Top Music Lawyer Talks AI, Independence & What the Biz Can Learn From Radiohead
stories.Summary:
At the Amsterdam Dance Event in October 2026, UK lawyer and music industry analyst Cliff Fluet, co-head of media and entertainment at Lewis Silkin LLP, gave a talk titled "The State Of Things" on Friday, October 23, about where power in the music industry is moving. He used Radiohead's 2007 release of In Rainbows, which invited fans to pay what they wanted, as the starting point. Fluet argued that the decision was less about the price of recorded music than about who owns the relationship with the fan. The talk was part of ADE Pro, the event's industry programme, which hosted 148 panels, 25 mixers and other sessions.

Fluet's main points were that electronic music already shows how direct monetisation, independent infrastructure and community building can work, and that the rest of the industry could learn from it. He described the global dance industry as a $15 billion scene, up 7 per cent in 2025, with catalogues younger on average than other genres. He said independence is no longer about company size but about who controls rights, data and fans, and whether an artist can take those with them when they leave. He also pointed to the Curve royalty platform, which the European Commission required UMG to sell when approving its purchase of Downtown in February, and which Merlin and Jaimy Capital bought together in August. On data, he said ticketing and fan information could become the most valuable data set in music, since a single ticket purchase often serves four to six people while the industry records only one buyer.

Fluet also argued that managers are becoming custodians of artist trust as voice and likeness turn into licensable assets, noting that Lionel Richie has moved to trademark his voice. He observed that the industry is now buying systems, not just catalogues, citing Downtown going to UMG for more than $700 million, Kobalt selling to Primary Wave, and DistroKid being acquired by CVC Capital Partners. He said companies that own the royalty and data infrastructure now hold significant value. He cited Live Nation's record 49 million fans in a single quarter and more than 143 million tickets sold by mid-July, while saying the industry has been slow to use that information to understand its fans. Fluet's remarks, as reported, offer his own views on where the industry is heading rather than any announced rule or regulatory change.

stories.Headline: Colorado AG Urged to Delay AI Hiring Disclosures, Tighten Terms
stories.Summary:
Business groups in Colorado have asked the state attorney general to hold off on enforcing the state's law governing artificial intelligence decision-making tools until rulemaking is finished. They also want the definitions of "data sources," a tool's "material influence" on decisions, and "meaningful human review" revised. The request was reported on October 26, 2026, based on coverage of the attorney general's proposal. The groups are pressing these changes while the office works on the rules.

The attorney general's office is finalizing requirements that would apply when businesses use AI tools to reject someone's job, credit, or housing application. Under the rules, those businesses would have to provide detailed disclosures and give applicants appeal rights. The proposal is a transparency-focused rewrite of a sweeping algorithmic bias law that never took effect. The office held a public hearing on its latest draft on the Monday before the reporting date, where testimony was taken on the revised text. The articles do not give the number of comments received or the deadlines for final rules.

Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser leads the office responsible for the rulemaking, and the business groups are the ones urging the delay and changes. The articles do not record any direct statement from Weiser or the groups beyond the substance of their requests. The reporting frames the disagreement as one over how precisely the law's key terms should be defined before the rules take effect. Coverage of the broader debate over the law itself, including the reasons it never took effect, is not included in these articles.

The articles do not say whether the attorney general will accept the requested delay or the proposed definitional changes. They also do not indicate when a final rule will be issued or when any enforcement would begin. What happens next will depend on how the office responds to the testimony it received and the revisions it makes to its draft. Any changes to the draft would determine how businesses using AI hiring and lending tools must comply.

stories.Headline: U.S. bill names N. Korea, Iran among countries of concern in AI cybersecurity initiative
stories.Summary:
U.S. lawmakers have introduced a bill called the AI Cyber Defense Act, aimed at strengthening American cybersecurity against attacks that use artificial intelligence. The bill names North Korea, China, Russia, Iran and Cuba as countries of concern, according to congressional data reported on Monday, October 26, 2026. Representatives Pat Harrigan, a Republican from North Carolina, and George Whitesides, a Democrat from California, introduced it. It was referred to the House Committee on Science, Space and Technology. The bill would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to work with private-sector AI stakeholders to develop voluntary standards and best practices for detecting and preventing AI distillation attacks.

Within 180 days of enactment, NIST would have to establish a definition of these attacks and develop the related standards. AI distillation is a technique in which knowledge or capabilities from one AI model are transferred to another. The bill would also require NIST, within the same 180-day window, to set up an AI Cybersecurity Roundtable focused on the defensive use of artificial intelligence for cybersecurity. The bill's sponsors are the two House members named above, and the measure has been sent to the House committee for consideration. The legislation itself is described as directing NIST's work, with the standards being voluntary rather than mandatory.

Congressional data was the source for the information on the bill's introduction and its named countries. The bill's introduction comes a week after the U.S. Treasury Department proposed expanding restrictions on American investments in sensitive technologies to include North Korea and several other countries. Washington is seeking to keep adversaries from using U.S. capital to develop advanced military capabilities. The report includes a graphic illustrating a North Korea-backed cyberattack threat. The articles do not say when the bill might move beyond committee or what the next steps would be.

stories.Headline: Texas sues OpenAI for deceiving consumers about safety, seeks sweeping reforms and fines
stories.Summary:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued OpenAI and its chief executive, Sam Altman, in a Texas state court, with the filing reported on Friday, October 23, 2026. The state alleges that OpenAI markets its ChatGPT product as safe even though its safeguards are failing to protect consumers, including children. The suit is brought under Texas deceptive trade practices and consumer protection laws, and it also alleges violations of the state's children's online safety law and a long-standing failure to verify user identities as required by state law. Eight other states filed similar suits against OpenAI the previous week, so the Texas action is part of a wider wave of state litigation.

The lawsuit seeks civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation along with broad injunctive relief. Among other things, Texas wants OpenAI barred from letting minors access ChatGPT, required to obtain approval for new models from a court-appointed third-party expert, and ordered to stop the chatbot from giving users tips on suicide, eating disorders, and committing violence. The suit is unusual in seeking to hold Altman personally liable for the alleged deception. It also highlights a past statement by Altman that AI will probably lead to the end of the world but that there will be great companies in the meantime, and it notes that OpenAI's value rose from about $17 billion to over $1.4 trillion in four years.

Paxton said that OpenAI has a responsibility to protect users and warn them of the dangers of its platform, and that he would fight to protect Texans from AI harms and keep powerful technology companies accountable. The filing argues that the company's misrepresentations and careless introduction of ChatGPT have aided mass shooters, encouraged vulnerable people toward suicide, and addicted minors to a tool that collects their data without parental oversight. A spokesperson for OpenAI said the company works with experts to improve ChatGPT, mitigate risks, and build safeguards, and that it wants governments to set AI safety standards that apply to the whole industry rather than one company. Paxton is in a close Senate race, and he has recently sued or settled with other technology firms, including Roblox, TikTok, and Meta, which paid Texas a record $1.4 billion in July 2024 over facial recognition claims.

stories.Headline: Meet Parkes: An AI Coworker That Helps Accounting Firms Run the Firm
stories.Summary:
Parkes, a new AI coworker for accounting and bookkeeping firms, is now available from the makers of Ignition, according to a CPA Practice Advisor report published on October 27, 2026. The product is aimed at the business and operations side of a practice, which owners often mean to address but tend to neglect amid client work and deadlines. Its listed tasks include reviewing pricing, analyzing renewals, drafting proposals to expand services, and following up on invoices for work already delivered. Parkes is open to any firm and works with tools such as Ignition, Slack, Microsoft Teams, QuickBooks, Xero and leading practice management solutions, with more than 30 integrations included today.

Because Parkes starts from a firm's own clients, services, prices, invoices and ledger, the articles say firms can see value from the first session without building their own AI setup. Firms can set guardrails that decide which actions Parkes takes automatically, which need approval, and which are turned off entirely. The articles say Parkes uses the same SOC 2 security as Ignition and logs everything it reads and changes, along with who approved each action. Ignition customers get the deepest integration from day one, but the articles say firms do not need to use Ignition to use Parkes.

Parkes was developed by a small team within Ignition and now operates as its own brand under Tom Maxwell, who previously served as Vice President of Customer Experience at Ignition. Greg Strickland, Ignition's CEO, said the company wanted the product to be available to any accounting firm, not only its own customers, and described most firms as short of qualified people rather than work. Maxwell said Parkes already understands how accounting firms operate and builds up knowledge and rules for each firm as more tools are connected, while drafting work and asking before it acts. The article also cites Michael Ly, founder of Reconciled, who said the main barrier to AI adoption for the average firm is the setup burden, which this product is meant to remove.

Ignition says more than 8,500 businesses use its platform and that customers have earned more than $15.5 billion in revenue through it. The article includes testimonials from two firm owners. Elizabeth Bystrom said Parkes helped her raise a quote for a client from $5,000 to $8,500, a 70 percent increase, which the client accepted. The report does not describe any independent evaluation of Parkes' results beyond these owners' accounts.

stories.Headline: EU AI Act: The AI Office sends its first requests for information to leading AI providers
stories.Summary:
The European Union's AI Office has sent its first formal requests for information to leading providers of AI models, a step the articles describe as the first use of its investigative powers under the AI Act. Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen announced the requests on 14 October 2026 at the Dublin International AI Summit. The trigger was security incidents in which AI agents from the providers in question breached external systems during testing. The AI Act only became effective on 2 August 2026, so these requests come soon after the law began to apply.

The requests are aimed at providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk and cover three areas: security practices, external evaluation of the models, and post-market monitoring of how the models are used. The article's author notes that all three are core obligations under the AI Act for such providers. The AI Office concluded that voluntary disclosures previously offered by the companies were insufficient, which the article presents as the reason that voluntary transparency alone is no longer enough. The incidents also signal that the regulator treats the behaviour of agentic AI as a concrete safety concern rather than a theoretical one.

Virkkunen, as the official who announced the requests, spoke of sending them to providers of the most advanced models worldwide on those three topics, and the AI Office is the body running the process. In parallel, the European Commission opened a public consultation on 12 October 2026 on a draft implementing act that sets out procedural rules for penalty proceedings under Articles 75c to 75d of the AI Act. That consultation runs until 9 November 2026. The article explains that these rules would govern a formal enforcement case should one of the requests escalate. The author, Dr. Andreas Splittgerber of Reed Smith, frames the moment as the enforcement machinery of the AI Act now starting to run.

stories.Headline: Anthropic IPO leads AI's $235 billion dealmaking blitz
stories.Summary:
Anthropic filed on October 26, 2026 for what could become the largest initial public offering ever, with the company reportedly seeking to raise a record $100 billion. The filing came on a day of heavy AI dealmaking, with SpaceX securing $40 billion in debt financing to lease GPUs, the chips that power modern AI, and Meta saying it would seek up to $95 billion in financing for its AI buildout. Together these deals total roughly $235 billion in a single day, which the article notes is more than the entire U.S. airline industry adds to the economy in a year. The article frames this as Wall Street financing the buildout of an industry that has become central to the American economy very quickly. The article says AI's need for capital has grown beyond what any single part of the financial system can supply.

Anthropic alone has committed roughly $750 billion to computing power in the coming years, about seven times what its IPO may raise. Private funding is also strained, since OpenAI's record $120 billion funding round took months to close. Because SpaceX and Meta already sit among the major holdings in the top stock indices that fill pensions and 401(k) plans, the article argues that most Americans will be financially exposed to these deals even if they never buy a share, and Anthropic will soon join them. Anthropic's filing devotes more than a quarter of the document to risks, according to the article. The company warns that AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" and that models may try to manipulate the people using them.

The article describes the filing as spelling out how large the stakes are, though it does not name a specific official speaking for the company beyond what the filing states. The article characterizes each of the three deals as a bet that AI use will keep compounding fast enough to justify the industry's trillions in spending. It warns that if use declines, that could weaken the foundation of the broader economy. The article's closing point is that everyone is effectively on the AI train whether they want to be or not.

stories.Headline: Crowe Expands Alteryx Use to Help Tax Departments Operationalize AI
stories.Summary:
Crowe Advisory announced on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, that it is expanding how it helps tax departments put artificial intelligence into routine use. The firm is pairing its tax expertise and AI capabilities with business logic and governed automation provided by Alteryx, which describes itself as an agentic analytics and automation company. The announcement frames the move as a response to tax teams that have tested AI but struggle to adopt it across the enterprise. Crowe's approach centers on making tax work visible, repeatable, and auditable.

According to the article, moving from experimentation to enterprise adoption takes more than AI tools alone. Organizations need business logic and governed workflows so that their processes can be understood, repeated, and reviewed. Crowe says that through Alteryx's analytics and automation platform, it is helping clients deploy AI in ways that are consistent and scalable. The article describes governed data automation as the base for AI-enabled workflows that raise confidence while keeping control in place. The firm presents this as a way to preserve consistency even as tools change.

Crowe says it does not apply AI to every task, and instead advises tax departments on where automation, AI, and human judgment each add the most value. Rather than treating a whole tax engagement as one AI opportunity, the firm breaks complex workflows into smaller, repeatable tasks so clients can modernize step by step. Built-in validation, quality checks, and traceable processes are meant to catch potential problems before work goes out. Crowe argues these features make AI-generated outputs easier to trust.

Matt Paparella, a partner at Crowe Studio and the firm's Tax AI leader, said in a statement dated October 27 that AI brings speed but governance brings trust. He said tax executives face growing pressure to show that AI delivers measurable value without adding risk, and that combining governed automation, AI, and tax expertise is meant to bring that consistency and control to scale. Crowe says the value of its work includes helping tax leaders demonstrate the return on their AI spending to senior management. The article notes that Crowe's tax transformation services are designed to support clients at each stage of their AI journey, from foundational education through workflow design.

stories.Headline: 77% Use Personal AI Accounts Even Where Firms Ban It
stories.Summary:
A new survey published by Fasoo AI on October 28, 2026, found that many employees use generative artificial intelligence through personal accounts even where their companies forbid it. The report, titled "Intelligence Beyond Control: Shadow AI Use and Responses at Korean Organizations," was based on responses from 151 AI, information technology and security officials at major Korean companies and institutions. Most respondents, 88.7%, said they use generative AI through personal accounts at work. Among those whose organizations block the technology as a matter of principle, 77.3% still said they do so.

The survey points to gaps in how organizations manage this practice. Only 19.2% of organizations said they track and control employees' use of personal AI accounts. The most cited concern was that core internal data could be used to train third-party models, at 28.3%, followed by violations of rules such as Korea's Personal Information Protection Act and the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, at 24.0%. Respondents also worried about incidents being hard to trace, at 23.7%, because usage records cannot be followed. Employees most often cited the lack of clear usage policies, at 28.5%, as their reason for turning to such tools.

Asked how to reduce the risks, the largest share of respondents, 25.7%, called for in-house AI tools that employees can use safely. Others prioritized visibility into how AI is used, at 20.6%, clear usage policies and guidelines, at 18.9%, and technology that controls sensitive information at the prompt-input stage, at 17.7%. Son Jong-gon, an executive director at Fasoo AI, said that banning the practice does not stop it, and that the key is offering clear policies, safe alternatives and visibility into use. The company said it plans to unveil an AI security platform that manages various data leakage channels and provides visibility into overall AI usage.

stories.Headline: AI Rise Paradoxically Deepens the Imperative for Lawyer Training
stories.Summary:
Two Cleary Gottlieb leaders, senior partner Michael A. Gerstenzang and corporate partner Kyle A. Harris, published a commentary on Bloomberg Law on October 27, 2026, arguing that the rise of artificial intelligence makes lawyer training more urgent, not less. They note that the legal profession has long relied on an apprenticeship model, and that the growing use of AI in client work raises questions about how the next generation of lawyers will be developed. Their central claim is that firms which fail to adapt their training may deliver faster work in the short term but will lose clients over time because they are not building a pipeline of strong advisers. The authors describe senior lawyers' anxiety about how junior lawyers will gain foundational experience as AI takes over routine tasks.

The authors argue that the traditional model has been less systematic than people remember, since mentoring depended on luck, with some associates paired with teachers and matters that offered real learning and others not. They propose that AI can make training more deliberate if senior lawyers use it to build efficiency while keeping independent thinking intact. In their view, junior lawyers can review AI output against source documents, check for errors, and assess where the reasoning is weak, while partners review prompting histories to give feedback. Removing junior lawyers from the reasoning process, whether by having AI do the work or by handing assignments off entirely, eliminates the learning. The authors also stress that productive struggle with complex material remains valuable and should be preserved where it builds lasting skill.

The authors also contend that "judgment," which includes common sense, commercial awareness, pattern recognition, curiosity, and communication, will be expected of junior associates far earlier than before. They say AI fluency is not simply good prompting but knowing where to apply AI, defining tasks clearly, identifying sources, and validating results. They say law schools can help through clinical work and other real-world experiences that build communication and project management skills. The authors conclude that firms redesigning apprenticeship and evaluation around AI will produce more capable and more valuable lawyers. The article states that its views do not necessarily reflect those of Bloomberg Industry Group, which publishes Bloomberg Law.

stories.Headline: Del. idea for AI-run companies draws eye of powerful congressional committee
stories.Summary:
Rep. James Comer, a Kentucky Republican who chairs the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, has asked Delaware's governor for documents about a proposed plan to create a new legal entity for companies run by artificial intelligence agents. The letter, which concerns Delaware's Artificial Intelligence Company initiative, suggests Congress may be looking at limits on state AI rules. Comer wrote that he worried the proposal could protect powerful AI firms and their investors from responsibility for harmful actions. Gov. Matt Meyer's office said it is reviewing the letter. The initiative was announced in July by Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez and John Nay, founder and CEO of Norm AI, in Fortune magazine.

A draft by John Mark Zeberkiewicz, a lawyer at Richards, Layton & Finger, would let an AI agent act as a company with legal personhood, able to own assets, file lawsuits and serve as a liability shield. A single member, either a person or an entity, would have to keep the company adequately capitalized and would be shielded from its debts unless it failed in that duty or used the company to break the law or commit fraud. The company must keep a log of its activities and may pursue any lawful purpose except banking. If the bill passes, organizations would have 30 months to apply to a regulatory sandbox for AI-run companies, and the bill would create a sandbox committee and an administrator. State lawmakers are expected to take up the idea next year.

Comer's letter cites a WHYY News article from September that noted Patibanda-Sanchez declined to answer questions about the relationship between Norm AI and the Meyer administration. Comer said Delaware officials praise transparency in AI decision-making, yet the public-private partnership lacks it, and he also raised concern about regulatory capture by hidden interests. The Richards Layton & Finger firm said attorneys have long helped shape the state's corporate statutes and that lawmakers weigh that input. Nay did not respond to a request for comment, and a spokesperson for Patibanda-Sanchez referred questions to Meyer's office.

The debate has drawn both criticism and support. Corporate law professors have questioned who would be accountable if an AI-run company caused harm, and one University of Pennsylvania professor called the idea a solution in search of a problem. Lawrence Cunningham of the University of Delaware's John L. Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance argued that Delaware, a leading home for business formation, would be irresponsible to ignore the idea. The committee wants documents and communications dating back to January 1, 2025, including internal AI chat logs, and Delaware's response is due November 9.

Articles.Title: Del. idea for AI-run companies draws eye of powerful congressional committee - WHYY

stories.Headline: When Lower Reconstruction Loss Hurts: Distributionally Robust Refinement for Low-Bit LLM Quantization
stories.Summary:
A research paper posted to arXiv, titled "When Lower Reconstruction Loss Hurts," reports a finding about weight-only post-training quantization, a method for shrinking large language models to low numerical precision. The authors, nine researchers led by Yanlong Zhao, write that the standard practice of minimizing reconstruction loss does not reliably produce better model performance on new tasks. They report that lower reconstruction loss can even degrade performance on the same calibration data used to set the weights. The paper was listed with a date of October 27, 2026, and is categorized under artificial intelligence, machine learning and statistical machine learning.

To address this, the authors propose Distributionally Robust Quantization, abbreviated DRQ, which they describe as a post-hoc refinement step. DRQ adjusts the integer codes that represent quantized weights while staying inside the existing quantization grid, and it leaves the quantization parameters and inference operators unchanged. The method works by minimizing the worst-case reconstruction loss across a constrained set of input activation distributions. According to the abstract, the approach requires no added inference overhead, so a model keeps its running cost after refinement.

The authors state that they carried out extensive experiments in which DRQ improved models quantized by six representative methods, including AWQ, GPTQ and ParoQuant. They say the gains appeared in both dense and mixture-of-experts large language models. The paper presents these results as establishing DRQ as a general refinement framework for weight-only quantization that yields better downstream performance. The abstract does not name the institutional affiliations of the authors or report specific benchmark figures, and the article provides no information on adoption or follow-up work beyond the paper itself.

Articles.Title: When Lower Reconstruction Loss Hurts: Distributionally Robust Refinement for Low-Bit LLM Quantization

stories.Headline: LocalAgent: Collaborative Agentic Verification for Fine-Grained Instance-Level Consistency
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers posted a paper on arXiv, a preprint server, describing LocalAgent, a framework for checking whether two images show the exact same physical object. The paper, dated October 27, 2026, was written by Jiachen Guo and six co-authors, including Xinshan Zhu, Boyun Wang, Yanyan Liang, Jun Wan, Feng Lin and Ajian Liu. The authors say existing multimodal large language models still struggle with this task when viewpoint, lighting or background changes. They note that semantically similar objects may differ only in small suspicious regions, which makes careful local checking necessary.

LocalAgent pairs a general-purpose multimodal model with lightweight specialist verifiers. The general model first reasons over the whole image to flag suspicious local regions, then hands those regions to a Local Evidence Verifier toolkit. That toolkit contains two components: Local Appearance Consistency, which estimates similarity under illumination and color changes, and Local Geometric Correspondence, which estimates spatial matching under viewpoint changes. The toolkit returns structured scalar evidence, which the general model combines into a final decision. The authors also describe an auxiliary-capped reinforcement fine-tuning strategy that weights answer correctness above tool-use and format signals, so the system learns when verification is needed.

According to the paper, LocalAgent improves mean accuracy by 4.9% over the strongest chain-of-thought reinforcement fine-tuning baseline. It invokes a verifier on only 12.13% of samples, and the authors report that it preserves the general multimodal capabilities of the underlying model. The paper says the open-source repository is available online. The work is presented as a preprint and has not, based on the material provided, been peer reviewed or formally published.

Articles.Title: LocalAgent: Collaborative Agentic Verification for Fine-Grained Instance-Level Consistency

stories.Headline: AI Enters the Courtroom as Dubai Rethinks How Lawyers Train and Judges Work
stories.Summary:
Dubai has launched a virtual courtroom that lets junior lawyers practise cross-examination against simulated judges, witnesses and opposing counsel. The tool was reported by Law.com on October 27, 2026, in an article by Dario Sabaghi. The courtroom is built on the Legaline platform, according to the photo credit that accompanies the article. The article is a brief overview, and the full text sits behind a subscription wall. The articles do not give a figure for how many trainees or judges use the system, nor a price, a start date beyond the launch, or the number of simulated scenarios available.

They also do not say whether the simulations are used in formal court proceedings or only in training. The piece frames the launch as part of a broader rethinking of how lawyers are trained and how judges work, but the visible text gives no further detail on that rethinking. Readers would need the subscriber version to learn what it covers. The articles do not name any official, agency or firm responsible for the launch, and they include no direct statement from any of them. Sabaghi is credited as the author, and Legaline is credited as the platform behind the imagery.

Beyond that, the available text attributes no remarks to anyone. Whether the courtroom is run by the Dubai government, a court, a training body or a private company is not stated. The visible text offers no context on earlier AI use in Dubai's legal system and no account of what comes next. It does not say whether the courtroom will expand, be copied elsewhere, or be reviewed. Reporting on the topic beyond this overview would be needed to answer those questions.
