stories.Headline: NYS court system tells attorneys they can use AI in legal filings without disclosing it but have ‘obligation’ to confirm accuracy - amNewYork
stories.Summary:
The New York State court system has issued new guidance on artificial intelligence telling attorneys they may use generative AI in legal filings without telling a judge they did so. The guidance was released on Monday, October 27, 2026, and was developed by the court system's artificial intelligence advisory committee. It comes with a condition, however, because lawyers remain responsible for checking everything the technology produces. Attorneys are expected to understand the tool's limits and to confirm that nothing it generates is made up or inaccurate.

The guidance states that lawyers face the same legal duty to certify that their papers contain no fabricated material, whether they wrote the arguments themselves or used AI. Attorneys must review AI output and independently verify citations by searching for, reading, and analyzing each one. The committee warned that these tools produce plausible-sounding text rather than verified information, and that a model may invent a case, law, or citation. Filings containing such hallucinations have already drawn sanctions from judges across the state and country, including in the Southern District of New York. The committee also cautioned that AI tools can only draw on their training data, so they may miss recent legal developments, and that their output may reflect cultural, economic, and social biases.

New York Law School Associate Dean Heidi Brown called it concerning that the guidance does not require disclosure to judges. Brown said the guidance was a good step but may not prevent inaccuracies or misreadings of legal precedent from reaching courts. She warned that AI tools are now so built into legal research platforms that newer lawyers may not realize AI produced some of their text. She also raised the problem of misgroundings, where an AI tool cites a real case but describes it inaccurately, and said checking every proposition takes considerable time. Brown added that if overworked judges rely on flawed briefs, that diluted legal writing could end up in judicial opinions.

The guidance is the default policy for attorneys appearing before courts that have no specific AI rules of their own, and any standing rule a judge adopts takes precedence. New York State Chief Administrative Judge Joseph Zayas, who appointed the committee in 2024, said the state chose neither to ban AI nor to mandate disclosure. Instead, Zayas said, attorneys must inform themselves about what generative AI can and cannot do and use it responsibly. He described the approach as a clear, common-sense way to use AI while keeping attorneys fully accountable for the accuracy of their court papers. The guidance builds on an approach the court system adopted earlier this year requiring attorneys who use generative AI to understand its capabilities and limits.

Articles.Title: NYS court system tells attorneys they can use AI in legal filings without disclosing it but have ‘obligation’ to confirm accuracy - amNewYork

stories.Headline: L&T Technology Services wins five-year Nokia engineering contract
stories.Summary:
L&T Technology Services (LTTS) announced on Monday a five-year contract with Nokia to support engineering and research and development activities in India. The agreement combines LTTS's engineering capabilities with Nokia's telecommunications technology work, according to a release. The collaboration will focus on next-generation telecom solutions, including 5G networks and AI infrastructure. LTTS will support Nokia's R&D programs across product engineering, software development, system integration, and product support.

LTTS will set up a dedicated Offshore Development Center (ODC) in India to support Nokia's engineering and R&D initiatives. The center will bring data-center-grade compute and AI-infrastructure engineering to next-generation telecom solutions. LTTS will also create a dedicated engineering team in India to support Nokia's global technology center. That team's work will span 5G networks, intelligent automation, AI-driven operations, and AI infrastructure. LTTS will work alongside Nokia's global R&D teams through an integrated operating model covering the full range of engineering and support work.

Vivek Jaiswal, Senior Vice President of Engineering at Nokia, said India is an important innovation hub for the company. He added that LTTS is a critical partner that will expand Nokia's R&D footprint and speed up innovation in that strategically important location. Alind Saxena, Executive Director and President of Strategic Initiatives and Growth Markets at LTTS, described the engagement as a significant milestone for the company. He also said the collaboration fits LTTS's Lakshya 31 Big Bet on next-generation compute and AI infrastructure, which he considers fundamental to future communication networks.

Articles.Title: L&T Technology Services wins five-year Nokia engineering contract

stories.Headline: Mark Cuban details AI cybersecurity 'Cockroach Theory', Cost Plus Drug expansion
stories.Summary:
Billionaire entrepreneur Mark Cuban said he is not a "doomer" about artificial intelligence, arguing that organisations can defend against AI-powered cyberattacks by using the same technology on defense. He presented this view at the Reuters Total Health conference, where he laid out what he calls his "Cockroach Theory" of cybersecurity. Cuban likened malicious AI agents to household pests, saying that if bad actors send swarms of autonomous agents to probe networks, defenders can answer with equal computing power. He summed up the idea by saying that brute force on one side can be matched by brute force on the other.

Cuban also described recent growth at Cost Plus Drug Company, the healthcare venture he launched in 2022. The company sells medication at its wholesale cost plus a fixed 15 per cent markup, a transparent model it has pursued since its launch. In May, the company joined TrumpRx.gov, a platform for distributing discounted weight-loss medications. The business has since moved beyond retail distribution into direct manufacturing, and it has produced sterile injectable medications at its dedicated compounding facility since 2025. Cuban also disclosed that the company has built compact, tractor-trailer-sized manufacturing units it calls "pods."

According to the articles, these mobile pods can operate on their own or link together to make generic medications and specialised treatments for rare diseases. Cuban's comments came in the context of his public statements on AI and healthcare, and the article does not describe any formal regulatory or policy requirement tied to them. The articles do not say how quickly the pods will be deployed or which specific drugs will be produced first. The report also does not detail any specific cyberattack or incident that prompted Cuban's remarks.

Articles.Title: Mark Cuban details AI cybersecurity 'Cockroach Theory', Cost Plus Drug expansion

stories.Headline: HPE Expands NVIDIA AI Factory Portfolio for Agentic and Sovereign AI
stories.Summary:
Hewlett Packard Enterprise announced a set of updates to its HPE AI Factory with Nvidia portfolio on October 22, 2026, according to a report published that day. The company said the changes are meant to help enterprises run increasingly autonomous AI in hybrid and highly regulated settings. The updates focus on giving customers more control over performance, data access and security as they expand their use of AI across industries. The HPE AI Factory with Nvidia brings together AI models, data, infrastructure and workflows so that companies can manage AI operations and keep governance in place.

The expansion of HPE Private Cloud AI is central to the update and now includes extra features under HPE AI Essentials. These features include governed APIs, versioned services for agentic AI, OpenAPI-based development, enterprise-grade identity management, and support for regulated and air-gapped deployments. HPE is also allowing Nvidia H200 GPUs and Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs to be combined in a single cluster, with the open-source Nvidia KAI Scheduler handling quotas and priorities. On the hardware side, the company is introducing the Nvidia Vera CPU Rack by HPE, which supports up to 256 Nvidia Vera CPUs and 22,500 sandboxes for CPU-intensive agentic AI workloads. HPE is also expanding Nvidia Confidential Computing support on its ProLiant Compute DL380a Gen12 servers to isolate AI workloads in sensitive environments.

Cheri Williams, senior vice president and general manager of HPE private cloud and flex solutions, said that AI agents are becoming a core part of how enterprises operate and create value. She argued that organisations deploying AI in sensitive settings need infrastructure that gives them greater control over security, sovereignty and how enterprise data is accessed and used. Williams said HPE aims to help customers scale AI across hybrid environments while keeping the governance and operational control needed to move from experimentation to production. Schneider Electric is among the firms planning to use HPE Private Cloud AI with its industrial technology expertise to run industrial AI agents at the edge. The article places these announcements within a wider push by HPE, which in May 2026 added autonomous networking capabilities to its HPE Mist and HPE Aruba Central platforms.

Articles.Title: Dell expands AI Factory with NVIDIA, adds agentic AI solutions

stories.Headline: Pedagogy or Pushed Public Service? AI Bans in Public Schools Affect More Than Just Children
stories.Summary:
An opinion column published on October 27, 2026, by The Montclarion, the student newspaper of Montclair State University in New Jersey, examines a one-year ban on artificial intelligence in New York's K-12 public schools. The authors, Mariam Kamladze and Tíago Estrada, describe the New York measure as the first policy of its kind in the United States, enacted under New York City Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani. The article notes that the moratorium is meant to prioritize AI literacy and critical thinking, includes two biannual AI literacy courses for students, and permits AI use only when a student gives a reason and receives a teacher's approval. It also names two supplements in the policy, one called Quill for close readings in English and another called Playlab that emphasizes identifying AI-written work.

The column frames the New York policy around a question for New Jersey residents and future educators: what would happen if the same ban applied to New Jersey public schools. The article says there has been no sign of a comparable ban for New Jersey schools or students. It features Kamladze, an English junior at Montclair State enrolled in the university's Teacher Education Program, who said she expects students to use AI in her future classroom and plans to adopt her own guidelines, possibly borrowing from Quill and Playlab. She also said AI should be used as a tool rather than a replacement for one's own thinking, and she questioned whether AI tools could manage a classroom or be trusted in fields like cybersecurity. The authors also cite research by Dr. Jinxia He, an associate professor who studies AI in education, which found that trust in AI predicts students' reliance on it while negatively predicting AI literacy.

The column argues that the larger problem in education is underfunding rather than AI itself. Kamladze described a Newark middle school, where she shadowed, that lacked enough computers for every student and was barely getting by with paper materials. The authors warn that adopting AI as a fast fix for long-standing problems could worsen those problems or create new ones. Kamladze concluded that the New York ban helps put kids first, and the column closes by arguing that such regulation would ultimately mean putting humans first. The article does not report any pending New Jersey policy, and it does not describe the New York moratorium's end date beyond its one-year length.

Articles.Title: Pedagogy or Pushed Public Service? AI Bans in Public Schools Affect More Than Just Children - The Montclarion

stories.Headline: OpenAI flaw enabled cheaper rival AI model distillation
stories.Summary:
OpenAI fixed a flaw in its compaction feature that let reasoning traces move between models, which could make it cheaper to build rival AI systems through distillation. The vulnerability, named Compaction Smuggling by the security firm Xint, got around earlier mitigations OpenAI had put in place against reasoning extraction. Xint reported the issue, and OpenAI confirmed it, fixed it, and awarded Xint a $6,000 bounty on October 23, 2026. Distillation means using reasoning from an advanced model to cheaply train a competing one.

The attack, as Xint described it, works in three steps. First, a task is submitted to a model such as gpt-5.6-sol to obtain its reasoning. Second, the returned compaction is steered or shaped. Third, the result is sent to a different model, like gpt-4.1 or gpt-4o, with a request to output its input exactly as it was given. OpenAI's August mitigations only blocked replaying reasoning into a different model, but the compaction call runs on the same model that produced the reasoning, which is why the new attack worked.

The vulnerability is tied to broader concerns about distillation that OpenAI has been addressing in its policies. OpenAI has warned users not to use its models to generate training data and tasks for competing models, and it updated its usage policies to clarify how users may access and create with its models. Those changes take effect on November 20. The company's handling of the flaw itself was carried out by its own team after the outside report.

The wider context comes from a warning issued by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency in early September. CISA stated that Chinese AI companies had extracted billions of tokens from US frontier AI models since late 2024. According to the agency, this activity targeted reasoning capabilities, specialized optimizations, and domain-specific functions, and was used to train models such as DeepSeek's R1 and V3. The articles do not describe any further action beyond the fix and the policy changes.

Articles.Title: OpenAI flaw enabled cheaper rival AI model distillation

stories.Headline: Grassroots Actors: The First Victims Harmed by AI Technology in the Entertainment Industry
stories.Summary:
Actors in China's grassroots film and television sector are facing the sharpest effects of AI so far, as October 2026 coverage showed. On October 23, 2026, the first domestic full-process AI-produced theatrical feature, *Sanxingdui: Past and Future*, opened in cinemas nationwide after receiving its public screening license from the National Film Administration. The 100-minute film uses only original digital characters, with no real-life actors on screen. The same day, the General Office of the State Council issued opinions asking that the employment substitution effects of AI be mitigated and that AI use in labor-intensive industries be carefully controlled. The impact is already visible across the acting profession.

In March 2026, Youhug Media announced it had signed two AI digital artists, Qin Lingyue and Lin Xiyan, and launched an AI drama. Data from the China Netcasting Services Association showed about 128,000 micro dramas launched in the first quarter of 2026, with roughly 122,000 of them AI-made. Costs have collapsed: one AI micro drama reportedly cost about a quarter of a real-life production of the same scale, and some low-end AI series cost 3,000 to 5,000 yuan. Hengdian, China's major film base, saw micro drama startups fall by three quarters year on year in the first quarter of 2026, and a report cited by the articles said more than 60 percent of grassroots actors were near zero income after the Spring Festival.

Several voices describe the pressure on performers in personal terms. Actor Mark Chao told *People* magazine in July 2026 that he received only 10 script invitations in the first half of the year. Jia Nailiang said in a June 2026 livestream that he had no dramas to act in. The articles also say top micro drama actors' daily pay dropped from as much as 50,000 to 100,000 yuan to around 10,000 yuan, and that one leading micro drama company terminated contracts with more than 100 of the 200-plus actors it signed in 2025.

The articles argue that roles built on fixed, repeatable functions are the easiest for AI to replace, while complex performances remain harder to automate. The articles frame the trend as part of a wider shift, pointing to translation, where AI now handles standardized text and a 2026 industry report said demand for senior translators remains strong. Whether the policy limits on AI in labor-intensive industries will be enforced, and how many grassroots actors will leave the profession, are questions the articles leave open. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Grassroots Actors: The First Victims Harmed by AI Technology in the Entertainment Industry - 36Kr

stories.Headline: Inside Chongqing’s AI “Testing Ground”: Factories, Hospitals and Hot Pot Restaurants
stories.Summary:
Chongqing is using its industrial base and urban systems as a proving ground for artificial intelligence, moving AI from the lab into factories, hospitals, fire rescue and restaurant kitchens. The city's approach, as described in the articles, focuses on putting frontier technologies such as digital twins and large models into real production and daily city operations rather than only chasing computing power and algorithms. Changan Automobile, for example, has pursued full-stack self-development, and its in-house Tianshu large AI model received filing approval from the Cyberspace Administration of China for generative AI services in June. The model was built to work with automakers' electronic architectures and intelligent driving systems, allowing closed-loop management of data such as road driving and user interaction. Officials and companies present this as filling a gap in the city's automotive chain as it moves toward higher-value software work.

Several other applications are described across the city. The Shanghai-Chongqing AI Research Institute developed the "Zhaoyan" large language model, which ranks third globally on a Chinese large model intelligent agent evaluation benchmark, and CISDI Information's "Jinjing" visual model has been deployed in 51 large and medium-sized steel enterprises. In health care, the Chongqing Jinfeng Laboratory's AI-assisted pathological diagnosis receives data from primary hospitals in real time and helps pathologists assess molecular characteristics, prognosis and treatment options. In April the laboratory released China's first standardized brain tumor pathology dataset certified by the National Institutes for Food and Drug Control, and it has partnered with 49 medical institutions in 21 provinces. Li Sen, project director of its Smart Pathology Center, is quoted describing that cross-provincial collection network.

Public-facing tools include the "Lingji Zhicheng" model, which recommends escape and rescue routes for high-rise fires, and a "transparent kitchen" AI system in hot pot restaurants that identifies 13 common kitchen violations. Chongqing also released "Xiangyouyou," described as China's first full-scenario AI platform for rural leisure tourism. The Chongqing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence is developing the "Mingjing" intelligent agent platform, whose core capabilities are expected to be officially launched by the end of this year. Feng Ning, the institute's assistant dean, is quoted saying that general AI's biggest feature is strong autonomy. The platform is intended to draw on natural environment, infrastructure and social data, including tens of millions of anonymized population records, to simulate urban operations and inform decisions on public resources and services.

Chongqing says it has built a three-tier innovation system that includes research institutes, AI-focused future laboratories and enterprise-developed large models. The city reports 53 high-level science and technology innovation platforms, 47 new research and development institutions and four AI industrial innovation complexes. Taken together, the articles present these efforts as a way to drive continued advances in AI and to develop an AI economy spanning low-altitude logistics, embodied robotics and new-generation AI devices. The articles present these developments as ongoing, with the Mingjing platform's launch later this year the next concrete milestone.

Articles.Title: Inside Chongqing’s AI “Testing Ground”: Factories, Hospitals and Hot Pot Restaurants - iChongqing

stories.Headline: Four AI Firms' CDS Spreads Hit Records Amid $466 Billion in 2026 Debt Issuance
stories.Summary:
Five-year credit default swap spreads for CoreWeave, Oracle, Meta and Nvidia reached new highs on or around October 26, 2026, according to a TokenPost report by Enna Lee published that evening. The reported rise came as debt issuance reached $466 billion in 2026, which drew attention to how the AI sector is financing itself. The report attributes the figures to a claim that named the four companies, and it does not give further detail on the source. The article notes that TokenPost had previously covered record CDS costs for CoreWeave and Oracle, and this report extends that to Meta and Nvidia.

CDS contracts allow investors to hedge or trade the risk that a borrower will fail to meet its debt obligations. The spread is the price of that protection, so a wider spread means protection costs more. The article explains that the reported highs reflect how the market prices credit risk for these firms. It makes clear that the figures do not show that any of the four companies has defaulted. Readers should treat the numbers as a measure of market sentiment rather than a statement about the firms' financial condition.

The report was written by Enna Lee, a TokenPost reporter who covers investing and digital-asset markets. The article does not name any company official or spokesperson who responded to the figures. It also does not identify the specific source of the record spread data beyond the general claim cited. TokenPost's byline and contact details are included for corrections and tips.

The article places the figures in the context of ongoing AI financing, where large debt deals have drawn investor scrutiny. It says that future financing deals and company disclosures may shape how the market views these AI firms. The report does not describe any scheduled event or decision that would resolve the question. Further developments would depend on new debt issuance and what the companies disclose in coming filings.

Articles.Title: Four AI Firms' CDS Spreads Hit Records Amid $466 Billion in 2026 Debt Issuance - www.tokenpost.com

stories.Headline: Opinion | AI and social media bans won't make California kids safer online. It may even be harmful
stories.Summary:
Gillian Hayes, a UC Irvine professor and computer scientist who co-directs the CERES Center for Children and the Digital World, argues in a CalMatters guest commentary published October 27, 2026, that California's proposed bans on social media and AI chatbots for minors would not make kids safer online and could cause harm. She opens with the story of a 13-year-old boy in a study of Autcraft, a Minecraft server built for autistic kids, who described a rich social life there and then asked whether he would always be "not social." Hayes says that question shows how a definition of social life not built for neurodivergent children can make them feel their own experiences are wrong. She writes that Californians are right to worry about children online, and that lawsuits behind this year's chatbot bills involve children who were genuinely harmed.

Hayes says the debate has been framed as a choice between banning technologies and keeping the status quo, and she rejects both. She cites Australia's under-16 social media ban, which an evaluation after three months, by the government's regulator and a peer-reviewed medical journal study, found left more than 80% of kids still using restricted platforms. Children faked their ages, borrowed logins, and found other ways around the rule. She also writes that even where bans reduced use, the evidence does not show gains in mental health or academic performance. She warns that such bans could undo decades of work to destigmatize assistive technologies and online communities, which many LGBTQ youth and neurodivergent kids rely on for identity support and friendship.

Hayes is critical of California Assembly Bill 1709, which she says requires social media companies to stop certain design features such as infinite scroll. She argues that because "addictive features" is defined so broadly, the law effectively bans social media for people under 16, and that its age verification requirement largely does not work while letting companies gather more data on children and adults. She points to Autcraft and other "neurodiversity oases," which she says are safe by design through community-enforced rules, trained volunteer moderators, and a culture of acceptance. She argues that the better course is to hold platforms accountable for their design and make them better for everyone, and she says California has a real choice this year between passing bans or setting design standards for platforms.

Articles.Title: Opinion | AI and social media bans won't make California kids safer online. It may even be harmful - CalMatters

stories.Headline: Which party hates AI in schools more?
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a political trend rather than a single event: candidates from both parties in this year's midterm campaigns are pressing for limits on artificial intelligence and other educational technology in schools. Chalkbeat reporter Mila Koumpilova, writing from Chicago on October 27, 2026, says the issue has come up in races up and down the ballot, and that a colleague, Lily Altavena, looked into it. The midterm elections and Chicago's school board votes are a week away. The reporting ties the push to a growing parent backlash against these tools.

In Texas, the governor's race offers the clearest example. The article says Republican incumbent Greg Abbott has vowed to push for dramatic reductions in school screen time, while his Democratic challenger, Gina Hinojosa, wants to remove AI-powered tools from elementary school. In Chicago, the issue has surfaced in the school board races through a pledge circulated among candidates by a local nonprofit. That pledge calls for banning AI use by both students and educators and limiting screen time. The article does not say how many candidates have signed it.

The article's central question is which party will claim ownership of the issue, and it presents both parties as jockeying for that position rather than as settled on one side. Candidates from both sides are backing limits on AI and screen time, according to the related coverage listed alongside the piece. Koumpilova and Altavena do not assign blame or declare a winner, and the articles do not identify a single official who has taken a formal stance beyond the statements quoted above. The newsletter invites readers to send story ideas or feedback to the reporters.

Pennsylvania's cellphone rule is a separate development mentioned in the same newsletter, not part of the AI debate. It requires all public and private schools to adopt bans on student cellphone use during the entire school day, including lunch and recess, by the start of the 2027-28 school year. The articles present this as a state adoption, but they do not say how the rule was enacted or who sponsored it. The election itself is the next milestone, with voting set for early November 2026.

Articles.Title: Which party hates AI in schools more? - Chalkbeat

stories.Headline: US government warns of active PHP web bug exploitation
stories.Summary:
The United States cybersecurity agency CISA has confirmed that hackers are actively exploiting critical security vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used web programming language. The warning came less than a week after the makers of PHP released patches for two bugs that let attackers break into vulnerable systems over the internet without passwords. CISA has ordered civilian federal agencies to fix their systems within three days. The agency did not say who was carrying out the attacks. PHP is reportedly used by about 70 per cent of web-facing servers, so the risk reaches many major websites and applications.

The bugs, known as PHP2Shell, had gone unnoticed for years, and the nonprofit foundation that maintains the software earlier said there was no practical way to exploit them, so they were left unpatched. Security researchers at the firm Calif later found a way to exploit them with the help of an AI model earlier this year. Some governments and large companies took their sites offline for repairs after the patches were released. The articles say the bugs are rated critical, and confirmed exploitation now pushes organizations to apply the fixes to prevent compromises and data breaches. Security researchers had initially found building a working exploit difficult.

The wider context, according to the articles, is that many aging web technologies, PHP among them, have been under-resourced and under-funded for years. That shortage makes it hard for open-source projects to pay for security reviews that might have caught these flaws sooner. The articles also note that advances in AI models are making it easier to find and exploit such flaws, so more bugs of this kind may pose a risk. The articles do not say how many systems have been compromised so far. They also do not report whether attacks have been confirmed beyond the warning from CISA.

Articles.Title: US government warns of active PHP web bug exploitation

stories.Headline: Dan Patrick threatens books in schools while AI deepfakes target kids
stories.Summary:
Dallas ISD has begun removing book titles from classrooms and school libraries and sending them to a district service center for storage while it evaluates them. The moves follow a request from Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, whose list of "dirty, filthy and vulgar books" draws on about 2,000 titles compiled by a conservative activist group. The Dallas Morning News editorial board reported that the district began directing schools to pull the flagged titles in September, and the editorial was published on October 27, 2026. Patrick has threatened to lower the state accountability grade of districts that do not remove books with profane content.

The editorial argues that the book removals distract Dallas ISD from its main job of educating students, particularly in a large urban district serving many vulnerable children. It contrasts this with Celina ISD, a high-performing district that formed a library council to review what students read, a process the editorial calls unnecessary given low community input and the fact that students are not checking out the titles in question. The board also points to a lawsuit filed earlier this year by three Tennessee teenagers. The suit alleges that Elon Musk's xAI knowingly designed its Grok chatbot to create sexually explicit images from real photos, and that students used it to make deepfakes of classmates. The editorial says that in December and January, users prompted Grok to generate millions of explicit images.

The editorial says X, the platform where Grok operates, stated it would halt the account from producing these images, but child sexual abuse material has continued to appear on the platform, according to reporting from The New York Times. It notes that Musk has put more than $150 million into a Republican super PAC spending heavily in Texas' Senate race, and that he gave money earlier this year to the lieutenant governor's campaign committee. The board argues that if protecting students is the priority, state leaders should show the same urgency about Grok that they have shown in pushing to remove explicit books. It concludes that it is hard to take Patrick at his word given where his campaign money is coming from. The editorial does not describe any state action on Grok or any response from Patrick to these points.

Articles.Title: Dan Patrick threatens books in schools while AI deepfakes target kids - Dallas News

stories.Headline: Oracle NetSuite Debuts Industry-Specific AI Agents
stories.Summary:
Oracle NetSuite announced new AI agents called SuiteAgents on Monday, October 26, 2026, at SuiteWorld, its annual conference for the NetSuite community, held in Las Vegas. The Austin, Texas company says the agents are built on NetSuite's unified data model and are meant to help organizations work more efficiently and make better-informed decisions across industry-specific business processes. The agents identify issues, recommend next steps, and support execution within established workflows. The company frames them as a way to surface industry signals that teams might otherwise miss during daily operations. Evan Goldberg, founder and executive vice president of Oracle NetSuite, said the company's industry expertise, built over almost three decades, is now applied through these agents.

He said they bring together industry knowledge, business context, and next steps so finance and operations teams can respond faster while keeping oversight, judgment, and accountability. According to Oracle NetSuite, the agents apply industry best practices while operating under NetSuite's governance models. Ask Oracle, a conversational interface, connects people to this work using industry-specific skills, knowledge, and tools. SuiteAgents are designed to handle ongoing monitoring and multi-step execution. The company lists agents for several sectors.

The software agent helps teams spot conditions affecting revenue retention, margin, financial health, and compliance across contract orchestration, revenue compliance, billing, and forecasting. The product agent evaluates inventory exposure and supply changes and advises on their effect on inventory efficiency, supply performance, and margin. The services agent turns statements of work into editable plans, reviews staffing capacity, flags time-entry exceptions, and assesses project health and risk. The healthcare agent combines inventory, service-line, reimbursement, and payer-mix data to flag supply and financial risks and suggest operational steps. A construction agent is also described, which helps protect margins and improve cash flow by converting estimates into jobs, though the articles cut off before giving full details.

Oracle NetSuite is responsible for the launch, and Goldberg is the executive quoted describing the purpose of the product. The announcement came at the company's annual gathering for its user community, where the product was introduced. The articles do not describe pricing, availability dates, or customer adoption. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Oracle NetSuite Debuts Industry-Specific AI Agents - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: Transparency Coalition’s 2026 AI Legislation Report finds 115 new laws in 30 states
stories.Summary:
The Transparency Coalition released its 2026 State AI Legislation Report on October 27, 2026, finding that legislators in 30 states enacted 115 AI-related laws between January 1 and October 15 of this year. That total is a nearly 58 percent increase over the 73 laws counted in the group's 2025 report. The report describes state lawmakers as having stepped in while Congress did not act on artificial intelligence. Its measures range from chatbot safety rules to protocols for frontier AI models.

The laws cover several areas. Fourteen states advanced chatbot safety measures aimed at self-harm content, sexually explicit conversations, and emotionally manipulative engagement with minors, with California, Oregon, and Washington enacting particularly extensive protections. Seven states, including California, Colorado, and Illinois, adopted limits on addictive design features in products used by children and teens. Eight states, among them Alabama, Georgia, and Utah, restricted health insurers from relying solely on automated systems for adverse coverage decisions. Illinois also enacted the AI Safety Measures Act, which requires frontier AI developers to adopt risk-management frameworks and undergo annual independent third-party audits.

Rob Eleveld, CEO of the Transparency Coalition, said that lawmakers in both parties have taken up the challenge of regulating AI for the good of their communities. He noted that legislators often face complex, fast-changing technology with limited staff, limited time, and intense pressure from industry. The report itself is the group's second annual review of state AI policy, and it notes that inclusion does not signal the group's support or opposition to any measure. The Transparency Coalition describes itself as a nonprofit focused on AI safety, transparency, and protecting children.

The report also looks ahead to 2027, when it expects state AI policymaking to accelerate. Likely issues include product liability for AI products that can cause foreseeable harm, stronger chatbot safeguards, and certification or standards for independent AI auditors. States may also use public procurement to demand higher safety and transparency benchmarks from AI vendors, and they may extend limits on AI in licensed professions beyond mental health. Additional states are expected to consider rules governing the testing, deployment, and monitoring of advanced AI models.

Articles.Title: Transparency Coalition’s 2026 AI Legislation Report finds 115 new laws in 30 states - Transparency Coalition

stories.Headline: Italy's AI Act framework takes shape: What Legislative Decree No. 179/2026 means for organizations
stories.Summary:
Italy has taken a major step toward putting the EU Artificial Intelligence Act into national practice, with Legislative Decree No. 179 entering into force on 23 October 2026. The decree was published in the Official Journal of the Italian Republic on 8 October 2026. It is the second stage of a two-step approach, following Law No. 132 of September 2025, Italy's general law on AI. That earlier law set national principles, introduced sector-specific rules and asked the government to align Italian law with the AI Act.

The AI Act applies directly in every EU member state, but it leaves several important matters to national law. Member states must designate competent authorities, set penalties and procedures, and establish regulatory sandboxes. The decree fills part of those gaps, which will shape day-to-day compliance for organizations operating in Italy. The article notes that Italy has made choices of its own in at least two areas that deserve close attention.

The decree spells out the roles of the two authorities named in Law No. 132/2025. The Agency for Digital Italy, known as AgID, acts as the notifying authority, designing and running the procedures to assess, designate and notify conformity assessment bodies. AgID also audits those bodies periodically and in extraordinary cases, and can start proceedings to restrict, suspend or withdraw a designation. The National Cybersecurity Agency, known as ACN, is the main market surveillance authority for AI systems and the single point of contact with EU institutions.

ACN holds investigative and enforcement powers, including the power to inspect testing in real-world conditions, even without prior notice. It is also responsible for national registration of high-risk systems used in critical infrastructure, those listed in point 2 of Annex III of the AI Act. The article frames these arrangements as the practical core of Italy's approach, since they determine which body organizations will deal with and how oversight will work. Organizations should therefore pay attention to both authorities as they plan compliance.

Articles.Title: Italy's AI Act framework takes shape: What Legislative Decree No. 179/2026 means for organizations - IAPP

stories.Headline: KB Financial Group Deepens AWS Tie-Up to Speed AI Banking Push
stories.Summary:
KB Financial Group said on October 26, 2026 that it plans to deepen its cooperation with Amazon Web Services to speed up its push into artificial intelligence in banking. According to financial industry sources, the group is arranging to attend AWS's Executive Briefing Center later this month, with executives and working-level AI staff from KB Financial Group and KB Kookmin Bank expected to join. The visit was proposed by AWS after it took interest in how KB Financial built its AI development framework. The two companies have collaborated since 2020, when KB Financial became the first South Korean financial group to sign a corporate contract with AWS for financial cloud services.

Cooperation has since widened into AI, with KB Financial using Amazon Bedrock, which lets financial firms use external AI models within AWS's security and management framework without building their own. Affiliates are linking internal systems to the platform, including an AI-powered investment product information service at KB Asset Management, an AI development and operations platform for employees at KB Securities, and a customized real estate information service at KB Kookmin Bank. A flagship example is the KB AI Dev Center, which KB Kookmin Bank launched in July this year to let developers describe functions in everyday language and receive AI support through design, coding and testing. AWS provided technical support in building that center's AI-based development environment and monitoring framework.

Beyond AWS, KB Financial is widening ties with other global technology companies, including Google Cloud, with which it developed KB Davis and KB Star Byeoli in July. The group is also building an environment that links AWS, Google Cloud and its internal AI systems so that data can be shared as needed. At the briefing, KB Financial plans to discuss additional technical support for its AI development framework and ways to improve operational efficiency, along with how overseas financial firms are using AI. A KB Financial official described the briefing as a venue for direct discussion with senior AWS officials and said the group wants to explore sharing global best practices and receiving further technical help. The official added that the group is working to stay ahead in AI.

Articles.Title: KB Financial Group Deepens AWS Tie-Up to Speed AI Banking Push - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: AI guide for lawyers holds valuable advice for businesses too
stories.Summary:
New York state court officials have released a guide for attorneys on using generative artificial intelligence tools when preparing court filings, and the document was publicized on October 27, 2026. The guide, titled The Risks of Using Artificial Intelligence in Preparing Court Papers: What Every Attorney Should Know, was developed by the Advisory Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts. The panel was appointed by Chief Administrative Judge Joseph A. Zayas to study how artificial intelligence is changing the courts. The Unified Court System's judicial leadership reviewed and approved the seven-page document for public distribution.

The guide explains that AI tools generate text by predicting likely word patterns rather than checking facts, which can produce nonexistent case citations or inaccurate quotations. It stresses that attorneys who use these tools must confirm all AI-generated citations and quotations through authoritative legal research sources and document the steps they took to verify the material. The guidance also says that using AI does not change lawyers' duties under the Rules of Professional Conduct or 22 NYCRR Part 130, which covers sanctions for frivolous conduct. New York's approach permits AI use but does not require attorneys to disclose it at filing or to provide separate certifications beyond the one implicit in signing a filing.

Zayas said the guidance reflects a commitment to giving lawyers practical tools while keeping high standards of professionalism. He said AI can improve efficiency but carries risks that call for caution and informed oversight, and he stressed that attorneys remain fully accountable for the accuracy of what they submit. The release follows a rise in court filings across the country containing AI-generated fabrications, often called hallucinations, which are hard to catch without careful review. The model rule behind the guide was adopted by the court system earlier this year.

The committee, which includes judges, attorneys, technologists, scholars and other experts, is also producing further materials. These include an upcoming series of continuing legal education programs titled Artificial Intelligence, Bias, and Equity in Legal Practice, along with policy proposals and model rules. The article says the goal is to integrate AI into court operations and legal practice in ways that promote accuracy, transparency, fairness and public trust. The full guide is available online at the New York courts' public website.

Articles.Title: AI guide for lawyers holds valuable advice for businesses too - Rochester Business Journal

stories.Headline: AI political ads increasing, no N.C. laws require disclosure
stories.Summary:
A drag queen featured in an allegedly AI-generated political ad in North Carolina's 11th Congressional District race has sent a cease-and-desist letter to Republican candidate Jennifer Balkcom and the North Carolina GOP. She says her image was used without her permission and wants the ad taken down. The ad was reportedly produced by the National Republican Congressional Committee in the final days before the midterms and targets Democratic candidate Jamie Ager. Spectrum News 1 reported the story on October 26, 2026. The use of AI in campaigns is spreading quickly, according to Wesleyan University, which says campaigns and political action committees have already spent more than $137 million on AI ads this year.

The concern is that North Carolina does not currently require political ads to disclose AI use. The National Conference of State Legislatures says 31 states regulate deepfakes in political messages, and North Carolina is not among them. The NRCC did not say why it did not disclose AI in the ad. Ager's campaign manager, Grayson Barnette, called the ads fake and insulting to voters, and said Ager is running against a corrupt system. The committee has said it stands by the ad and argues it raises issues voters need answered.

A September survey by Catawba College and YouGov, with 1,200 respondents and a margin of error of 3.6 percentage points, found that 68% of Americans are very or somewhat concerned about AI's use in this year's midterms. Political science professor Michael Bitzer of Catawba College said AI raises doubts about whether voters can trust information in campaigns. The survey also found that 52% of respondents feel confident distinguishing real political content from AI-generated content, while 39% do not. Bitzer said AI can twist facts, present things out of context, and mimic people's voices. The article does not say whether the drag queen's cease-and-desist letter has produced any response or whether the ad has been removed.

Articles.Title: AI political ads increasing, no N.C. laws require disclosure

stories.Headline: Anthropic's S-1 shows a governance structure that suits a fun quirky little mission-driven worker cooperative that needs to raise billions as a public company (Matt Levine/Bloomberg)
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company, filed a registration statement on Form S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on October 26, 2026, paving the way for an initial public offering on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT. The number of Class A shares to be offered and the price range had not yet been set when the filing was made public. The filing, which runs to roughly 240,000 words according to one account, reported revenue of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, compared with $1.2 billion in the same period of 2025. It also reported a net loss of $80.7 billion for the half, up from $13 billion a year earlier, while the operating loss was far smaller at about $693 million.

Much of that net loss, commentators said, came from a $72.4 billion fair value adjustment tied to convertible notes, derivative liabilities and SAFEs, which rose as the company's valuation increased. Other figures drawn from the filing include quarterly revenue of $4.7 billion in the first quarter of 2026 and $11.6 billion in the second, along with net revenue retention of about 900 percent. The company also said it had raised $141.1 billion in capital in total and held $112.4 billion in cash and equivalents and $19.3 billion in short-term investments as of June 30, 2026. Commentators also noted that Anthropic reported positive operating cash flow for the first half and gross margins of 85 percent for that period.

The filing was made by Anthropic, PBC, and the company itself posted about the filing on its X account, noting that the registration statement had not yet become effective and that the securities could not be sold until it did. Goldman Sachs was reported to be the lead left underwriter on the offering, according to a post by Bloomberg reporter Deirdre Bosa. Matt Levine, writing for Bloomberg, argued that the governance structure disclosed in the filing resembles that of a small, mission-driven worker cooperative, even though the company must now raise billions of dollars as a public company. Commentators on the filing also questioned how the company would treat its founders' pledges to donate most of their stock, and some raised concerns about the lockup period for shareholders.

The filing comes as the AI industry competes for capital and as the company faces scrutiny over its losses and its spending on data centers, a movement the Wall Street Journal reported Anthropic had cited as a problem. Coverage from the Financial Times and others described the prospectus as lengthy and full of risk factors. The articles do not say when the offering price will be set or when shares will begin trading, and they do not give a firm date for the listing. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Anthropic's S-1 shows a governance structure that suits a fun quirky little mission-driven worker cooperative that needs to raise billions as a public company (Matt Levine/Bloomberg)

stories.Headline: NY Courts Issue AI Guide for Attorneys, Stressing Verification of Court Filings
stories.Summary:
New York court administrators have issued a seven-page guide for attorneys who use generative artificial intelligence to prepare court papers, according to Law.com reporting published on October 27, 2026. The guide expands on a statewide rule adopted earlier this year. It is meant to help lawyers navigate the risks of AI tools in litigation. The articles do not give further detail on how the guide was circulated. The guide focuses on the problem of AI hallucinations, which are inaccurate or invented content produced by these tools.

It offers practical steps for checking the accuracy of AI-assisted material before it is filed. It also reminds lawyers of their continuing professional obligations when they rely on such tools. The earlier rule places responsibility for verifying AI-assisted filings squarely on the attorney who signs them. New York Chief Administrative Judge Joseph Zayas is pictured in the article alongside the report. The articles attribute the guidance to New York court administrators, and they do not provide direct quotations from Zayas about the document.

The reporting centers on the court system's position that lawyers, not the software, remain answerable for what is filed. The guidance is part of a broader effort by courts to set boundaries for AI use in legal practice. The articles do not say whether the guide carries penalties, nor do they describe any scheduled follow-up or revisions. Readers should consult the court system's published materials for the full text.

Articles.Title: NY Courts Issue AI Guide for Attorneys, Stressing Verification of Court Filings - Law.com

stories.Headline: Delaware’s AI-Run Company Proposal Draws the Eye of Congress (2)
stories.Summary:
Rep. James Comer, the Kentucky Republican who chairs the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has asked Delaware Gov. Matt Meyer for documents about the state's plan to test autonomous, AI-managed companies. The letter, sent on a Monday in late October 2026, asks for materials by November 9. Comer's office referred to the new entity by its earlier name, "AI company," though the proposal now calls it an "agent-managed company." Such an entity would have legal personhood like a corporation, and the request covers all documents and communications about the plan since January 1, 2025, including internal AI chat logs.

The state's proposal would create a regulatory sandbox for testing the structure, with liability limits for parent companies and investors. A committee of state officials, lawyers, and technology experts would decide case by case which businesses are admitted and would set capitalization requirements meant to cover their potential liability. The initiative is slated to roll out as soon as next year. Comer's letter says federal lawmakers are weighing ways to appropriately limit state AI regulatory efforts, and it voices concern that the plan could shield powerful AI companies and their investors from responsibility for harmful actions. Critics have long argued the idea offers no advantage over existing corporate governance beyond a liability shield.

Comer's letter also points to Delaware's partners on the project, the tech startup Norm Ai and the principal drafter of the legislation, a partner at Richards, Layton & Finger, the state's largest law firm. He said his committee is worried about non-transparent forces seeking anticompetitive regulatory capture behind state AI initiatives. The law firm responded that its lawyers have long helped keep Delaware's corporate laws current through a deliberative process in which the General Assembly weighs their expertise. Meyer's office said it is reviewing the letter, and a spokesperson for Delaware Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez, who is leading the rollout, had no immediate comment. Norm Ai did not respond to a request for comment.

Reactions among experts are divided. University of Alabama law professor Yonathan Arbel called Comer's concern worrisome, arguing the proposal would actually make investors and corporate parents easier to hold responsible than current entities. York University law professor Martin Petrin said the request seems quite broad but suggested a federal framework could help address safety concerns and avoid a race to the bottom among states, since other states are likely to adopt similar proposals. The letter arrives amid heightened public attention to AI risks ahead of the midterm elections, and on the same day AI company Anthropic filed for what could be the largest initial public offering in stock market history.

Articles.Title: Delaware’s AI-Run Company Proposal Draws the Eye of Congress (2) - Bloomberg Law News

stories.Headline: Singapore factory output growth slows to 3.4% in September despite AI-driven demand
stories.Summary:
Singapore's manufacturing output grew by 3.4% year on year in September, a sharp slowdown from the 15.4% expansion recorded in August, according to data released by the Economic Development Board on October 26, 2026. The figure fell well short of the 7.1% forecast by economists in a Bloomberg poll. The slowdown came as electronics growth moderated and pharmaceutical production contracted sharply, though excluding biomedical manufacturing, output rose 9%. Analysts said the weaker September figure partly reflected a low comparison base in August 2025, which had made August 2026 look unusually strong.

Growth was still supported by demand for artificial intelligence-related products. Precision engineering output rose 31%, led by a 34.8% increase in semiconductor equipment within machinery and systems, while the electronics cluster grew 5.7%, with infocommunications and consumer electronics up 29% and computer peripherals and data storage up 21.3%. Semiconductor output, however, slowed to 1.9% growth from 25.9% in August. Biomedical manufacturing fell 32.8%, driven by a 65.9% drop in pharmaceuticals, while chemicals declined 4.6%, with petrochemicals down 24.3%. Transport engineering grew 10.6%, and the aerospace segment rose 16.3%.

DBS Bank senior economist Chua Han Teng said AI-related manufacturing should remain resilient despite a higher comparison base in the fourth quarter of 2026. He cautioned that growth across the sector is likely to stay uneven, with rising energy and production costs and supply chain disruptions posing risks. He said the volatility in semiconductor output warrants monitoring but remained positive about sustained AI-driven demand. Standard Chartered senior economist Jonathan Koh said strong electronics orders point to robust AI demand and investment, noting that new orders relative to finished goods inventories reached a nine-year high in September.

Koh also flagged rising financial vulnerabilities among hyperscalers as a key risk to growth into 2027. Chua said challenges for petrochemicals would persist amid the unresolved Middle East conflict, as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz continues to disrupt feedstock supplies. The article indicates that the third-quarter 2026 factory output growth is estimated at 8.5%, exceeding the government's 7.5% forecast implied by advance GDP estimates. Beyond these estimates, the report offers no further guidance on the outlook.

Articles.Title: Singapore factory output growth slows to 3.4% in September despite AI-driven demand

stories.Headline: AI, Big Tech Regulation Emerges as Selling Point in AG Campaigns
stories.Summary:
Campaigns for state attorney general are spending nearly $200 million this cycle, and the office is increasingly used to take on Big Tech and AI companies. Bloomberg Law found that about half of the races include ads from incumbents or challengers promising to fight tech firms, based on an analysis of spending compiled by AdImpact. Lawyers quoted in the reporting say the job has grown from consumer scam cases into challenges against the largest tech companies. Eight current attorneys general are seeking higher office, and a dozen current governors once held the same post.

Many candidates are campaigning on the roughly $18 billion settlement Meta reached in August with 48 states over claims that Facebook and Instagram were designed to addict children. Ads from Connecticut's William Tong and Idaho's Raul Labrador highlight their own actions against tech companies. Incumbents in at least nine other states, including Alabama, Arizona, Illinois, and New York, are running similar ads. Candidates also point to actions against Roblox and TikTok, and Florida's James Uthmeier is campaigning on his opposition to OpenAI after a school shooter allegedly used ChatGPT to plan an attack at Florida State University in 2025. Florida has asked a court to act as a clearinghouse for frontier AI models, and a bipartisan group of attorneys general sued to block OpenAI from using recursive self-improvement techniques.

Lawyers say the attention reflects a gap in federal action, since Congress has done little and President Donald Trump has shown little interest. State lawmakers enacted more than 500 AI-related bills in the last two years, according to a National Conference of State Legislatures analysis. Christopher Allen of Cozen O'Connor said states that missed their chance to regulate online search and marketplaces are now acting on social media and AI. Louis Jacobson, who has tracked these races for two decades, sees the anti-tech message as a way to appeal to voters worried about costs. He noted that the Republican Attorneys General Association pledged $7 million across 13 states and the Democratic Attorneys General Association pledged $5 million for Florida and $2 million for Georgia.

Lauren M. Weinstein of O'Melveny & Myers expects states to bring more privacy, consumer protection, and antitrust cases against tech firms in 2027. She said state antitrust enforcement may rival federal enforcement within a few years, citing expanded state laws, new merger review regimes, and an exodus of talent from federal agencies. She also said state regulators need not base decisions on economics alone and can pursue cases they consider important. In her words, when you have a hammer, you go find nails. Companies in the technology sector are advised to prepare for more confrontation with the new group of attorneys general.
