stories.Headline: The long bill for cheap software and AI apps
stories.Summary:
A commentary in The Business Times, published on October 27, 2026, argues that choosing which software applications to keep, improve or close deserves the same management attention as approving new ones. The writer, who ran an IT department at a previous company, recalls a colleague who built more than 200 applications on a low-code platform before moving to another unit. The applications stored private employee data in several locations without any record of where it lived, and many performed overlapping functions, so the writer's team had to untangle the duplication and clean up the data. The piece says AI now makes it even easier to build software, and it points to a security firm's 2026 tests in which about 44 per cent of AI code-generation tasks introduced a security flaw.

The writer says that building an application is only the start of a long commitment, and that the work of maintaining it is easy to underestimate. A sales team's renewal tracker, for example, may be built in an afternoon, yet it can later clash with a finance report over what counts as a renewal, need changes when pricing or currency rules shift, and require checks for security after every revision. Gartner first used the term "citizen developer" in 2009, and its September 2026 guidance on AI citizen development, the writer notes, still stresses ownership and support after launch. The article argues that the business team that benefits from an application should help direct and fund its future, and that each application needs an owner with time and resources, plus a record of where its data is stored and who can access it.

The writer places the responsibility on business owners and IT departments together, with IT working out how to change a system and business staff explaining what the change should do, and does not describe any particular legal or regulatory requirement. The writer suggests testing whether an application actually improves colleagues' working week, since saving minutes on data entry can add hours of reconciliation elsewhere. The piece also recommends planning for retirement, including moving needed records and removing what is no longer used. The writer concludes that, as building gets cheaper, more attention will need to go to deciding what should stay, and that the real cost of an application lies in the years of decisions that follow its creation.

Articles.Title: The long bill for cheap software and AI apps

stories.Headline: Latham & Watkins Lends Lawyer Funds Expertise for Harvey AI Tool
stories.Summary:
Latham & Watkins has agreed to work with the legal AI startup Harvey to design an artificial intelligence tool aimed at private funds work. The plan was announced on a Tuesday, and the article is dated October 27, 2026. The tool is meant for Latham lawyers handling limited partnership agreements, side letters, subscription documents and comment memos. The arrangement deepens an existing relationship between the firm and Harvey.

Harvey plans to sell the technology to other law firms, but Latham will not receive any share of that revenue. According to the article, the firm's benefit lies in using the tool for its own clients and in having a say in how the technology develops. The article's text is cut off at that point, so further details of the terms are not available. Nothing in the available text gives figures for the deal's cost or timeline. The piece offers only the broad outline of the partnership.

The announcement came from the two companies, and the article reports the plan as a joint effort in which Latham helps shape the product. Harvey is the party that will commercialize the tool for the wider legal market. The article does not include direct statements from either company beyond what is summarized. Its wider context and any next steps beyond the announced design work are not described in the material provided.

Articles.Title: Latham & Watkins Lends Lawyer Funds Expertise for Harvey AI Tool

stories.Headline: AI Governance Is Not a Checkbox: Five Practical Lessons for Organizations
stories.Summary:
The article is a Law.com opinion piece by Christine Chasse of Spencer Fane, published October 27, 2026, arguing that responsible use of artificial intelligence is an ongoing risk-management discipline rather than a one-time technology decision. It notes that AI is already embedded in everyday business work, from email and research to clinical decision support, and that adoption often outpaces governance. The piece frames governance as requiring visibility, accountability, testing, and documented oversight. The excerpt available here cuts off before the five lessons are laid out, so the specific steps and their details are not available from this text.

The central point is that governance cannot be treated as a box to tick once. Organizations that deploy AI tools need to know where those tools are being used, assign clear responsibility for their outcomes, test them before and during use, and keep records showing that someone is overseeing them. The article presents these as continuing obligations, not a single compliance event. Because the full text is behind a subscription wall, the article does not specify timelines, thresholds, or named regulatory requirements in the portion visible here.

The author is Christine Chasse, identified in the byline as a lawyer at Spencer Fane. The article's stated view is that adoption tends to run ahead of governance, and that closing that gap takes sustained discipline. The related coverage listed alongside it includes a piece on smaller, sovereign AI for law firms and a report that the Fifth Circuit reassigned a case after a judge relied on AI to draft a ruling containing errors, which illustrates the risks the governance argument addresses. The visible text does not say what further steps the author recommends beyond the general principles above.

Articles.Title: AI Governance Is Not a Checkbox: Five Practical Lessons for Organizations

stories.Headline: Stacy Garrity talks AI, skill games and measles in Pennsylvania's governor race
stories.Summary:
Republican Pennsylvania Treasurer Stacy Garrity sat down with KDKA-TV reporter Josh Taylor ahead of the November 3 election for governor. In an interview published October 27, 2026, she answered questions for about 30 minutes about artificial intelligence, skill games, affordability, federal cuts to SNAP and Medicaid, and a measles outbreak in the state. The interview covered her campaign against incumbent Democrat Josh Shapiro. It also included a discussion of a political ad about Shapiro that was made with AI.

Garrity defended the AI-generated ad, saying its content was accurate and that the ad states up front that it was made with AI. When asked whether it was ironic to use AI in an ad given growing criticism of the technology, she pointed to Shapiro's campaign finances, saying he had received $5.7 million from data center developers and used that money to run ads against her. She also said Shapiro's ads against her were false. On skill games, she criticized the state for letting an October 13 deadline pass without a resolution, which forced American Legion posts, VFW halls, fire halls, gas stations, convenience stores and some pharmacies to remove the machines.

Garrity said the games supported thousands of jobs and returned millions of dollars to local communities, and she argued that a real leader would have acted before the deadline. On federal cuts to SNAP and Medicaid, she said the state should lower its error rate so taxpayers pay less, and she said that benefits should go to pregnant mothers, single parents, caretakers and people with disabilities. On measles, the Pennsylvania Department of Health has reported nearly 1,300 cases along with the state's first measles-related deaths in years. Garrity said Shapiro ran to a camera before he had the facts, and she said a leader should first console families and then gather facts and be transparent.

KDKA invited Shapiro to sit for a one-on-one interview before Election Day, but according to the report he has not accepted. The article does not indicate any response from Shapiro's campaign to Garrity's specific criticisms. The report notes that the interview was part of local coverage of Pennsylvania's gubernatorial race. It does not describe further steps in the race beyond the November 3 election date.

Articles.Title: Stacy Garrity talks AI, skill games and measles in Pennsylvania's governor race

stories.Headline: Reed Union schools to develop age-based framework for screens, AI
stories.Summary:
The Reed Union School District board used its first look at a districtwide technology plan to ask whether students from preschool through eighth grade spend too much time on screens. The discussion came four months after the board approved the district's first artificial intelligence policy. Jonathan Weller, the district's director of information systems, educational technology and innovation, told the board on Oct. 13 that a framework setting age-appropriate limits on devices and AI will return to the board in February. Board members raised their concerns during an update on curriculum pilots. They questioned how much learning should rely on technology in the classroom.

Board member Mike Ghaffary said classrooms should use real textbooks and paper and pencil whenever possible. He said the whole world had overrelied on technology. Ghaffary argued it would be hypocritical for parents, teachers and the board to warn students about device addiction outside school while requiring devices in class and for homework at night. His remarks gave the screen discussion its sharpest edge. The article does not record any formal vote on the framework at that meeting.

The Ark reported the story in its Oct. 27 coverage, and the article is written as a single report of the board discussion. The district's plan, as described, will be presented in February and will set limits by age on devices and AI use. The article does not say what those limits will be, how they will be enforced, or whether they will apply to every grade level in the same way. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Reed Union schools to develop age-based framework for screens, AI - The Ark newspaper

stories.Headline: Pa. law doesn't regulate AI-generated candidates in election ads, but some hope to change that
stories.Summary:
A recent campaign ad in Pennsylvania has renewed questions about whether artificial intelligence deepfakes are legal in political advertising. Republican gubernatorial challenger Stacy Garrity's campaign released an AI-generated video depicting her Democratic opponent, incumbent Governor Josh Shapiro, as the midterm elections approached less than a week away. The ad opens with a figure resembling Shapiro in the governor's office, and the synthetic Shapiro refers to sexual harassment scandals before pointing to a real New York Times headline. The video contains no watermark or on-screen text disclosing its artificial origin, and the fake Shapiro does not reveal that he is not the real candidate until about 45 seconds in. Near the end, the synthetic figure says the ad was created with AI, crediting "big beautiful data centers."

A spokesperson for the real Shapiro called the ad "cheap" and "dishonest" in a statement to Axios. Garrity told KDKA-TV that she stands by the ad. Under current Pennsylvania law, there is no prohibition on deepfakes in political ads and no requirement for a disclaimer. State Sen. Lisa Boscola announced in May that she planned to introduce legislation barring AI-generated or AI-altered video, audio or images of a candidate during the 90 days before an election, but that bill had not yet been introduced. A separate bill to regulate deepfakes in campaign ads passed the state House last year but did not clear the state Senate.

The reporting places the issue in a broader regional context, noting that several neighboring states, including Delaware, Maryland and New York, have laws that either prohibit election deepfakes or require a disclosure that content is AI-generated. Pennsylvania, by contrast, currently has neither. The article does not say whether Boscola's proposal or any other measure will advance before the election. It also does not indicate what penalties, if any, the Garrity ad could face under existing law.

Articles.Title: Pa. law doesn't regulate AI-generated candidates in election ads, but some hope to change that

stories.Headline: Oakley planners approve A.I. data center ban
stories.Summary:
On October 20, the Oakley Planning Commission voted 4-0 with one abstention to recommend that the City Council approve a total ban on data centers. Commissioner Adam Sterud abstained, and the commission also approved several other projects at the same busy meeting. The City Council will make the final decision at a later meeting. The ban would cover both artificial intelligence and non-AI data centers, though small auxiliary server rooms used by businesses would be exempt. Community Development Director Ken Strelo said data centers have grown rapidly amid rising public opposition, and Oakley wanted to act quickly while state and federal rules were still being written.

The City Council passed a 45-day moratorium on April 14 and extended it to one year on May 12. Joint City Council and Planning Commission work sessions were held on July 21 and September 15 to guide staff on drafting the ban ordinance for all zoning districts. Many residents spoke against data centers, though one resident, Jason Lester, argued a ban would cost jobs and let China dominate the field. Lester asked for only a temporary ban, but Commissioner Sean Ireland said a moratorium could last no longer than one year and that a future council could repeal the ban if needed. Also at the meeting, the commission approved the Peixoto Ranch subdivision at 5321 Sellers Avenue, which will divide a 20.1-acre lot into 110 lots along with a stormwater basin, a central park, and a landscaping corridor.

The developer, Meritage Homes, will connect it by road to its Machado subdivision. The commission also approved a General Plan amendment and rezone of 5801 Bridgehead Road to light industrial, which is part of the 164-acre Bridgehead Industrial Project approved by the council in March. An A.I. data center had been a possible use for that space but was withdrawn before approval. The commission gave a design review and conditional use permit 5-0 for a Panda Express and Quick Quack car wash at the southeast corner of Main Street and Neroly Road, one of Oakley's primary gateways. Associate Planner Evan Gorman said the applicant redesigned the project several times at staff's request, adding a stone wall between it and the nearby mobile home park.

Panda Express will operate from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. and Quick Quack from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m., and the operators must control litter and graffiti. The city-owned parcel was once a PG&E maintenance station, and if developed, its sale proceeds would go toward the city's outstanding bond debt and to organizations such as school districts.

Articles.Title: Oakley planners approve A.I. data center ban - thepress.net

stories.Headline: Why boutique law firms can beat the big names in AI search
stories.Summary:
Fewer people are starting their search for a lawyer on Google, and a growing number are asking AI assistants instead. A 2026 study of 1,110 US consumers by legal marketing firm iLawyer Marketing found that use of ChatGPT to research lawyers rose from 28.1% to 41.9% in a year, while Google use fell from 86.7% to 71.9%. Similar shifts appear elsewhere, with JUSTICE finding that around one in six people in the UK with a legal problem had used an AI chatbot, rising to 26% among 18 to 24 year olds. In Australia, the University of Melbourne and KPMG report that half of people now use AI regularly. An AI answer functions much like a referral, naming a few firms and explaining why, so a firm that is absent from that answer is effectively off the list.

The article argues that small and mid-sized firms can compete because AI tools reward clear, specific and consistently verified answers rather than simply the largest marketing budget. It describes three related approaches: SEO to rank in Google, AEO to structure pages so AI tools can quote them, and GEO to build outside proof such as directory listings, reviews and media mentions. Its practical steps include writing pages around specific client questions that name the state or territory, giving every lawyer a verifiable profile, and checking entries in law society directories and Google Business Profiles. It also recommends careful review handling, earning mentions when the law changes, adding structured data, ensuring AI crawlers are not blocked, and testing monthly what the AI assistants say about the firm. BrightLocal's research is cited as showing 45% of consumers use AI tools to find local business recommendations.

The article is written by Tiffany as an expert contribution on Dynamic Business, and it cautions that visibility must never come at the cost of compliance. It cites Rule 36 of the Australian Solicitors' Conduct Rules, which prohibits false, misleading or offensive advertising, along with the Australian Consumer Law and some state-based restrictions in areas such as personal injury. Firms are advised to keep content educational, avoid guarantees about outcomes, and state that general information is not legal advice. The piece concludes that people still want a lawyer they can trust, but the first introduction is increasingly made by an AI assistant summarising what the internet says about a firm.

Articles.Title: Why boutique law firms can beat the big names in AI search

stories.Headline: Charlotte Extends Data Center Moratorium Until 2027: What It Means for Residents, Electricity Costs and AI - Creative Loafing Charlotte
stories.Summary:
On October 26, Charlotte City Council voted unanimously to extend its temporary moratorium on new data center development until October 18, 2027. The pause was first approved in June and covers new applications for telecommunications and data storage facilities in the city and its extraterritorial jurisdiction. Projects approved before the initial restrictions took effect are not automatically shut down. The vote came as the city weighs how such facilities should fit into its future.

The extension gives city officials more time to study electricity demand, water consumption, noise, land use and neighborhood compatibility. Large facilities can require substantial electrical capacity, cooling systems and backup generators, and the articles say the central question is who pays for the infrastructure needed to serve them. Water use depends largely on cooling technology, so the articles suggest that project-specific disclosures would help the city judge expected consumption. Local reporting also cited about 5.5 million square feet of hyperscale development in the pipeline, which raised concern that new rules may not reach every previously approved facility.

Councilmember Renee Johnson raised the issue of that hyperscale pipeline, according to WCCB. City officials, including the task force, are examining the effects on residents and infrastructure while state law may limit how far local zoning can change. The articles note that Charlotte's Unified Development Ordinance has permitted data centers in several employment, commercial and industrial districts. Officials have also pointed to the difference between temporary construction jobs and permanent employment, along with the tax revenue such facilities can generate.

The extension runs until October 18, 2027, unless the city ends it earlier by adopting an acceptable regulatory framework. In the meantime, the articles list open questions, including whether facilities will face setbacks from homes and how economic benefits will be measured. They also ask whether hyperscale campuses will be regulated differently and what protections can apply to projects already approved. The outcome could shape how North Carolina handles the infrastructure demands of artificial intelligence.

Articles.Title: Charlotte Extends Data Center Moratorium Until 2027: What It Means for Residents, Electricity Costs and AI - Creative Loafing Charlotte

stories.Headline: L.A. Film School Escapes Whistleblower Lawsuit as Judge Punishes Lawyer for AI Use
stories.Summary:
A federal judge has dismissed a whistleblower lawsuit against the Los Angeles Film School and fined the claimants' attorney for filing a brief written with ChatGPT. The ruling was issued Friday by Judge Stanley Blumenfeld, who dismissed the suit with prejudice. The judge found that much of the alleged conduct fell outside the six-year statute of limitations. The case was reported by Variety on October 26, 2026.

The two former school executives, Dave Phillips and Ben Chaib, filed a false claims suit in 2024. They alleged the school paid outside vendors to hire its own students for short jobs, inflating its job placement figures. The complaint said the school used those figures to keep its accreditation and its eligibility for federal student loans. The school had paid $1 million in 2020 to resolve a Department of Education audit, but the executives said it had lied to investigators and hidden the full scope of the fraud.

The judge imposed a $5,000 fine on attorney Mark Kleiman for submitting a 76-page brief in April without disclosing that AI wrote it. The brief cited a nonexistent case, and two real cases that did not support the points they were cited for. Phillips later acknowledged he had drafted the brief himself with ChatGPT and given it to Kleiman to review. Kleiman has not responded to a request for comment, and the judge did not sanction Phillips or Chaib because they are not lawyers, though he said they were "not blameless."

The ruling leaves the broader allegations against the school unresolved on their merits, since the court dismissed the case largely on timing and on the poor quality of the opposition brief. The complaint also named CEO James "Bill" Heavener, who owns the school and Full Sail University in Florida, though the judge found no details offered about that second school. Other for-profit colleges have paid multimillion-dollar settlements in similar False Claims Act cases, which let whistleblowers share in recovered funds. The articles do not say whether the claimants plan to appeal.

Articles.Title: L.A. Film School Escapes Whistleblower Lawsuit as Judge Punishes Lawyer for AI Use

stories.Headline: The Bear Hug of Artificial Intelligence: Risks and Responsibilities in Patent Practice—The Israeli Perspective - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
The articles supplied are a single long analysis piece on AI in patent practice, not a news report of a discrete event, so I cannot write a breaking-news story about an event. What the text does carry is a set of legal risks, doctrines and recommendations. I have written it as a feature summary below, with paragraphs of four to five sentences each. The article is cut off partway through its discussion of scenario C, so the summary covers only what appears in the text.

An article published October 27, 2026 by The National Law Review, written by Kfir Luzzatto and Lilach Luzzatto Shukrun of Luzzatto Group, examines how artificial intelligence tools used in patent work create legal risks under Israeli and other patent systems. The authors say AI now handles tasks such as prior-art searching, translation, summarizing technical material and drafting assistance, which saves time but can expose inventions. They focus on confidentiality, public disclosure, novelty, inventive step, sufficiency of disclosure, inventorship and evidence in litigation or opposition. They argue that AI should be treated as a useful but indiscreet assistant, appropriate for administrative work but risky during inventive activity or claim strategy. The piece says it closes with best-practice recommendations for practitioners, though those recommendations fall outside the portion provided.

The authors note that the United States, Europe and Israel all require inventors to be natural persons, a position reinforced by the DABUS decisions in those jurisdictions, so an AI system cannot be named as an inventor. They caution against treating AI as a neutral tool, because some systems may use user inputs for training or may retain abstractions of confidential material that could later appear in outputs for others. The authors also say that users often treat chatbot exchanges as private consultations, which encourages them to share half-formed concepts and claim strategies that they would not disclose to an outside party. This raises possible breaches of confidentiality duties, which in many jurisdictions are broader than privilege. The article adds that providers' contractual assurances may be hard to verify, since it is difficult to prove what was stored, used for training or later produced.

The central doctrinal question, the authors explain, is whether feeding an invention to an AI system could count as making it available to the public under Article 54 of the European Patent Convention, under Section 4 of the Israeli Patent Law, or as prior art under 35 U.S.C. § 102. They note that neither system has yet produced a precedent directly addressing AI chat disclosures, though both already have tools for functional equivalents. Under European practice, a disclosure is public if at least one member of the public could access and understand it without confidentiality obligations, and the mechanism of disclosure does not matter. The authors argue that an AI output given to an unbound user could be treated as a public teaching, and they stress that there is generally no grace period for an inventor's own pre-filing disclosures outside the United States. In the United States, a one-year grace period exists for inventor-derived disclosures, but the authors point out that proving derivation depends on logs that providers may not produce, and that the protection does not extend abroad.

The authors illustrate the risk with three practical scenarios: an inventor asking an AI to assess patentability and draft claims, an engineer asking for a solution to a specific technical bottleneck, and a practitioner asking for improvements to a draft application that contains proprietary details. In each case they say the disclosure could later support a novelty attack, a dispute over obviousness or a challenge to the invention's origin. The article identifies the authors as Israeli patent practitioners at Luzzatto Group, whose stated view is that AI offers efficiency but tightens around the rights it is meant to protect. The text provided ends mid-discussion of the third scenario, so the specific recommendations and any further guidance on what courts or offices are expected to do are not available in the material supplied.

Articles.Title: The Bear Hug of Artificial Intelligence: Risks and Responsibilities in Patent Practice—The Israeli Perspective - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: Intuit Unveils Custom Financial AI Tools for Nonprofits and Manufacturers
stories.Summary:
Intuit announced new and expanded financial intelligence tools for the nonprofit, manufacturing and construction sectors on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, according to a press release the company issued. The new capabilities were added to Intuit Enterprise Suite and QuickBooks Online Advanced. For nonprofits, the update builds fund and grant accounting directly into the platform instead of requiring spreadsheets. For manufacturers, it adds workflows for multi-location inventory and production, including pick-pack-ship and multi-level bills of material, while construction businesses receive deeper industry-specific capabilities.

Intuit described the tools as powered by its Intuit Intelligence platform, which combines AI, machine learning, deterministic code, human expertise and permissioned financial data. The announcement came at the company's Intuit Connect event, where Intuit also introduced several other products. These included Agentic Books Close, which automates more of the monthly close process for accountants, along with Firm Playbooks and portfolio intelligence tools. The company also said a ProPartner program would launch in 2027 to offer training, certifications, rewards and client connections.

Intuit Chairman and CEO Sasan Goodarzi was quoted in the release saying the tools let businesses and accountants manage greater complexity and scale with confidence. He said the company is harnessing AI so that businesses can keep pace with what he called the largest technology disruption in the company's history. In an August earnings call, Goodarzi said 75% of Intuit Enterprise Suite users were using the company's AI agents every month. Intuit first introduced Intuit Intelligence in October 2025, describing it as a system that would unify business data and provide a team of AI agents across financial tasks.

Articles.Title: Intuit Unveils Custom Financial AI Tools for Nonprofits and Manufacturers

stories.Headline: NY court officials release AI guide for lawyers
stories.Summary:
New York state court officials released a seven-page guide for attorneys on using generative artificial intelligence tools when preparing court filings. The document, titled The Risks of Using Artificial Intelligence in Preparing Court Papers: What Every Attorney Should Know, was developed by the Advisory Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts and was reviewed and approved for public distribution by the Unified Court System's judicial leadership. The article was published on October 27, 2026. The release came as courts across the country report a rise in filings containing AI-generated fabrications, such as nonexistent case citations and inaccurate quotations.

The guide explains that generative AI tools predict likely word patterns rather than verify facts, which can produce fabricated cases or misleading legal statements. It says attorneys remain bound by the Rules of Professional Conduct and by 22 NYCRR Part 130, which governs sanctions for frivolous conduct in New York civil litigation, and that AI use does not change those duties. Under the state's approach, attorneys may use AI but must independently verify any AI-generated content. They are not required to disclose AI use when filing or to provide separate certifications beyond the implicit certification made when signing a filing. The guidance urges attorneys to confirm AI-generated citations and quotations through authoritative legal research tools, check AI-generated text for bias or inappropriate content, and document the steps they took to verify material.

Chief Administrative Judge Joseph A. Zayas, who appointed the advisory committee to examine AI's role in the judiciary, said the release reflects the court system's commitment to giving attorneys the tools to adapt to changing technology while upholding professional standards. He said AI tools can improve efficiency but carry risks that call for caution and informed oversight, and that the document reinforces the principle that attorneys remain fully accountable for the accuracy of what they submit. The article notes that the guidance follows a model rule adopted by the court system earlier this year, which requires attorneys using generative AI to understand those tools' capabilities and limits and to independently ensure the accuracy of the information they produce. The committee, made up of judges, attorneys, technologists, scholars and other experts, is also developing an upcoming series of CLE programs titled Artificial Intelligence, Bias, and Equity in Legal Practice, along with policy proposals and model rules. The guide is available from the court system.

Articles.Title: NY court officials release AI guide for lawyers

stories.Headline: Key facts: TSMC (2330) ups CoWoS prices 10–20%; U.S. interposers
stories.Summary:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, listed as TSMC (2330), has reportedly planned a price increase of 10% to 20% for its CoWoS advanced packaging service. The move follows strong demand for artificial intelligence chips and limited available capacity. The reporting gives the date as October 28, 2026. The same reporting also says GlobalFoundries will produce silicon interposers in the United States for TSMC's CoWoS packaging. The articles say TSMC expects CoWoS output to exceed 130,000 units per month in 2026 and reach about 200,000 units in 2027.

Nvidia, AMD, and Apple are cited as customers driving that demand. The U.S.-based interposer work would add a domestic supply source for components used in TSMC's advanced packaging. The summaries do not state the exact capacity or cost terms of the GlobalFoundries arrangement. The articles attribute the pricing plan to TSMC and the interposer arrangement to GlobalFoundries and TSMC. They do not include direct statements from company executives about either decision.

The available text is a short automated summary that draws on two sources and carries a disclaimer urging readers to verify details with original reporting. The context is a tight market for advanced chip packaging, where AI-related orders are pushing demand above available supply. The articles do not say how the price increase will be implemented or when customers will face it. They also do not describe further steps in the interposer plan or any response from the named chip designers.

Articles.Title: Key facts: TSMC (2330) ups CoWoS prices 10–20%; U.S. interposers - TradingView

stories.Headline: Elvis Presley AI Lawsuit, Neil Young Trump Case, Drake Spotify Ruling & More Music Law News
stories.Summary:
The owners of Elvis Presley's music sued the AI company Anthropic last week, accusing it of training its models on hundreds of the rock legend's songs without permission. The case, filed in federal court, claims the company used "Can't Help Falling in Love," "A Little Less Conversation," "Don't Be Cruel" and more than 270 other Elvis tracks. Billboard describes it as the most high-profile legal action an individual musician has filed over AI so far. The article's author, Bill Donahue, frames it as part of a broader industry fight over artificial intelligence that has been running for years. Days before the Elvis suit, Reservoir had filed its own cases against Anthropic and Suno over AI training on music by Madonna, Johnny Cash and Joni Mitchell.

The Elvis complaint centers on the claim that Anthropic trained its models on the songs without authorization, and the article links to the full filing for readers who want the details. The article does not say what remedies the plaintiffs are seeking or how the court is likely to rule. Billboard's newsletter also covered several other music law stories that week. Neil Young sued President Trump again for playing "Rockin' in the Free World" at rallies, telling a federal judge the song is "the opposite of everything that Donald J. Trump stands for."

A federal judge also dismissed a class action that claimed Spotify allowed billions of fake bot streams of Drake and other artists. The articles identify the parties making these claims, including the owners of Elvis's catalog and Reservoir, but they do not quote representatives of Anthropic responding to the Elvis suit. Neil Young's position in his case is paraphrased from his filing as opposition to the president's use of his song. The Spotify ruling was described as a dismissal that ended the class action for good, with no further details on the plaintiffs' arguments.

Other items in the newsletter, such as the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders suit against My Chemical Romance and the Stevie Wonder eviction case, were reported without further developments. The Elvis case is at an early stage, and the articles do not indicate a schedule for filings or a trial. Billboard says modern music stars may take similar legal action over AI, though no specific artists are named as doing so. The newsletter itself is a weekly roundup, and the article notes that more cases are being tracked as they develop.

Articles.Title: Elvis Presley AI Lawsuit, Neil Young Trump Case, Drake Spotify Ruling & More Music Law News

stories.Headline: The dark side of AI regulation is unrestrained government control
stories.Summary:
The Hill published an opinion piece on October 27, 2026, by economists Georgy Egorov and Konstantin Sonin, arguing that the push to regulate artificial intelligence carries its own dangers. The article notes that fear of AI is spreading and that momentum is building in the United States for a regulatory framework that would slow progress at the technological frontier. Industry leaders, according to the authors, sound open to slowing down. The authors say the central problem is that any effective regulation of this kind would create risks of its own.

The authors separate two kinds of rules. Specific uses of AI, such as fraud, privacy violations, copyright infringement, and liability for damages, can be regulated in the ordinary way. The harder case is regulation that tries to halt private firms from developing capabilities that officials consider too dangerous. Enforcing such a slowdown, they argue, would demand an unusually intrusive government with broad access to companies' research, computing resources, training runs, data centers, and internal evaluations. Because frontier AI changes quickly, that monitoring would have to be continuous and would reach into what firms were planning, not just what they had built.

Egorov and Sonin contend that firms would have strong incentives to evade such rules, since AI promises large profits and even a short-lived technological lead could be very valuable. Unlike a factory that cannot hide a new plant or a bank that cannot secretly double in size, a company could keep an AI advantage out of sight while gaining lower costs or better products. They warn that a regulatory agency capable of watching the frontier would need rare expertise and access to valuable commercial information, creating large conflicts of interest and openings for capture and corruption. They also point to the historical record, noting that many authoritarian states justified their power by promising to control risks.

The authors further argue that an American slowdown would make little sense if rival powers kept racing ahead, and they doubt that arms control treaties could work well here. Cold War agreements limited weapons that could be physically observed, while AI progress is far harder to monitor, and they question whether China would accept comparable American oversight of its technology. That leaves Washington with a dilemma: follow rules its competitors might ignore, or drop its own once it suspects cheating. The authors conclude that AI safety debates should ask not only how much power private companies hold but also how much power society is prepared to grant the government that would police them.

Articles.Title: The dark side of AI regulation is unrestrained government control

stories.Headline: Republican candidate defends AI-generated ad targeting Iowa governor rival
stories.Summary:
Republican Iowa gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn released an advertisement featuring an AI-generated likeness of his opponent, Democrat Rob Sand, according to a report by KCCI published October 26, 2026. The ad includes the line "He was a European model for real" and says Sand called himself extremely liberal in college. Some voters reportedly saw what appeared to be Sand, though the figure was an artificial likeness created with AI. The ad carries a disclaimer in its bottom right-hand corner telling viewers that it contains AI-generated content.

Lahn has said he stands by the ad and defended its accuracy, pointing to the disclaimer as proof he disclosed the use of AI. He argued that the central question is whether the ad's content is true, and said the content is accurate regarding positions Sand has supported, including on transgender books and classrooms and gun control. Lahn's position is that the substance of the claims, rather than the method of presentation, should determine whether the ad is fair. The reporting makes clear that this is his stated defense and does not independently verify the claims in the ad.

Sand's campaign responded sharply to the advertisement. In a statement, the campaign said Lahn was using AI to try to trick Iowans into believing Sand is someone he is not, and it predicted the tactic would fail. The campaign's response frames the ad as a deception rather than a legitimate comparison of records. The exchange places the disputed ad at the center of the race's closing stretch, with each side presenting the other as misleading voters.

Articles.Title: Republican candidate defends AI-generated ad targeting Iowa governor rival

stories.Headline: Anne Arundel schools superintendent seeks community input on AI policy and electronic devices ban plan
stories.Summary:
Anne Arundel County Public Schools Superintendent Mark Bedell has started gathering community feedback on a proposed ban on electronic devices during the school day and on how artificial intelligence should be used in schools. The first public session took place on a Tuesday, and Bedell began hosting Community Connection Sessions at high schools across the county to hear from teachers, parents and community members. The county school board has introduced a new policy to set parameters for AI use and is also considering a ban on cell phones, smart watches and other electronic devices during the school day. Both issues have drawn considerable discussion in the community. Bedell said he wants people to feel they have a voice before decisions are made, noting that residents have complained in the past that they learned about policies only at board meetings.

At the first session, parents and residents were split into small groups to share their views on AI in schools, a subject on which opinions run strongly on both sides. Bedell said he wanted to meet people face to face to hear their thoughts directly. He also said he wants students to become skilled users of AI rather than being used by it, and that the conversations would help the district balance traditional instruction with preparing students for a future that involves the technology. Bedell described the proposed device restrictions as a matter of how class time is used. He said students spend only about 19.3 percent of the week in school, and he wants that time devoted to teaching and learning and collaboration, while the state law the district must follow leaves the remaining time for students to decide how they use their technology.

The personal electronics ban would begin next school year, and the small groups discussed what that would look like in practice. Bedell urged parents and community members to attend so the district understands the expectations for educating students. The remaining sessions are scheduled for 6 to 8 p.m. on the following dates: Monday, November 2, at Glen Burnie High School; Thursday, November 5, at Northeast High School; Tuesday, November 10, at Arundel High School; Thursday, November 12, at Southern High School; Tuesday, November 17, at Annapolis High School; and Thursday, November 19, at Meade High School. The article does not say what decisions will follow the feedback process or when the board will vote on the AI policy.

Articles.Title: Anne Arundel schools superintendent seeks community input on AI policy and electronic devices ban plan - WMAR 2 News

stories.Headline: Duolingo slapped with class-action lawsuit alleging AI efforts, relentless ads hurt user growth
stories.Summary:
A class-action securities fraud lawsuit was filed earlier this month against Duolingo, the language-learning app, in US District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania by the law firm Levi & Korsinsky, LLP. The suit covers investors who bought Duolingo shares between May 2, 2025, and Feb. 26, 2026, and those investors are eligible to file as claimants. It accuses the company's executives of hiding from investors how aggressively they were pushing paid subscriptions and of rolling out low-quality AI features that they allegedly knew would frustrate customers. The Post reported the lawsuit on October 27, 2026.

The complaint says free users were forced to watch unskippable ads after each lesson, with some spending as much or more time on ads than on lessons. It also says Duolingo replaced its old Hearts system with an Energy system that drains energy on every answer, right or wrong, so that users can refill it by watching more ads, waiting until the next day, or paying for a premium tier. According to the suit, the real goal was to create friction that would push free users into subscribing. The lawsuit names no specific individuals as defendants in the portion summarized here, and it describes executives' statements to investors rather than any formal findings.

The suit says CEO Luis von Ahn told investors that the company's main focus was boosting user engagement and that it would smooth out sources of frustration, while calling daily active user growth probably the most important metric in the company. The lawsuit accuses executives of misleading investors on these points, and it says the company described its AI features as improving quality rather than cutting costs. The complaint also points to a drop in daily active user growth to 36 percent in November 2025, followed by a preliminary figure of 30 percent in January 2026 and a February report confirming the slowdown would continue through 2026. Duolingo did not immediately respond to The Post's request for comment, so the company's position is not yet known.

Duolingo was founded in 2011 at Carnegie Mellon University by von Ahn and a graduate student, and it teaches more than 40 languages along with subjects such as math and chess. Its paid tiers, Super and Max, cost roughly $12.99 and $30 a month, respectively, before annual discounts, and the stock was last trading near $138.60 a share, down more than 20 percent so far this year. The stock fell 25 percent after the November 2025 user growth report and dropped further after the January and February announcements, including the departure of chief financial officer Matthew Skaruppa. Further developments in the case were not described in the articles.

Articles.Title: Duolingo slapped with class-action lawsuit alleging AI efforts, relentless ads hurt user growth

stories.Headline: The Outlook for the Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Predictive Toxicology Market Strengthens as Global Demand Increases - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
The article is a market-research press release, not a breaking news story, so it does not describe a single event with a clear actor, date and consequence. It reports a forecast from The Business Research Company, published by EINPresswire on October 26 and 27, 2026, that the market for artificial intelligence in predictive toxicology will grow rapidly. The release says the market is expected to exceed $2 billion by 2030, roughly 21 percent of an AI-in-pharma sector projected at about $11 billion that year. It also projects a compound annual growth rate of 29 percent through 2030.

The release breaks the forecast down by region and by country. Asia-Pacific is projected to reach about $0.80 billion in 2030, up from $0.18 billion in 2025, at a growth rate of 34 percent a year. The United States is expected to hold the largest national share, at about $0.69 billion in 2030, up from $0.22 billion in 2025, growing 26 percent a year. The solutions segment is expected to account for 63 percent of the market, or about $1 billion in 2030. The release also names Certara Inc. as the leading company in 2025, with a 4 percent share, and says the top 10 firms held 23 percent of revenue that year.

The release attributes the expected growth to several drivers: pharmaceutical firms' demand for faster drug discovery, the growing availability of toxicological, genomic and clinical data, and public concern about reducing animal testing and meeting regulatory standards. It estimates these drivers would add about 1.3, 1.0 and 0.8 percentage points of annual growth, respectively. The forecast is the work of The Business Research Company, which the release presents as the source of its figures. The article describes no regulatory action, no legal requirement and no change in law, and it gives no information about what will happen next beyond the 2030 projections.

Articles.Title: The Outlook for the Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Predictive Toxicology Market Strengthens as Global Demand Increases - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: Long Beach Unified Surveys Families on AI as Parents Push for a Moratorium
stories.Summary:
Long Beach Unified School District has opened a survey asking students and families what they think about artificial intelligence and computer screens in classrooms. The survey opened earlier in October and probes how families feel about the effects of classroom technology on learning, well-being, privacy and attention. It closes on November 6. The move comes as parents and students have spent months pressing the district to rein in classroom technology.

The district may develop new technology policies in response to that public pressure, according to Long Beach Post. Groups pushing for limits argue that heavy technology use harms learning and development while draining the budget. The district says it spent $2.5 million on laptops during the 2025-26 school year and projects another $2.5 million for the current year. A district workgroup will review the survey results once the survey closes. The workgroup will include teachers, students, guardians, administrators and industry experts.

Long Beach parents helped start a local chapter of Schools Beyond Screens, a national group that advocates limiting screen use in classrooms. Kim Tashkin, who helps lead that chapter, said she hopes the district passes an AI moratorium as soon as possible. The district adopted a policy in 2025 to curtail phones and personal devices, but some parents say it did not go far enough. At an October 7 board meeting, students told members that unchecked AI use could leave them unable to think independently.

Student surveys and national research point to widespread AI use. A student campaign survey found that 91% of respondents had used, or seen someone use, AI to cheat on assignments, and 85% had seen or heard about teachers using AI in class. A 2025 RAND study found that 54% of students and 53% of teachers reported using AI for school. Long Beach is not alone, since Los Angeles Unified and New York City Public Schools have both passed AI moratoriums. Spokesperson Eric Mitchell said the workgroup's findings may help shape policy recommendations.

Articles.Title: Long Beach Unified Surveys Families on AI as Parents Push for a Moratorium - Hoodline

stories.Headline: SGA swears in new leadership, advances bills on AI access and addresses procedural efficiency
stories.Summary:
The Johns Hopkins University Student Government Association held its tenth general body meeting of the semester, the first since former Student Body President Jason Yu resigned, and it swore in new leadership and advanced several bills. Sumire Sumi was sworn in as Student Body President by a member of the SGA Judiciary Branch, and Shreemann Patel was then elected Student Body Vice President in a closed session. The meeting opened with a virtual presentation from the Office of International Services about its work supporting international students and faculty. Patel had previously served as Senate Vice President and Chair of the Internal Affairs Committee, and both of those posts are now vacant.

The Senate moved several bills through the first reading stage. Senator Isaac Zhang introduced one bill to create a digital database for student performances, which was referred to the Student Services Committee, and a second on equity in access to artificial intelligence tools, which was referred to the Academic Affairs Committee. Senator Boyi Chen presented a bill on procedural reforms, which was sent to the Internal Affairs Committee. Senator Sophia Baleeiro introduced a bill to create a caucus senator position for LGBTQ+ students, which was also referred to Internal Affairs. The only bill in second reading, from Senator Aishani Garg, concerned an SGA tabling event to raise awareness about the construction of the Data Science and Artificial Intelligence Institute building, and the Senate passed it.

Sumi and Patel delivered cabinet reports in their new roles once the session reopened to the public. Several senators also gave reports, including Mahima Sanghera on a bingo-themed student well-being event and Julia Lee on civic engagement. Committee on Student Organizations Chair Kevin Xu outlined the committee's next initiative, "Spotlight Fridays," which is meant to help students discover student organizations. Patel discussed a survey of SGA members on internal effectiveness, and Senator Noah Sokol described a separate survey on internship opportunities for freshmen. The meeting adjourned soon after the Senate passed the tabling bill.

Articles.Title: SGA swears in new leadership, advances bills on AI access and addresses procedural efficiency - Indiana Daily Student

stories.Headline: AI Image Laws Impacting Apartment Listings
stories.Summary:
Two artificial intelligence disclosure laws, one in California and one in Wisconsin, take effect on Jan. 1, and the California measure was signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom on Sept. 27. The California law requires that any listing photo using altered images be labeled as such and include the original, unaltered image for comparison. Similar proposals have been introduced in Washington, D.C., and have surfaced in New York and New Jersey. The rules follow a surge in AI-altered listing photos, and multifamily owners and brokers are now scrambling to prepare. Industry leaders say they support more transparency about altered photos but warn of new costs, legal exposure and operational strain.

Kevin Donnelly, executive director of the Real Estate Technology & Transformation Center, estimated that "thousands" of apartment communities in California alone would need new photography to comply, and he has heard per-property cost estimates as high as thousands of dollars. He argued that disclosure and false advertising protections should be kept, but that the record production mandate is infeasible as written. Donnelly also pointed to the Multifamily Information Transaction Standards data model, created by the National Multifamily Housing Council, as a way to share updated fee information across platforms. Anthony Paganucci, CEO of Brynson, said understaffed teams and outdated technology make consistent listings hard to maintain. Jonas Bordo, co-founder and CEO of Dwellsy.com, said many listings may go without updates given the cost, and he expects some legal action.

Jay Harris, a partner at Hudson Cook, said many California clients who acquired properties do not have the original images and worry about the cost of reshooting ads. He noted that a single violation under California's law is a misdemeanor, while repeat violations could expose owners and brokers to misrepresentation claims and, in egregious cases, civil and criminal penalties. The California Department of Real Estate's Assistant Commissioner, Christina Jimenez, said the agency takes all violations seriously and is committed to consumer protection. Donnelly has asked for a grace period or safe harbor after Jan. 1 so owners can update their listings. Bordo argued the issue should be self-policing, since landlords who alter photos mainly hurt themselves.

The debate comes as apartment marketing has become more digital, with virtual tours and 3D photography now common, and as about 8% of leasing still happens remotely. California's rules build on a similar law for single-family homes that took effect Jan. 1, 2026, and owners and industry groups have been asking the state for guidance. NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani, announcing an AI imagery proposal at a July event, said renters should not have to wonder whether the apartment they view online is real. Donnelly said the industry is comfortable with greater transparency but needs policymakers to set realistic timelines so it can comply.

Articles.Title: AI Image Laws Impacting Apartment Listings - Bisnow

stories.Summary:
