stories.Headline: How Are Schneider Electric, Nscale and Start Campus Using NVIDIA Digital Twin Technology to Develop AI Data Centers?
stories.Summary:
Emerald AI released results from a pilot run with Nvidia and Nscale at Nscale's data center in Iceland, with the figures shared during Nvidia's GTC event in Berlin in the week of October 23, 2026. According to the companies, Emerald AI's Emerald Conductor platform, working together with Nvidia's DSX power-management technology, cut the power use of the AI server racks by about 25 percent. The reduction was held for 30 minutes before the site returned to normal operations. It was the first time Emerald Conductor had been fully integrated with DSX, which is designed to get as much computing as possible out of every watt of energy. It was also the seventh test Emerald AI has carried out, following three in the US, in Santa Clara, Phoenix and Chicago, and one in the UK with National Grid.

Separately, Schneider Electric said on October 23 that it is launching new prefabricated power modules and power skids. They are based on a reference design developed jointly with Nvidia for its GB300 NVL72 AI server system, and they support power densities of up to 142 kilowatts per rack while integrating power management and liquid cooling controls. The modules use Schneider's Galaxy VXL uninterruptible power supply technology and come in three capacities, 2MW, 2.25MW and 2.5MW. The 2.5MW version is the company's largest single-container prefabricated power solution so far. Prefabrication means the equipment is built and tested at a factory before installation, which shortens construction time and lets operators add capacity module by module.

Varun Sivaram, founder and CEO of Emerald AI, said access to power has become the main constraint on Europe's AI build-out. He argued that the fastest way to ease it is to make AI factories flexible enough to use grid capacity that already exists, which also helps keep energy affordable for local communities. In his view, the pilot shows that AI computing can lower its power use on request, which utilities need to see before they can connect such sites faster. Emerald Conductor acts as a go-between for the grid and data centers, orchestrating AI workloads in real time so that sites can adjust their consumption while keeping compute performance acceptable. Schneider will build its new products at its facility near Barcelona, Spain.

On the wider picture, Emerald AI announced its first commercial project in October, with its software to be deployed at Nvidia's under-construction 96MW Aurora data center in Manassas, Virginia. The company raised a further $150 million in Series A funding in August, and earlier raised $25 million in seed extension funding. It belongs to Nvidia's Inception program for startups and is backed by Google's chief sustainability officer, Kate Brandt. Schneider plans to launch its power modules first in Europe, then in North America later in 2026, before expanding sales to the Asia-Pacific region. A commentary on Nscale put its contracted backlog at $103.4 billion against first-half 2026 revenue of $140.6 million and a net loss of about $1.02 billion, with Anthropic and Microsoft the main customers, and it raised the question of whether the company is overleveraged.

stories.Headline: AI for Lawyers: Avoiding Hallucinations and Preserving Privilege - New York State Bar Association
stories.Summary:
The New York State Bar Association is offering a free webinar titled "AI for Lawyers: Avoiding Hallucinations and Preserving Privilege," scheduled for October 27, 2026, from 3:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m., and it is offered virtually as a webinar. The program covers two areas of concern for lawyers using artificial intelligence: fabricated cases and quotations, often called hallucinations, that have led to sanctions against lawyers and firms in California and New York, and the data-handling questions that arise before client-confidential information is entered into an AI tool. The sessions will be led by three panelists, Marc Lewis of San Francisco, Arlo Devlin-Brown of New York City, and Rhick Bose, head of U.S. operations at Crimson AI, with Nitesh Daryanani moderating.

The program is sponsored by the association's Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies, Committee on Technology and the Legal Profession, and Committee on Continuing Legal Education. It carries 1.0 credit in ethics and professionalism. The first session reviews recent sanctions decisions in both states involving AI-fabricated citations and examines the duties they implicate, including competence, candor toward the tribunal, and supervision. Panelists will compare New York's court rule on AI use with California's AI-focused amendments to its Rules of Professional Conduct, and they will discuss verification workflows for AI-assisted research.

The second session turns to confidentiality and privilege, looking at the obligations that apply when client information goes into an AI tool. It also considers how courts are beginning to address whether AI use affects privilege and work-product protection, and it covers what lawyers should look for in an AI vendor, including training on user data, retention, security, and contractual protections. The closing segment is an audience question-and-answer period followed by remarks from the moderator. The page lists a non-member price of $395.00, while association members may attend for free.

The association is the organizer of the program, and the articles name the panelists and moderator as the people presenting its content. The page itself does not describe any specific sanctioned lawyer or firm by name, and it does not report on any particular court ruling beyond saying that sanctions decisions exist. The page also advertises the association's Annual Conference 2027, with early-bird registration ending November 2. The article does not say what the outcome of any future court decision will be, and it does not indicate whether the regulatory approaches it compares are expected to change.

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania House passes bill requiring AI disclosure in healthcare
stories.Summary:
The Pennsylvania House of Representatives approved House Bill 1925 on September 30, voting 144 to 59 to pass it. The bill sets rules for artificial intelligence in clinical care and in health insurance coverage decisions. Its disclosure rules cover healthcare facilities, and it limits how insurers may rely on AI during utilization review. The amended bill was referred to the Senate Institutional Sustainability and Innovation Committee on October 14 and remains pending in the Senate.

If enacted, the bill would require healthcare facilities, including imaging centers, to disclose their use of AI in clinical decision-making through website postings and written patient notifications. Those notifications would be needed once per episode of care rather than at every encounter. Facilities would also have to review AI system performance at least annually and make sure the technology does not override providers' independent clinical judgment. The bill extends disclosure requirements to certain personalized patient communications generated by AI.

It also covers Medicaid and Children's Health Insurance Program managed care plans, requiring that reviewers examine clinical records, document that review, and form their own judgment before issuing or upholding an adverse coverage determination such as a prior authorization denial. The articles do not name a specific sponsor or identify individual lawmakers who spoke for or against the bill. They report that the legislation is aimed at setting guardrails for AI in healthcare without hindering its development and adoption. The American College of Radiology has described state legislation as an important opportunity for radiologists and state medical societies to advocate for policies that protect patients and preserve physician decision-making.

The organization expects similar proposals addressing clinical AI during 2027 state legislative sessions. The proposed requirements could affect radiology practices that already use or plan to adopt AI in their workflows. The bill now moves to the Pennsylvania Senate, where it awaits action in committee. The articles do not say when the Senate might take it up or whether it will be enacted in its current form.

Articles.Title: Pennsylvania House passes bill requiring AI disclosure in healthcare - Radiology Business

stories.Headline: Weil Launches AI Training Program For Summer Associates
stories.Summary:
Weil Gotshal & Manges LLP has launched an artificial intelligence training program for its first-year summer associates, according to a Law360 report by Jake Maher published October 26, 2026. The firm said the program is meant to cultivate new attorneys experienced in AI. The article is a preview, and the rest of the text sits behind a paywall, so the full details are not available. What the program requires of participants, its length, and any cost or structure are not stated in the portion provided. Readers should treat the account here as limited to the opening summary.

The firm's stated goal is to let summer associates work directly with artificial intelligence tools during their time at the firm. That framing suggests hands-on use rather than classroom study alone, though the article's visible text does not spell out the format. No specific numbers, dates beyond the publication date, or named program participants appear in the material available. Anyone seeking those specifics would need the full Law360 article. Weil Gotshal & Manges is identified as the party behind the initiative, and the firm announced it through its own statement as reported by Law360.

The visible excerpt does not include direct quotations from firm leaders or other individuals. Responsibility for the program's design and rollout therefore rests with the firm as described in the report. The move comes as law firms increasingly look at AI skills in new hires, though the article excerpt does not make that broader trend explicit or cite other firms. stories.Headline: Federal Court Splits On Disclosure Of Expert Witness AI Prompts
stories.Summary:
A federal judge in Nevada has ruled that an expert witness's prompts to a generative AI platform are protected from disclosure, while the AI-generated case summaries the expert consulted must be handed over. The order, issued September 29, 2026 by District Judge Anne R. Traum in Villanueva v. Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department, came in a civil rights case over a plaintiff's detention at the Clark County Detention Center. The plaintiff's expert, Tom Melton, testified at an October 1, 2025 deposition that he had used a generative AI platform to help research and draft his report. The plaintiff had not disclosed that use in response to an earlier subpoena, and afterward refused to produce the platform's 40-page history log.

Magistrate Judge Albregts had first ordered production of the entire log, but Judge Traum held that this order was clearly erroneous or contrary to law and sustained the objection in part. The court relied on the Ninth Circuit's broad reading of "facts or data considered" and required production of the AI-generated case summaries, which the expert used as a quick reference. It held that the prompts are protected because a question is not something an expert can consider as facts or data, and because the prompts would reveal the expert's mental impressions and strategy. The AI-generated deposition outline was also shielded as trial preparation material, and outputs the expert pasted into his report were treated as protected drafts.

The court further ruled that using generative AI does not waive privilege, because the platform is not a person but a research, drafting, and editing tool. The ruling was written by the court, and the law firm Mayer Brown, which reported on it, notes that the decision departs from a June ruling in Conservation Law Foundation v. Shell Oil Company, where Magistrate Judge Thomas Farrish ordered an expert's AI prompts produced as discoverable methodology. The firm says the two decisions may be partly reconciled by how each expert used AI, since in the Conservation Law Foundation case the platform shaped which documents were reviewed.

Mayer Brown also says the courts disagree directly on prompts, with the Nevada court comparing them to online research queries. Experts and counsel are advised to keep AI uses in separate categories and to expect that even protected use may be probed at trial, including the risk of hallucinated citations. The firm reports that the Conservation Law Foundation objection is scheduled for oral argument on November 3, 2026. The law on expert AI discovery remains unsettled, and the outcome will likely depend on the jurisdiction and the facts of each case.

Articles.Title: Federal Court Splits On Disclosure Of Expert Witness AI Prompts - Mondaq

stories.Headline: Drag queen explores legal action over AI-generated Jennifer Balkcom political ad
stories.Summary:
An Asheville drag queen known as Nova is exploring legal action over an AI-generated political attack ad that places her in a scene with Democratic congressional candidate Jamie Ager. The commercial was paid for by the National Republican Congressional Committee and approved by Republican NC-11 candidate Jennifer Balkcom, and the ad shows a barn dance in which Ager appears to dance with what looks like Nova. Nova told News 13 that she was blindsided when she learned her image had been used, and she says she has never met Ager or been to his property. She has sent a cease-and-desist order to Balkcom's campaign demanding the ad be removed. The ad continues to run on television and remains posted on YouTube.

Mike Tadych, a First Amendment attorney and counsel to the North Carolina Press Association, said that if the campaign ignores the cease-and-desist, Nova could have grounds for a misappropriation claim. He said the ad implies she was somewhere she was not, and that a cease-and-desist is only a first warning. If the ad keeps running after the campaign has been told there was no consent, Tadych said, Nova could file for damages and possibly seek an injunction. He also cautioned that political advertising receives strong First Amendment protection and that a court might be reluctant to order the ad taken down, since that could be treated as prior restraint.

Dr. Chris Cooper, chair of the political science department at Western Carolina University, said North Carolina has no law requiring political ads to disclose when artificial intelligence was used to create them, though many other states do. He said the ad may be meant to motivate Republican voters who oppose Ager to turn out. A spokesperson for Ager called the ad "100% fake" and said Balkcom "can't win on the truth." Balkcom's spokesperson had not responded to News 13's request for comment, and the story was published October 26, 2026.

Articles.Title: Drag queen explores legal action over AI-generated Jennifer Balkcom political ad - WLOS

stories.Headline: China's industrial profits rise 15.5% in first nine months of 2026, driven by high-tech manufacturing, AI integration
stories.Summary:
Profits at China's major industrial firms rose 15.5 percent year on year in the first nine months of 2026, according to official data released on Tuesday. Firms with annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan ($2.8 million) reported combined profits of 6.03 trillion yuan from January to September. The National Bureau of Statistics said profits grew 14.4 percent in September alone. Industrial production stayed steady, and cumulative profit growth has remained in double digits this year. The electronics industry was the main driver, with its profits doubling year on year over the period and adding 9.6 percentage points to the overall gain.

Demand for artificial intelligence computing power and advanced memory technologies helped push up earnings, with electronic specialty material manufacturing up 220 percent and semiconductor device manufacturing up 51.7 percent. Optoelectronic component and electronic circuit manufacturing rose 69.8 percent and 62.5 percent. High-tech manufacturing profits jumped 52 percent, accounting for 25.5 percent of total industrial profits, up 6.2 percentage points from a year earlier. Optical fiber and optical cable manufacturing profits surged 570 percent and 110 percent, respectively, as computing infrastructure and data center construction expanded.

Raw materials manufacturing also contributed, with profits climbing 44.9 percent and adding 5.9 percentage points to overall growth. Strong demand for copper, aluminum and other metals from AI and new-energy industries lifted nonferrous metals profits by 79.7 percent. Mining profits rose 38.2 percent and manufacturing profits increased 17 percent across the broader sector. Chen Xi, a researcher at the Academy of Macroeconomic Research under the National Development and Reform Commission, said large-scale equipment upgrades, the integration of AI into manufacturing and tax policy support have helped firms cut costs and improve efficiency.

He also credited China's comprehensive industrial supply chains and quick response to market demand. The National Bureau of Statistics said it will focus on expanding domestic demand, improving supply and accelerating the shift from traditional to new growth drivers. The agency framed these goals as ways to strengthen the economy's internal momentum and advance high-quality industrial development. The articles do not specify further policy measures or timelines beyond these stated aims.

Articles.Title: China's industrial profits rise 15.5% in first nine months of 2026, driven by high-tech manufacturing, AI integration - Global Times

stories.Headline: Hong Kong's urban renewal body to set up HK$100 million 'AI-first' tender assessment subsidiary
stories.Summary:
Hong Kong's Urban Renewal Authority will spend up to HK$100 million to set up a subsidiary that will check tender applications using automated AI systems. The move comes after accusations of corruption linked to the deadly Tai Po fire. The sum is a third of the HK$300 million the government allocated to the authority in its 2026-27 Budget. The funds are meant to reform the authority's Smart Tender scheme.

The Smart Tender system was launched in 2016 to give property owners an electronic platform for recruiting contractors. Its design anonymises the tender process, which is meant to prevent interference and encourage competition. However, the system cannot control who takes part in a tender exercise or who withdraws from one. The new subsidiary would bring in a professional team and build an automated workflow for deeper data verification and analysis. The authority said the approach would be "AI-first".

The authority's managing director is among those who have spoken on the plan, which is described as a direct response to the corruption concerns. According to the article, the director explained that the start-up money will go toward the new unit and its staff. The reporting quotes the director's account of the scope of the work, though the excerpt available is cut short. Further details on who else is accountable were not included in the material provided.

The plan sits within a broader government effort to restore public confidence after the Tai Po fire, which was deadly and which prompted questions about how renewal contracts were awarded. The articles provided do not say when the subsidiary will begin operating or how its performance will be measured. They also do not give a timeline for the wider reform of the Smart Tender scheme. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's Unreleased AI Model Chains Flaws Into Working Chrome, Safari, Windows and Linux Exploits
stories.Summary:
Anthropic said in a research post published on October 28, 2026, that an unreleased internal AI model found security flaws in Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows and Linux and chained them into working proof-of-concept exploits. The company said these were built in its lab after the model was prompted, not drawn from any real attack, and that it reported every flaw to the affected vendor first, so all of them are already patched. One proof of concept opened the Calculator app on a stock Mac running Chrome within seconds of a page loading, with no further clicks. Anthropic's Frontier Red Team described five chains in the post.

The company presents the work as evidence that a single model can now find several separate flaws and combine them into a functioning exploit, a task it says previously required a few specialist teams. Each chain has its own requirements: the Chrome chain runs code outside the browser sandbox after one visit to a page, the Safari chain disables the same-origin policy without running code, the Windows chain is a denial-of-service attack, and the Linux chain runs commands as root over the network when the target runs a multipath TCP listener. Anthropic reported 62 Chrome flaws to Google, all rated critical or high, including 13 sandbox escapes, and says its Linux proof of concept took 48 minutes to leak a kernel address and five more minutes to reach a root shell. The company also points to a kernel use-after-free rated 9.8 that was fixed upstream on October 15.

Google and Apple have both publicly credited Anthropic and its Claude model for specific fixes, and those credits can be checked against vendor release notes. Google's notes credit a named Anthropic researcher, assisted by Claude, for certain Chrome fixes, though not for all 62 flaws. Apple credits two named researchers working with Claude at Anthropic for the Safari fix in iOS and iPadOS 26.5.2. Anthropic says the work needed only "initial prompting" and "little human involvement," but it does not describe what a person did at each step, and it refers to the model only as an unreleased internal research model.

Anthropic frames the publication as support for defenders under a coordinated disclosure policy that gives developers 90 days to patch and 45 more before details beyond a public advisory are discussed. It also points security teams to its Cyber Verification Program, which gives vetted professionals access to Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Mythos 5.1. In its own words, the company said publishing was warranted because models can now do this "with little human involvement" and produce a working exploit "that anyone can run and verify." The articles do not describe any further steps beyond these disclosures and program offerings.

Articles.Title: Anthropic's Unreleased AI Model Chains Flaws Into Working Chrome, Safari, Windows and Linux Exploits

stories.Headline: UNESCO stresses 7 actions against AI-enabled violence in education
stories.Summary:
UNESCO has published a technical brief, titled "Connected and safe," that urges education authorities to tackle online and technology-facilitated violence in schools through policies that link learner protection with the governance of education technology. The brief warns that generative artificial intelligence can make abuse easier to carry out and scale, pointing to sexually explicit deepfakes, image-manipulation tools, voice cloning and automated harassment. It cites research showing that around one in ten learners worldwide has experienced cyberbullying, and notes that images of 1.2 million children across 11 countries were manipulated into sexually explicit deepfakes within a single year. The report was published on 27 October 2026.

The brief sets out seven areas in which education systems can strengthen prevention and response. These cover planning a clear approach to technology-facilitated violence, recognising its effects on learners' safety, inclusion and outcomes, strengthening safeguarding systems and institutional procedures, and building staff capacity to respond to incidents. They also include embedding prevention in curricula and teaching, accounting for safeguarding and well-being when managing digital platforms, content, assessment and learner data, and tracking whether policies are implemented and effective. UNESCO further recommends building safeguards into decisions about buying and using education technology, and says awareness raising and digital literacy should be backed by institutional measures. It cautions against excessive surveillance or blanket restrictions that could undermine learners' rights, inclusion and participation.

UNESCO places responsibility on institutions, technology governance frameworks, learners and school staff, and says incidents often start on digital platforms outside schools' direct control while schools are left to deal with the consequences for learners' safety and well-being. The organisation calls for responses that join online and offline safeguarding and involve stakeholders beyond the education sector. The guidance draws on a UNESCO-led global dialogue held through a three-part webinar series between June and October 2025 and a Global Symposium in Bangkok, Thailand, in November 2025. The article suggests the recommendations could help education authorities account for AI-related risks when selecting and managing digital tools while protecting privacy, inclusivity and students' rights. It does not say what follow-up steps UNESCO or national authorities will take.

Articles.Title: UNESCO stresses 7 actions against AI-enabled violence in education - Digital Watch Observatory

stories.Headline: AI Diversion Theories Emerge as New Securities Lawsuit Risk Zone
stories.Summary:
Securities plaintiffs are filing a new kind of lawsuit tied to artificial intelligence, according to a Fried Frank analysis published by Bloomberg Law on October 28, 2026. Cornerstone counted 15 AI-related securities cases in the first half of 2026, against 16 for all of last year, putting this year on pace for nearly double. The authors describe a growing category of claims that companies concealed how shifting toward AI pulls resources and customers away from their core businesses. They call this the "AI diversion" theory.

The article walks through three recent complaints that illustrate the theory. In In re Microsoft Corporation Securities Litigation, the plaintiff alleges Microsoft diverted computing capacity from its Azure cloud business to Copilot development without telling investors. The complaint says capital expenditures reached $72.4 billion for the first half of fiscal 2026, largely from AI infrastructure and Copilot costs, without producing the expected Copilot subscribers. In Tejada v.

ZoomInfo Technologies, the plaintiff alleges customers shifted spending from ZoomInfo's seat-based software toward in-house AI tools, cutting into core license revenue. In Potter v. monday.com, the complaint says Google's "AI Overviews" and chatbot use reduced clicks to the company's website, eroding its paid search acquisition channel, and that executives described the effect as temporary or minor. The authors say the courts have not yet settled how to handle motions to dismiss these claims.

They point to In re Sprinklr Securities Litigation, where earlier this year the court dismissed a similar complaint after finding Sprinklr had adequately disclosed its resource realignment toward an AI-powered product line. The court also found the complaint relied on hindsight rather than particularized facts. The authors note that the Microsoft, ZoomInfo, and monday.com cases have not yet been decided on those motions. If they survive the pleadings stage, the authors expect many more complaints pleading AI diversion claims against other companies.

Articles.Title: AI Diversion Theories Emerge as New Securities Lawsuit Risk Zone

stories.Headline: AI in Psychotherapy: An Evolving Regulatory Landscape - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed California Senate Bill 903 on September 30, 2026. The bill would have prohibited companies from offering psychotherapy through artificial intelligence chatbots and would have limited how far clinicians could rely on AI tools. Supporters said the measure kept clinicians involved in patient care, while opponents said it would force clinicians to review and sign off on AI activity even when that activity was routine. Newsom said the bill was overly broad, invited a narrower version, and stressed the need for guardrails on AI in healthcare.

The veto leaves the national debate over AI's role in psychotherapy unsettled. Supporters argue that AI can expand clinician capacity and improve access to care, while lawmakers have cautioned against over-reliance and several states have acted to regulate it. Many states permit AI use in healthcare but have passed laws barring health plans from relying on AI for clinical decisions without clinician involvement. Some states also require providers or plans to disclose when AI is used in a patient's care or claims. The article's authors describe the resulting landscape as evolving, with new legislation expected in 2027.

State approaches to AI in psychotherapy vary considerably. Nevada bars AI providers from representing their tools as capable of psychotherapy and bars making AI mental health chatbots available, while Colorado forbids representing AI as a therapist and instead bars health plans from paying for AI psychotherapy services. Tennessee prohibits representing AI as a therapist without the further bans, and Illinois, Maine, Rhode Island, and Vermont require psychotherapy to come from a qualified professional. Utah expressly permits AI mental health chatbots if they disclose that they are AI. The rules on clinical use also differ, with Nevada generally limiting psychotherapists to administrative AI uses, while Colorado and Maine allow AI to make recommendations so long as a clinician reviews and approves the output.

Governor Newsom said that even with a review-and-approval exception, SB 903 went too far because it would limit clinicians' use of tools, including by requiring routine screening determinations to receive direct approval. Senator Padilla, the bill's author, said he would reintroduce the legislation in the coming session to prevent AI from providing psychotherapy. The 2027-28 California legislative session convenes on December 7, 2026, and the authors advise providers to monitor legislative developments in their jurisdictions. They also note that the requirements for AI-assisted psychotherapy could change substantially over the next year.

Articles.Title: AI in Psychotherapy: An Evolving Regulatory Landscape - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: How Should Schools Adapt to AI?
stories.Summary:
Only one article was supplied, a transcript of a KQED Forum episode dated October 26, 2026, titled "How Should Schools Adapt to AI?" It describes a radio conversation rather than a breaking event, so the story below summarizes what educators said about AI in classrooms and is not a news report of a single incident. The discussion featured Daniel Herman, a humanities teacher at Maybeck High School in Berkeley, and Kip Glazer, principal of Mountain View High School and author of a guide for school leaders on AI. Herman said his classroom has changed little, but he has rethought assignments so they emphasize process over finished products, such as research presentations and interview projects that show students thinking on the page. Glazer described some teachers banning the technology while others admit they do not have all the answers, and she said students react to both approaches differently.

Herman argued that AI can be useful for learning but is poor at replacing a student's own thinking. Both educators stressed honesty and dialogue with students about whether and how they use chatbots. Herman said he asks students to tell him when they use AI, though he cannot confirm they all do. Glazer said some students avoid the tool entirely for fear of being labeled cheaters, and she pointed to students noticing when teachers use AI to grade work while forbidding it for students.

Glazer also raised concern about accelerating expectations, noting seventh graders contacting her about preparing for high school two years early. The episode included guests from Digital Promise, Alpha Schools and Prospect Sierra School, whose views were not summarized in the transcript provided. The host, Alexis Madrigal, framed the questions as open, asking how schools can gain AI's benefits without weakening students' reading, writing and critical thinking. The transcript ends before any firm conclusions are reached, so the articles do not say what schools will ultimately decide.

Articles.Title: How Should Schools Adapt to AI? - KQED

stories.Headline: BBAI Stock Climbs As $225M Federal AI Contracts Fuel Momentum
stories.Summary:
BigBear.ai shares rose about 11.32 percent in trading on October 27, 2026, as investors reacted to a run of federal contract announcements. The stock had earlier gained roughly 4.6 percent after the contract news, and it was trading near $2.36 that day. Coverage describes the move as a momentum-driven rally tied to positive AI headlines rather than a sudden gap or crash. The stock was held steady through the session, climbing from the low $2.18s to the mid $2.30s by midday.

The company has built up more than $225 million in total contract value since July across U.S. homeland security, defense, intelligence, and federal civilian agencies. It has also won more than 25 new generative AI awards from customers including the FBI, NASA, the U.S. Coast Guard, the Department of Energy, and the Department of Veterans Affairs. Recompete wins and renewals with U.S. Customs and Border Protection were also cited as reinforcing its role in national security and trade and travel. The articles say the company's next scheduled step is its Q3 2026 earnings release and conference call, where investors are expected to look for details on backlog, margins, and AI growth.

The articles do not name a specific person as responsible for the stock move, and they attribute the rally to market sentiment around the contract flow. Jack Kellogg is listed as the author, with Tim Sykes and Ellis Hobbs named as reviewer and fact-checker. The company's financial picture is described as mixed: quarterly revenue was about $36.7 million, with EBITDA near -$18.6 million and net income near -$25.7 million, while the balance sheet carries little debt and over $31.9 million in cash and short-term investments. The articles also note that Form 4 insider filings in the coverage did not state whether transactions were buys, sells, or awards, so they were treated as unclear.

The context is that BigBear.ai is still losing money despite a rising contract pipeline, which makes the stock a volatile, news-driven trade. The articles say free cash flow last quarter was roughly -$22.5 million and that the company has enough liquidity to keep operating while it works toward profitable scale. The Q3 2026 earnings release is presented as the next key catalyst for the shares. The articles stress that the price action and contract news are not investment advice.

Articles.Title: BBAI Stock Climbs As $225M Federal AI Contracts Fuel Momentum - Timothy Sykes

stories.Headline: AI bots flooded 2023 UK government consultation on disposable vapes ban
stories.Summary:
Researchers have revealed that AI bots flooded a 2023 UK government consultation on banning disposable vapes with tens of thousands of fake responses. Three-quarters of the responses to the consultation on the tobacco and vapes bill were machine-generated, and the research was published on Tuesday in the journal Tobacco Control by Dr Nason Maani of the University of Edinburgh and Prof Anna Gilmore of the University of Bath. The Department of Health and Social Care used bot-detection methods to find that 90,835 of its 118,756 responses, or 76%, came from bots. Nearly all of these automated responses opposed the plan of the previous Conservative government under Rishi Sunak to ban disposable vapes, and they were often duplicated and sent at high frequency from a small number of IP addresses. The researchers described it as the first documented case of large-scale automated interference in a formal public health policy consultation.

The department excluded all of the 90,835 automated responses from its decision-making. The Labour government of Keir Starmer inherited the tobacco and vapes bill in 2024 and passed it into law, including the ban on businesses selling or supplying disposable vapes. The researchers warned that the greater danger lies in future campaigns that are harder to detect, since they could make a handful of powerful interests appear to be a mass movement. Health groups and experts also raised concerns about the risk of commercial interests exploiting new technology to undermine public health rules. The articles give no specific figures for any further changes to the rules beyond the ban itself.

Caroline Cerny, deputy chief executive of Action on Smoking and Health, said the evidence was deeply concerning and that safeguards were needed against the use of technology to serve commercial interests. Azzurra Moores, associate director for information ecosystems at the thinktank Demos, called the findings pretty alarming and said that interference of this kind undermines trust in the process. She also said there is no easy fix, because barriers that keep bots out can also make it harder for real people to take part. The department said its robust controls identified the attempt, that the fake responses were removed, and that the consultation helped inform the government's smoke-free generation action. It said it would remain alert to such interference and would not be deterred from doing what is necessary to promote healthier living.

Articles.Title: AI bots flooded 2023 UK government consultation on disposable vapes ban - The Guardian

stories.Headline: First Harmonised Technical Standard Published Under the EU AI Act
stories.Summary:
On 14 October 2026, the European Commission published the first harmonised standard under the EU AI Act, EN 18286:2026, a standard on artificial intelligence quality management systems. The publication was made through Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274. Providers of high-risk AI systems can rely on this standard to demonstrate compliance with Articles 11(1) and 17(1) of the Act, which cover technical documentation and the quality management system. The standard was prepared jointly by CEN and CENELEC after a formal request from the Commission.

The standard requires providers to identify the AI Act requirements that apply to them, define the scope of their quality management system, and adopt a documented regulatory compliance strategy. That strategy covers the essential requirements of Articles 9 to 15, conformity assessment, modifications, post-market monitoring and serious-incident reporting. The standard builds these obligations into management processes covering leadership, competence, the AI lifecycle, supply chain controls, handling of non-compliance and management review. It follows the same high-level structure as ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO 9001, so it can be layered onto existing management systems. Applying it does not change the conformity assessment route for most high-risk systems, though it matters for biometric systems under Annex III, point 1.

The Commission has said the standard is designed to sit on top of existing international standards rather than replace them. Adherence to those other standards alone, however, will not give a provider the presumption of conformity. The legal duties under the Act remain binding, and providers stay responsible for assessing all risks of their AI systems. The Official Journal publishes only the reference to the standard, and the full text is sold by national standardisation bodies such as AFNOR, DIN, UNI and BSI. The paid-access model has drawn criticism and is legally contested, given the standards' role in legal compliance.

EN 18286 is the first of a wider set of standards planned under a Commission standardisation request, which identifies 10 areas including risk management, data governance, human oversight, cybersecurity and conformity assessment. These areas relate mainly to Articles 9 to 15, 17 and 43 of the Act, and several deliverables may address a single area. The remaining standards are at different stages of development and adoption. Providers of high-risk systems are advised to assess their current arrangements against EN 18286 to benefit from the presumption of conformity under Article 40, and to watch for further standards as they are published.

Articles.Title: First Harmonised Technical Standard Published Under the EU AI Act - Orrick

stories.Headline: To make AI morally good, tech companies are turning to religion. But some say it isn't that simple
stories.Summary:
Tech companies are increasingly turning to religion to help decide how their AI models should behave morally. Executives such as Anthropic's Chris Olah have said these questions cannot be answered in a lab and that traditions with millennia of moral reflection have a role to play. Companies including Anthropic, Meta, Google, Amazon and Microsoft have met with faith leaders, philosophers and ethicists, with Anthropic saying in a May blog post that it had consulted scholars and clergy from more than 15 religious and cross-cultural groups. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said last year that ChatGPT should reflect a weighted average of humanity's moral views. The approach reflects growing anxiety about AI's risks and a desire to give models a sound moral footing.

Critics argue that this approach misunderstands religion. Anthropologist Webb Keane of the University of Michigan has argued that religion is not simply a rulebook that can be separated from daily life, culture and politics. If companies treat religion as a source of extractable moral principles, he and others warn, they may favor traditions that see themselves as systems of ethics, particularly scriptural faiths like the Abrahamic religions, while distorting others. Experts also note that different traditions often contradict one another, so a blended average of moral views may not reflect how religious people actually reason. Doctrine, ritual and relationships, they say, are central to religious life in ways a list of rules cannot capture.

Some participants describe the engagement as serious and thoughtful. Meghan Sullivan, a philosopher of religion at the University of Notre Dame who leads an initiative on ethics and AI there, attended an Anthropic meeting earlier this year that included Christians from different denominations. She said the company's staff were intellectually curious and that the meetings were structured in two parts, first explaining the models in layman's terms and then hearing feedback from faith leaders. She said she was impressed by Anthropic's rigorous engagement, which she contrasted with conversations she had with other tech companies. Anthropic is widely seen as the AI company taking ethics and safety most seriously, according to the article.

The article also places the debate in a broader historical context. Scholars such as the late Jonathan Z. Smith have argued that the modern idea of religion as a category for comparing distinct world traditions dates to roughly the 19th century, and that Buddhism and Hinduism were not originally seen as clearly bounded traditions. Many scholars therefore question whether companies can treat religions as comparable, extractable systems. The article indicates that the companies plan to broaden the range of traditions they consult, though it does not say how that expansion will be carried out or how any input will be weighed in model design.

stories.Headline: Datavault AI Expands WiSA Patent Portfolio with 13 U.S. Patent Milestones in 2026
stories.Summary:
Datavault AI Inc. (NASDAQ: DVLT), a Philadelphia company that describes itself as an artificial intelligence platform business, announced on October 26, 2026 that it has recorded 13 U.S. patent milestones for its WiSA wireless audio intellectual property so far this year. Those milestones include three patents the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office has issued and ten applications that have received Notices of Allowance. The company says the work is aimed at reliable, low-latency, synchronized multichannel wireless audio for modern consumer electronics and connected devices. The patents cover areas such as wireless audio transmission, synchronization, speaker localization, error concealment, multi-speaker speech processing, interoperability, and simplified pairing.

The three issued patents are No. 12,581,257, issued March 17, 2026, on audio source localization in multi-speaker systems; No. 12,696,035, issued July 28, 2026, on concealing discontinuities in audio blocks; and No. 12,711,979, issued August 18, 2026, on multi-speaker speech processing. The ten applications span wireless audio transport, audio timing and synchronization, device interoperability, enhanced interoperability, audio error concealment, data transmission, and one-button device pairing. The company says the Notices of Allowance mark substantial progress in examination and are expected to lead to additional issued patents, subject to completing the remaining requirements. Datavault AI links the portfolio to possible licensing, technology partnerships, and standards work across televisions, soundbars, speakers, smart home devices, gaming platforms, and professional audio products.

Chief Executive Nathaniel T. Bradley said each milestone helps build a foundation for how synchronized multichannel wireless audio will be built in the next generation of consumer electronics, and that the 13 milestones give the company a broader body of intellectual property to offer manufacturers and technology partners. Dean Becker, the company's Chief Licensing Officer, said interoperability and spatial high-definition audio transmission have been the focus of years of engineering at WiSA. He added that the acoustic and internal IP teams, working with counsel, have built a licensing program for acoustic technology that will be supported by WiSA certification systems. The company says it plans to keep evaluating ways to bring its intellectual property into licensing structures and collaborative standards efforts, subject to applicable policies.

The announcement is framed as a step in building a broader intellectual property monetization platform, though the company stresses that outcomes depend on the scope and enforceability of the patent rights, market adoption, and negotiations. Its press release includes standard forward-looking statement cautions, noting that actual results may differ materially from its expectations. The company also describes itself as a data monetization and digital asset firm with acoustic sciences and data sciences divisions, and it lists WiSA, ADIO, and Sumerian among its patented technologies. Future steps the articles mention include the potential issuance of patents from the ten pending allowances and new licensing or partnership arrangements, but none are confirmed by the materials.

stories.Headline: Meta Platforms Just Delivered Great News to AI Stock Investors
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms, which trades under the ticker META, has become a major driver of the AI trade in recent weeks. In September the company launched its Muse personal AI agent, which shot to the top of the download charts on Apple and Android and pushed up the stock and the broader AI sector. After its second-quarter earnings report, however, the shares fell sharply when the company disclosed its first quarter of negative free cash flow, as investors questioned its heavy AI infrastructure spending. Meta also announced it would create a new class of non-voting shares to raise money for its AI plans, and it has moved quickly since then.

This week Meta announced several stock offerings, including a $22.5 billion offering that was upsized to $25 billion. The company also plans to sell $12.5 billion in preferred stock and $60 billion of the new non-voting Class C stock, bringing the total to $97.5 billion in new funds. The move comes as investors have grown jittery about AI financing amid rising interest rates and a sell-off in neocloud and AI infrastructure stocks after CoreWeave's bond yields reached as high as 15%. Elon Musk also recently commented that finding financing was becoming difficult, which he expected would pressure smaller companies. The articles note that Meta's choice to raise equity rather than debt reflects that backdrop.

According to media reports, Meta's offering was oversubscribed by five times, meaning demand could have supported $125 billion in stock sales. Nvidia and AMD were among the investors in the round, and the articles suggest they expect Meta to spend some of the money on their chips. The Motley Fool's Jeremy Bowman, the author of the Yahoo Finance piece, wrote that this level of demand points to continued strength for AI stocks and AI infrastructure funding. He also noted that Meta trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of around 21 after its post-earnings sell-off, which he described as cheap. He suggested that some of the excess demand could flow to Anthropic, which is reportedly seeking a public listing at a valuation of around $2 trillion next month.

Bowman argued that Meta's move could encourage other AI companies to tap equity markets, though he acknowledged that not every company can dilute shareholders by roughly 5% to raise about $95 billion, and said neocloud firms such as CoreWeave likely cannot. A separate Motley Fool article from October 25 makes a related point, noting that SpaceX reported third-quarter revenue of $14.6 billion, up 161% year over year, with its AI segment, Super Intelligence, rising 830% to $7.6 billion, and that SpaceX's capital spending on the segment reached $16.4 billion. That article presents Nvidia and CoreWeave as beneficiaries of continued AI compute demand, while flagging CoreWeave's heavy debt and customer concentration as risks. Taken together, the articles suggest that strong demand for AI compute and funding could persist, though the sources differ on how much risk remains for smaller AI companies.

stories.Headline: AI-driven disinformation running rampant on social media before US midterms, experts warn
stories.Summary:
AI-driven disinformation is spreading widely on social media ahead of the November 2026 US midterm elections, and experts warn that many false posts are slipping past moderation. The Guardian reported on October 27, 2026, that social media companies have scaled back efforts to shield voters from election-related lies. Trust and safety teams were cut back after a backlash from the right over fears of speech restrictions, a backlash that grew after Elon Musk bought X and Donald Trump won the 2024 election. Artificial intelligence has made such campaigns cheap and easy to run, while platforms increasingly rely on AI rather than human reviewers to respond.

Frances Haugen, a former Facebook data engineer turned whistleblower, said operatives can evade content rules by slightly altering posts each time they publish them, so some will get through. Campaigns in Pennsylvania and Texas have struggled to respond to false claims that spread quickly online, and they are unsure whom to turn to when falsehoods circulate. Meta and X did not respond to requests for comment, while YouTube said all users are subject to the same guidelines. The Texas case involving Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico shows the problem: after he took time off to recover from the flu, a false claim that he was being treated at a mental health facility in Ohio spread for several days, and it later mutated into a Spanish-language claim that he had attempted suicide. The Digital Democracy Institute of the Americas said platforms enforce their rules less consistently in Spanish, and Roberta Braga, its founder, said AI moderation is likely letting even more content slip through.

Other examples include a Republican campaign ad using AI-generated footage of Talarico and a Pennsylvania case in which a false claim that an immigrant arrested in the state was a campaign worker for Democrat Janelle Stelson was amplified by an official statement from the Department of Homeland Security. Charles Wall, deputy director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, made a statement about Stelson, and the campaign released records showing the man had no paid position on her campaign. The Stelson campaign sent cease-and-desist letters, and a watchdog group filed a complaint alleging the Department of Homeland Security violated the Hatch Act, which limits political activity by government employees. Nora Benavidez of the nonprofit Free Press said Trump has leveraged federal agencies in ways that concern her.

Major platforms have written policies on election misinformation, but they are narrow. Meta requires disclosure of AI-generated content in election ads and bans misrepresentation of voting dates, locations, and requirements, while doing little active moderation of political commentary. YouTube stopped removing claims that past elections were marred by widespread fraud, and it bans only specific voting-related falsehoods. X replaced internal safety reviews with its crowdsourced Community Notes program, and experts argue its rules on synthetic media mean little without enforcement. Haugen argued that the focus should shift to how content is distributed and to the feedback systems that let communities respond.

stories.Headline: ZenaTech Unveils its Proprietary AI Software Suite Designed to Accelerate Land Survey Delivery for Drone as a Service Commercial, Municipal and Infrastructure Clients
stories.Summary:
ZenaTech, Inc., a Nasdaq-listed company that makes AI drones and offers drone-based services, announced on October 24, 2026 that it has unveiled a proprietary artificial intelligence software suite. The company plans to link this software with its land survey operations under its Drone as a Service division, pairing it with high-density LiDAR data collected by its ZenaDrone aircraft. The goal is to shorten survey data delivery from days to as little as minutes for commercial, municipal and infrastructure clients in North America and elsewhere. The combined platform is still in development and testing, so the company has not yet rolled it out. The software, called ZenaAI, is meant to take the billions of 3D measurement points a drone captures over a site and process them automatically.

Its planned functions include classifying points to build digital terrain models, extracting features such as curb lines and pavement edges for export into CAD and BIM formats, and filtering out noise while tagging assets like manholes, hydrants and utility poles. The company says the suite could cut post-processing work by as much as 80 percent, allowing teams to deliver classified data within hours of a flight. Testing is expected across land surveying, infrastructure monitoring and utility inspection projects next year. Chief executive Shaun Passley said that manual post-processing has limited how many projects survey teams can finish, and that automating classification and linework would let the same crews and drones deliver results faster and more consistently. He said the company expects the software to improve operating efficiency and support the recurring revenue model behind its drone services strategy.

ZenaTech describes that strategy as acquiring local service providers and combining them into a global network, with the software applied across the businesses it acquires. The announcement comes as ZenaTech pursues its acquisition-led strategy to digitize service industries such as land surveying and inspections. The company's release includes a safe harbor warning that these forward-looking statements carry risks, including the development and accuracy of AI models, drone regulations, customer adoption and the ability to complete acquisitions. The company said it will provide updates on the launch and rollout as milestones are reached.

stories.Headline: Ascendion Expands AI Advisory Community with Four Global Business and Technology Leaders
stories.Summary:
Ascendion, an AI-native software engineering company, announced on October 28, 2026 that it has appointed four global business and technology leaders to its AI Advisory Community. The new advisors are Andy Gamble, Jack Madrid, Julieta Ross, Ph.D., and Joseph Sirosh, Ph.D., and the company announced the appointments through a PR Newswire release datelined Basking Ridge, New Jersey. The company says the group brings a mix of perspectives, including executives who have answered to boards, regulators, and C-suites, a builder of AI and data platforms at global scale, and a leader who helped shape a large technology-services ecosystem. The advisors' experience covers banking, high-tech, media, and retail. Each will work directly with Ascendion's regional and engineering leaders.

Each advisor is assigned to a different part of the business. Julieta Ross, former Global CTO of Banco Santander, will work on executive relationships, go-to-market strategy, and growth, and will help the company meet the governance, regulatory, and risk expectations that banking leaders place on AI. Andy Gamble, former Group CIO of Currys plc, will advise on work across Europe and the UK, focusing on consumer goods, manufacturing, and retail. Joseph Sirosh, former Microsoft CVP and CTO of AI, will advise engineering leadership on the evolution of AAVA and its platform strategy. Jack Madrid, former President and CEO of IBPAP, will advise on Asia-Pacific markets and on how AI is reshaping global delivery, skills, and workforce models.

Ascendion's chief executive, Karthik Krishnamurthy, said in the release that enterprise leaders have moved past experiments and want AI that delivers outcomes boards can measure and risks they can manage. He said the new advisors know where transformation succeeds and will challenge the company's thinking and raise its ambition. The company describes itself as serving more than 250 enterprise clients and says the advisors will inform how it applies its Engineering to the Power of AI approach to commercial models, platform design, service execution, and workforce development. The release frames the appointments as part of a broader shift in which enterprises are moving AI from experimentation to governed, production-scale outcomes. Ascendion did not give terms for the appointments, and the release does not describe any next steps beyond the advisors' ongoing work with the company.

The announcement frames the honor as evidence that mobile brands and enterprises need to move from manual security and anti-fraud work to systems that run on AI agents. Frost & Sullivan judged companies through benchmarking across strategy effectiveness and strategy execution, and it said Appdome performed well in both.

The platform's central change is that it does the engineering work itself instead of advising human teams. According to the release, Security and engineering teams define the protections, policies and outcomes they want, and Appdome codes, integrates and maintains any of more than 400 protections directly in Android and iOS applications. Those protections cover security, anti-fraud, anti-malware, anti-bot, social engineering prevention, API and identity needs. The system also takes in threat and operational data from apps running its protections, and administrators can use separate agents to examine the decisions the platform makes.

The company says this keeps people in charge of governance throughout the process. Frost & Sullivan analyst Ozgun Pelit is quoted calling Appdome's agents more than traditional AI assistants, since they carry out security tasks and assess whether protections still fit current threats. CEO Tom Tovar is quoted arguing that cybersecurity teams need to match the speed of agentic engineering teams and agentic threats, and that the older model of several manually maintained point products is too slow and fragile. Tovar said teams in the agentic age should set objectives and let the agents do the required work.

Appdome describes itself as serving thousands of mobile brands and drawing on a live feedback loop of 1.3 trillion threat events from 4 billion installs per month, figures the release attributes to the company itself. The release is a promotional item distributed through NewswireToday, which says it does not vouch for the accuracy of the content and that the company bears responsibility for it. Frost & Sullivan presents this recognition each year to firms that show measurable gains in market share, customer satisfaction and competitive position, though the release does not give Appdome's specific figures on those measures. stories.Headline: OpenTelemetry essential for AI observability interoperability
stories.Summary:
OpenTelemetry, the open standard for collecting telemetry data, is being presented as essential to AI observability interoperability, a theme covered by TechGig on October 27, 2026, and by The New Stack on October 26, 2026. The articles describe how engineering teams can standardise the data their AI systems produce so that it can be compared across different models, frameworks and providers. The coverage frames this as a way to deliver useful AI outcomes reliably and at lower cost. The reporting does not describe a single incident or a single event; it is an analysis of where AI monitoring is heading.

Standardised telemetry matters because AI applications involve many moving parts, including model providers, orchestration frameworks and evaluation services, and these change often. The TechGig piece says that shared conventions reduce the need for separate data models and integration work, and that they make it easier to compare quality, cost and risk. It also notes that interoperability lowers the cost of changing parts of an AI application. The New Stack piece makes a similar argument, stressing that interoperability is what will decide which AI observability approaches succeed. Both articles treat common data formats as the practical requirement for teams that want to swap components without rebuilding their monitoring.

Both articles point to specific practices and tools. TechGig cites OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions, which describe common concepts for conversations and messages and allow large content to be stored externally with references kept in telemetry, and it names Splunk's Agent Observability work, built on OpenTelemetry and AGNTCY standards, as one vendor-neutral example. It also quotes the argument that cost per business outcome is more useful than cost per token, since token counts alone do not show whether spending produced useful work. The New Stack article, which is largely a discussion of interoperability as the central contest in the field, is framed around the same idea that open standards will shape the market. The pieces were published by technology news outlets and attribute these views to the authors and the cited vendors rather than to any regulator.

What happens next is not spelled out in detail by either article. TechGig suggests that agent observability can support guardrails that block harmful actions when connected to enforcement systems, and that shared telemetry can link those controls to evidence about an agent's steps and business impact. The New Stack article predicts that the AI observability race will be decided by interoperability, but it does not give a timeline or specific milestones. The reporting therefore describes a direction of travel toward shared standards and measurable business value, while leaving open how quickly organisations will adopt them.

stories.Headline: Tsinghua University & NVIDIA Unveil New AI Video Model Ranking: Exposing Shortcomings of 38 Real-Time Generative AI Video Systems
stories.Summary:
Tsinghua University, NVIDIA and several other universities and research institutions have jointly released StreamEval, a new benchmark for streaming interactive AI video generation. The ranking covers 38 models, and the researchers presented it in late October 2026 as the first evaluation of its kind in the industry. Existing tools such as VBench and EvalCrafter judge a single prompt and the video it produces, which leaves them unable to test how these systems handle instructions that keep arriving during generation. StreamEval was built to close that gap by testing the systems under conditions closer to real use.

The benchmark spans five task types: digital human dialogue, virtual human performance, world generation, instruction editing and reference editing. Each type has 60 test cases, run at durations of 15, 30, 60, 120 and 300 seconds, and each case is run three times by the same model. The full dataset includes 1,347 online events released step by step along the timeline, so a model sees only the input available at that moment. Performance is scored across four dimensions and ten indicators, each rated from 0 to 100, and the five task types are ranked separately rather than merged into one overall list. All code, datasets and scoring rules are open source, and developers can submit their own models to the leaderboard.

The results show that a model producing stable video does not necessarily follow changing instructions. In digital human dialogue, Vidu S2-Avatar reached the top overall score among participating models that support custom images, at 93.98 after a 5-point bonus. In virtual human performance, the same system scored highest overall at 81.71, yet its instruction-following score was only 36.90, the highest value among seven models but still low. In world generation, the top overall scores were held by different models on different measures, which the researchers say shows that visual quality, instruction response and long-term continuity must be judged separately. The reference editing task was the hardest, with the best overall score at 39.02 and an edit success rate of only 15.00.

A separate report from the same period describes Cadence Design Systems and NVIDIA announcing a partnership and the Maestro AI model family, fine-tuned on NVIDIA's Nemotron models to work with Cadence's electronic design automation tools. Cadence's Paul Cunningham said that somewhere between 20 and 30 percent of chips under development are now designed with help from AI agents, a share he expects to keep growing. Cadence claims early testing showed up to a 30 percent gain in output quality and up to five times better token efficiency compared with general-purpose foundation models. The Maestro platform can be accessed through an API, run in a secure virtual private cloud, or deployed on premises, with customization on customer data offered as a managed service. The same report links this trend to the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, which has driven a series of new Nvidia-based supercomputers.

stories.Headline: Georgia High School Students Weigh Learning Without Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Georgia high school students at Arabia Mountain High School in Stonecrest are working on assignments without artificial intelligence in some classes, and reporter Sofia Robertson described how students are adjusting. Teachers set limits on when AI can be used, so students now spend more time working problems out themselves. Some say this helps them learn, while others admit the work has become harder. The change has affected students differently, with some barely noticing and others spending longer on each assignment.

Under DeKalb County School District guidelines, teachers decide when students may use AI, and students cannot turn in AI-generated work as their own without permission. Teacher Robert Calloway described the challenge as finding a balance between using technology and making sure students are actually learning. Senior Gabrielle Montgomery said assignments take longer when she gets stuck, but that working alone forces her to learn the material. Senior Melissa Mendoza said her critical thinking has sharpened and she now pays more attention in class, though independent work takes more time away from friends. Senior Mariam Dukuray uses Khan Academy and YouTube when confused and said those videos still teach her step by step.

The students agreed that AI should not be removed entirely from education. Montgomery suggested a difference between using AI to do an assignment and using it to understand a hard topic or prepare for a test. Mendoza thought AI could help with creative group projects and with explaining information more clearly. Dukuray said teachers should also consider how they use AI, since students may lose motivation when teachers rely heavily on it for classroom materials. Their views show the question is less about whether to use AI than about how schools can keep the technology from doing the learning for students.

The district's guidelines also flag inappropriate uses such as creating deepfakes, impersonating others, harassment, and unauthorized help on tests, which can lead to consequences under the Student Code of Conduct. At the same time, the district offers its Gemini AI Certification Program, which covers AI safety, digital citizenship, writing effective prompts, and real-world use. The article notes that schools will have to decide how to prepare students to use AI while still encouraging independent thinking. The students' experiences suggest that knowing an answer is not the same as understanding it.

stories.Headline: AI-powered cyberattacks on websites surge
stories.Summary:
Reports from Japan indicate that cyberattacks aimed at companies through publicly accessible websites and apps have more than doubled compared with last year. According to Macnica, a Yokohama-based cybersecurity firm, 216 cases of confirmed or suspected data breaches have been reported so far this year, which is 2.6 times the total for all of last year. Of these, 101 cases came to light in October alone up to the reporting date. At a ministerial meeting on cybersecurity held on Monday, officials presented an analysis showing that attackers are increasingly scanning web-based systems to find entry points and steal personal information quickly, and a government official said AI was likely being used.

The attacks exploit weaknesses in websites and apps themselves, so hackers can reach customer information without first breaking into a company's internal network. In some cases, attackers log in as legitimate users and try to view other customers' data. Targets have also broadened beyond e-commerce sites to include membership websites, booking platforms, library catalog systems, sightseeing train reservations and university facility booking systems. Macnica's Yutaka Sejiyama said companies need to find and fix weaknesses in their own systems, since vulnerabilities specific to individual sites cannot always be patched by updating common software. Hiroshi Tokumaru of EG Secure Solutions noted that websites not handling confidential data or payments often receive lower security priority.

Other reporting describes a wider wave between September and October that reached media organizations, logistics and financial providers, department stores, restaurant chains and government bodies including the Digital Agency and several prefectural police departments, and it also affected South Korean banks. A cybersecurity company affiliated with GMO Internet Group reportedly found that a Chinese AI software tool called ARTEX was exploited against Japanese companies, and CrowdStrike has said attacks in South Korea used instructions written in Chinese. The same reporting says attackers hide their origins by routing traffic through devices around the world, which makes identification very hard. One analyst, Ani Terada of AironWorks, estimated that Japan's total for the year could roughly double last year's 84 publicly disclosed cases, and said most of the 119 cases disclosed by October 6 came after July.

Terada attributed much of the rise to generative AI, which lets attackers write natural-sounding Japanese for phishing emails and fake sites, removing a long-standing language barrier. He also pointed to weak organizational security at many Japanese firms, which often spend less on cybersecurity and fewer companies appoint dedicated security executives than in the United States. Stolen Japanese identity documents reportedly sell for up to ten times the usual price, and criminals are diversifying into ransom demands, data trading and fraud, including AI voice impersonation. Experts also note that new active cyber defense legislation took effect on October 1, and that attackers may have timed their campaigns around it. Terada expects tracking perpetrators to grow harder and warns that attacks often rise toward year-end, urging both individuals and businesses to stay vigilant.

stories.Headline: AI shoppers get first say in South Korea’s retail race
stories.Summary:
South Korean retailers are now testing products on AI-generated shoppers before putting them in front of real customers, according to reports published on October 26, 2026. These "synthetic consumers" are built from large language models and consumer data to mimic real purchasing behaviour. Companies use them to predict buying decisions, fine-tune prices and spot flaws in the shopping experience, all without the time and expense of conventional consumer surveys. Firms involved include Lotte Members, Coupang, Naver and convenience store operator BGF Retail, along with several food producers.

Several projects carry specific figures and dates. Lotte Members began building an "AI Twin Consumer" in July with local AI firms Vibe Co and Zero to One Partners, combining purchasing data from about 45 million accumulated users of its L.Point membership programme with social media data. The aim is to capture the reasons and context behind purchases rather than relying on a basic persona such as a woman in her 30s or a man in his 60s. Coupang and Naver are using synthetic shoppers to simulate how customers move through an online store, and to find where they hesitate, lose interest or cancel a purchase. BGF Retail, which runs the CU convenience chain, has used them to evaluate new product concepts and is now working on virtual store simulations to test displays, customer traffic and merchandise assortments before changing real stores.

The technology provider Intellicia says it has completed 120 proof-of-concept projects with 50 companies. Food groups that have taken part include CJ Group, Daesang, Maeil Dairies, Pulmuone and Sangmidang Holdings. According to Intellicia, its synthetic consumers are generated from real interviews, surveys, commerce reviews and social media data rather than simply assigned demographic traits. The company claims a 91.2 percent correlation with a 500-person real consumer survey in its own benchmark testing, a figure that comes from the firm itself.

An unnamed official at a retail company said the approach suits a market where trends can appear and vanish within weeks, because retailers no longer need to recruit consumer panels and analyse responses each time a product idea changes. The official expected retailers to lean more on AI to weed out weaker concepts, refine products and simulate customer experiences before spending on production, advertising or physical store changes. Over the long term, the official said, companies may be able to make bigger decisions more quickly based on a large group of virtual customers. The articles do not say what comes next beyond this outlook.

stories.Headline: AI curriculum is being rolled out. But where are the working computers?
stories.Summary:
The Union Education Ministry launched CBSE's new curriculum on Computational Thinking and Artificial Intelligence for Classes 3 to 8 on April 1, 2026, with teaching set to begin in the 2026-27 session. The early years focus on puzzles, games and worksheets rather than screens, with computational thinking serving as the foundation for AI learning in later classes. A recent JAN AI survey of nearly 800 government school teachers across Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka, Jharkhand and Maharashtra found that 72% were positive about AI and 26% used it regularly. Fear of job loss from AI was virtually absent among those teachers.

The curriculum raises a practical question about hardware and connectivity. Students moving into higher classes will need working computers and internet access, and their teachers will need time to learn and practise the material. The UDISE+ data for 2025-26 shows that 63.1% of schools had a computer working for teaching, up from 57.9% in 2024-25, and internet access rose from 63.5% to 67.4%. Even so, 5,41,851 of the 14,67,000 schools in India, over one in three, had no working computer for teaching. In Jharkhand, 81.2% of schools reported a computer but only 57.1% had one that worked.

The gap between private and government schools is wide. About 74.0% of private unaided schools had a working computer for teaching, compared with 59.4% of government schools, and only 23.0% of government schools with Class 6 and above had a functional ICT lab. Government schools serve 48.1% of school children and employ half of the national teacher workforce. The data also shows large state differences: Meghalaya and West Bengal had fewer than 25% of schools with a computer available for teaching, while Bihar had internet in 91.0% of schools but only 38.4% with a working computer. The authors describe the JAN AI survey as showing that many teachers without school computers use personal phones, which they say creates a risk because most such use happens without institutional oversight.

The authors, Raunak Maitra of Azim Premji University and Karan Babbar of XLRI Jamshedpur, argue that the next stage should focus on states that are lagging and on maintaining the more than one lakh schools whose computers are unfit for teaching. They suggest that repair and support would cost far less than buying new equipment. They also call for teachers to receive guidance on safe use of AI, not just access to it. The article concludes that the coming years will determine whether, by the time today's Class 3 students reach Class 9, every school has the computers, connectivity and trained teachers that AI learning requires.
