He stressed that companies should ease employees' worries about being replaced by technology.

The survey found administrative support was the top use of AI, reported by about 72% of AI-using businesses, down four percentage points from last year. Still, 54% of businesses said AI was minimally integrated into their workflows. Brandon said the term likely covers simpler tasks such as scheduling and emailing, and he said AI-assisted email is the leading edge of that work because it resembles spell-check software that people already use. Among non-users, privacy and security concerns and a belief that AI did not apply to their business were each cited by 48%.

Economic uncertainty was the top barrier to business this year at 61%, while healthcare costs rose 14 percentage points from last year to 42%, becoming the third-leading barrier. Altsech said he hopes more research will clarify how AI is changing productivity, job satisfaction and consumer behavior, particularly through qualitative studies. He said AI is not a passing fad and has real value, but businesses have not yet fully taken advantage of it. The articles do not say what further surveys or studies are planned beyond these comments.

Articles.Title: More Madison area businesses are adopting AI, survey finds

stories.Headline: Exclusive: ‘Godfather of AI’ Geoffrey Hinton on the risks of artificial intelligence and the future of humanity
stories.Summary:
Armenpress published an exclusive interview on 27 October 2026 with Geoffrey Hinton, the British-Canadian computer scientist often called the "Godfather of AI." Hinton shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics with John Hopfield for work that enabled machine learning through artificial neural networks. The interview was conducted at the STARMUS VIII festival in Spain's Canary Islands. He left Google in 2023 so he could speak more openly about the dangers of the technology he helped build.

Hinton described two kinds of risk, the near-term ones caused by people misusing AI and the longer-term one of AI systems becoming smarter than humans and acting on their own goals. He said AI is already very good at cyberattacks, and because an attacker needs to succeed only once while a defender must succeed every time, he expects serious incidents within the next few years. He also warned that AI can now design new viruses, that autonomous battle robots are beginning to appear, and that fake videos could be used to corrupt elections. On the economic side, he said companies may replace many jobs with AI, which would raise unemployment and shrink the tax base that governments rely on to support people.

Hinton argued that AI companies should face regulation similar to the rules for new drugs, requiring them to show that a system is safe before its release. He said it is inconsistent that a sandwich faces more rules than an AI system that could, in his view, threaten humanity. He added that self-regulation by companies is not enough, and he blamed the lack of rules on wealthy people who have influence over American politicians. He also said scientists who helped develop AI have a duty to warn the public about its dangers rather than simply profit from it.

Hinton still sees real benefits in AI, including gains in healthcare, education, and productivity, and he said the outcome depends on whether the risks are managed. He described two possible futures, one in which AI is developed carelessly and harms humanity and another in which serious work goes into managing its risks. He expressed concern that many developers are focused on moving fast and making money rather than addressing those risks. Asked for the biggest scientific achievement of the 21st century, he answered simply: chatbots.

Articles.Title: Exclusive: ‘Godfather of AI’ Geoffrey Hinton on the risks of artificial intelligence and the future of humanity

stories.Headline: Jump Rolls Out New Claude Skills for Financial Advisors
stories.Summary:
Jump, an artificial intelligence provider for financial advisors, has announced an expansion of its work with Anthropic through Claude for Financial Advisors. The expansion adds purpose-built skills that turn client conversations into follow-up tasks, and it was reported on October 27, 2026. It builds on Jump's existing one-click Claude connector, which brings client meeting context into Claude. The new skills give advisors another way to put that context to use.

The Jump-built skills include Yesterday/Week in Review, Client Commitments, Decision Log, Meeting Recap, Meeting History, Recap Email and Document Lookup. According to the company, they are meant to organize recent conversations, surface commitments and decisions, locate client documents and prepare follow-up communications. Firms keep control over Jump settings, including recording options, transcript retention, consent and access. Anthropic launched Claude for Financial Advisors, its suite of connectors and workflow skills, in mid-September.

Parker Ence, CEO and co-founder of Jump, said that advisors get the best results from Claude when it understands their clients. He said Jump captures context from client conversations, documents and intake forms, and that the connector and skills let advisors use that context inside Claude. Peter Nolan, head of asset and wealth management at Anthropic, said the tool helps advisors across their daily work and can help them prepare for meetings and follow up with clients. The article does not report any response from regulators.

The expansion follows a busy year for Jump. In February, the company raised $80 million in Series B funding led by Insight Partners, bringing its total capital raised to $105 million. In March it launched an AI Operating System for Advisors with three products, Meet, Grow and Operate, and in September it struck deals with Northwestern Mutual and XYPN. In October, it partnered with FMG Suite on a workflow that surfaces compliance-approved FMG content based on client conversations for advisors to use in follow-up.

Articles.Title: Jump Rolls Out New Claude Skills for Financial Advisors

stories.Headline: The right device for every role in the AI and hybrid era
stories.Summary:
AI and hybrid work have changed how companies should match devices to employees, according to a sponsored BrandPost published by CIO on October 27, 2026. The piece argues that the old method of sorting staff into personas by department or stereotype no longer works, because AI keeps reshaping what roles need and hybrid work has spread where that work happens. The author, writing on behalf of MCPC, a managed IT services provider, says the principle of grouping employees into representative types still holds, but the inputs have changed. The new approach starts with the work itself rather than the org chart.

The method reads each role against the factors that determine what its device must do, including where the work happens, what it demands at peak load, and how much of the day runs through calls and cameras. It also asks what data the role touches, how fast the role is changing, and what an hour of downtime costs. Those questions form a sample of a fuller reading that the article says runs across eight dimensions. Applied across a workforce, the reading can reveal roles with little in common on paper that make the same device demands, so the fleet can use fewer, better-matched standard configurations that are easier to support.

The article's eight dimensions are mobility and environment, work demands, collaboration load, digital dexterity, data and access footprint, cost of disruption, volatility, and security and compliance. The article presents these as the basis for a well-built persona, and it describes persona work as an ongoing lifecycle discipline rather than a one-time setup. It says the match must be monitored as roles evolve, adjusted when work outgrows a configuration, and closed out when devices reach end of life. MCPC, which the article says has spent more than twenty years on device lifecycle management, promotes its new guidebook, built with HP, Microsoft, and AMD, as a step-by-step method for building personas.

Articles.Title: The right device for every role in the AI and hybrid era

stories.Headline: How To Measure Healthcare AI ROI
stories.Summary:
Many health systems are adopting artificial intelligence tools, but they often fail to see the financial returns they expected. A recent Deloitte report found that expectations about annualized cost savings, revenue growth and the break-even point have outpaced organizations' ability to demonstrably measure the monetary impact of their AI investments. Measuring return is a mix of soft and hard metrics that take time to appear, and benefits such as a less burned-out workforce can improve patient care and reputation over the long term. Kenneth Harper of Microsoft said the strongest results come from organizations that tie AI to strategic priorities, set clear success measures and ensure the technology eases clinicians' work instead of adding complexity.

The need for efficiency in healthcare is clear, since the article cites at least $20 billion a year in U.S. medical errors, administrative costs reaching as much as 35% of healthcare spending, and burnout estimated to cost at least $4.6 billion annually. Buying an AI platform is not enough, because the true cost also includes staff training and building a modernized data governance framework, since AI is only as reliable as its data. Cybersecurity and privacy controls are also required, because a breach could affect patient safety and sensitive records. Integrating the platform with existing electronic health record systems adds further expense and effort.

Atif Chaughtai of Strategy explained that clinical outcomes such as fewer readmissions, earlier diagnoses and lower mortality take a long time to show and require enough patient volume to be statistically meaningful. He noted that time saved on paperwork produces a financial return only if it becomes more visits or less overtime, and that relief from burnout rarely appears as a line item. Adoption also matters, and the article warns that tools may go unused if physicians were not consulted, if they do not fit existing workflows or if they cause alert fatigue. Leaders are advised to establish baselines before deployment and track leading indicators such as documentation time, error rates and clinician adoption.

Alex Sushko of Glean recommended linking each AI use case to a stated health system goal, such as monitoring heart failure patients to keep them out of emergency rooms. He argued that measuring hours saved or costs cut matters, but that the purpose behind those steps should be tied to the hospital's overall mission. The article concludes that AI return should reflect cost savings and financial integrity together with care quality, workforce sustainability and patient outcomes. Examples cited include St. Luke's University Health Network saving nearly 200 hours a month on phishing alert work, and DaVita Kidney Care reporting 108 million minutes saved.

Articles.Title: How To Measure Healthcare AI ROI

stories.Headline: AI Risk Considerations Move into OCC Credit Examinations
stories.Summary:
On June 25, 2026, the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued Bulletin 2026-29, revising its Lending and Loan Portfolio Risk Management booklet and folding the older Loan Portfolio Management booklet from 1998 and several legacy thrift issuances into one credit examination manual. Most of the content will look familiar to banks that have followed supervision since 2008. Three additions are new, and they add dedicated sections on model risk management and third-party risk management, plus a subsection on automated credit approval processes. Each addition corresponds to procedures examiners will apply during credit reviews. The result is that risks tied to models, third parties and automated decision tools will be assessed inside routine credit risk examinations.

The bulletin pulls model risk and third-party risk, which previously lived in separate guidance and separate exams, into the scope of credit examinations. Its model section notes that banks use models for underwriting, loan pricing, stress testing and portfolio monitoring, and it states that models used to underwrite and decide credit should be subject to sound model risk management. The third-party section, drawn from 2023 interagency guidance, identifies the providers examiners will review by function, including model providers, loan brokers and correspondents, and financial technology companies. The booklet never uses the terms artificial intelligence or machine learning, so it does not address governance expectations for some AI lending tools now in use. Automated underwriting is described only in terms of models and rule-based criteria.

Those tools are instead pointed to OCC Bulletin 2026-13, issued in April 2026 as the successor to the 2011 model risk guidance. That bulletin states that generative and agentic AI models are outside its scope and signals a forthcoming request for information on those tools. The article argues that banks should expect model risk, AI governance and third-party reviews to surface within asset quality examinations, even when supervisory activity titles do not mention them. It also observes that the guidance is principles-based and most relevant to banks above $30 billion in assets, which leaves smaller institutions running AI underwriting engines without a clear framework. The author suggests that, where the guidance is silent, banks should adopt an external standard and cite it, pointing to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, its Generative AI Profile, and the Cyber Risk Institute's Financial Services AI Risk Management Framework.

The article also cites a Consumer Financial Protection Bureau statement that adverse action notice requirements apply to all credit decisions regardless of the technology used. Its suggested questions for senior stakeholders cover a complete inventory of models and AI tools, the ability to give accurate adverse action reasons, and which named standard governs tools the guidance excludes. The article closes by noting that AI will likely be examined through the credit exam, the model risk review and the third-party review rather than through a separate AI examination. Examiners will look beyond policy documents to whether a bank's assurance functions confirm that its decisioning is accurate, free of bias and protective of consumers. The article's advice is that institutions should not wait for dedicated AI regulatory guidance before building those controls.

Articles.Title: AI Risk Considerations Move into OCC Credit Examinations

stories.Headline: GITEX Global 2026 to showcase advancements in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity
stories.Summary:
GITEX Global 2026 is set to return for its 46th edition in Dubai, drawing together a large gathering of technology and industry figures to discuss recent developments in digital infrastructure, according to information published by Biometric Update. The event runs from Dec. 7 to 11, 2026, and is expected to attract more than 200,000 tech executives from 180 countries. Organizers expect 6,800 exhibiting companies, 2,000 startups, and 400 government entities to take part. The summit opens with an invite-only session on Dec. 7 at the Dubai World Trade Centre, before the main exhibition moves to the Dubai Exhibition Centre at Expo City Dubai. Taken together, these figures show how large the event is expected to become.

The conference will include specialized tracks on artificial intelligence infrastructure, data centers, quantum technology, mobility, robotics, and cybersecurity. Its stated aim is to connect industry leaders with government representatives, which organizers believe will speed up business growth and build international partnerships. Attendees can also look at emerging solutions in agentic AI and energy technology. The articles describe these themes as reflecting how quickly the global digital landscape is changing. Together, the tracks cover a wide span of the sectors now shaping technology policy and investment.

The source for the event details is Biometric Update, which the SC Media article cites for its information. The article does not name a specific organizer or spokesperson who made statements about the goals. It instead presents the aims of the event as a platform for addressing modern security challenges and technological integration across sectors. The article also notes that the event is positioned as a critical meeting point for these discussions.

No further quotes or official comments are included in the coverage. The article is a short preview rather than a report on an event that has already taken place, so it gives no outcomes or results. It also includes a separate item noting that Lindsey Cerkovnik, a senior official at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, is leaving her post after nearly six years, based on reporting from Nextgov. The articles do not say what will happen next beyond the scheduled dates of the event.

Articles.Title: GITEX Global 2026 to showcase advancements in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity

stories.Headline: UT Austin unveils UT Dell Medicine as it bets big on new AI-native hospital
stories.Summary:
The University of Texas at Austin unveiled UT Dell Medicine on Tuesday, a unified academic health system that brings its clinics, Dell Medical School and the planned UT Dell Medical Center under one name. Claudia Lucchinetti, executive vice president for Medical Affairs and the executive leader of the new system, said it will be Austin's fourth major health system and its only academic one. The announcement came as site clearing began this month for a new AI-native medical center in North Austin. Existing care operations, previously known as UT Health Austin, will adopt the new name.

The medical center is slated to open in 2030 at an estimated cost of about $5 billion and will sit on a 27-acre anchor site within a larger campus of more than 300 acres. It will include a 300-to-500-bed specialty hospital, an outpatient clinic and a full emergency department. Its clinical focus will cover cardiovascular, cancer, neurological and transplant care, plus advanced intensive care, with cancer services provided through UT MD Anderson Cancer Center. The project is anchored by a $750 million gift from the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation. Over the next four to six years, the system plans to double its clinical capability and more than triple patient volumes once fully operational.

Lucchinetti and Mike Ryan, the university's chief healthcare technology, digital and data strategist, said the goal is to reduce the number of patients who leave Austin for complex care. They described the local market as highly fragmented, with multiple systems, electronic health records and physician groups. The planned facility will use 20,000 to 30,000 sensors, along with extensive robotics for moving medications, supplies, linens and food. Skidmore, Owings & Merrill is the architectural firm, and the design is past 50 percent completion of the schematic phase. Health system leaders declined to name the technology vendors they plan to work with.

Ryan said the building is being designed to adapt as technologies change, with wider hallways and elevators for robots and infrastructure that can support future tools. Lucchinetti argued that technology should stay in the background so that compassion and human connection remain central to care. The system also plans to use AI, predictive tools and supercomputing from the Texas Advanced Computing Center to support earlier detection and prevention. Leaders said they will train clinicians through simulated environments that teach human-machine collaboration. The articles do not say how the project's cost or timeline might change if plans shift.

Articles.Title: UT Austin unveils UT Dell Medicine as it bets big on new AI-native hospital

stories.Headline: New Report: Big Insurance, Big Tech, and the Hidden Use of AI in Health Insurance - HEALTH CARE un-covered
stories.Summary:
The Center for Health & Democracy Education Fund released a white paper on October 27, 2026, examining what is known, and unknown, about how health insurance companies use artificial intelligence. The report, titled Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: Spotlight on Health Insurers, draws on documents obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request by the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Its findings include Palantir Technologies' role as one of four companies in the consortium operating the Arizona WISeR vendor Zyter, and claims that Aetna, Cigna, Humana and Blue Shield of California already use Palantir products. The report also cites early WISeR data showing delays and low approval rates in Medicare prior authorization.

The authors say that in Washington, only 47% of prior authorization decisions issued by one contractor through March 30 were approved or affirmed. Patients in all six states in the pilot have reported waiting in pain while providers struggle to get decisions. Patent filings from UnitedHealth Group subsidiaries describe technologies that could generate prior authorization requests, approve or deny them, and review appeals, though the patents do not show these tools have been deployed. The report calls for prohibiting AI from making care-altering decisions, ending the WISeR model, and requiring transparency about insurers' technology vendors and their access to patient information.

The report was written by Rachel Madley, PhD, executive director of the Center for Health & Democracy, and Zena Wolf, a researcher. Madley previously worked for Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal, and Wolf previously conducted congressional oversight for Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Elizabeth Warren. The authors argue that regulating algorithms alone will not solve the problem. They say the deeper issue is the financial incentives that make denying and delaying care profitable. The articles do not describe any specific next steps or responses from the insurers or Palantir.

Articles.Title: New Report: Big Insurance, Big Tech, and the Hidden Use of AI in Health Insurance - HEALTH CARE un-covered

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Has A Big Problem: Nobody Wants To Pay
stories.Summary:
The AI sector is showing signs of financial strain, according to economist Dean Baker, writing on October 27, 2026. CoreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, lost 11.7% of its stock value in one week after losing more than 25% the week before, and its long-term debt now carries an interest rate above 16%. Oracle, a hyperscaler, has also struggled, with its stock down 12.7% over the past month and 55.0% over the past year, and its long-term debt yield nearing 9.0%. Baker notes that yields above 8.0% are generally considered junk bond territory. Baker says the trouble matters because these companies depend heavily on borrowing to fund the trillions of dollars needed for AI data center buildout.

Baker argues that the core problem is whether demand can justify that buildout at all. He points out that adoption is growing, but mostly for low-cost AI, and that Meta's Muse app, downloaded almost 11 million times in its first 40 days, is free. Using a hypothetical, he estimates that a lawyer paying $20 a month for an Anthropic system brings in only $240 a year, and that even if a million lawyers subscribed, the total of $240 million would be far short of the hundreds of billions in annual lease commitments. He also cites an analysis from the investment firm Apollo finding no evidence of returns from AI outside the tech sector. He adds that Ramp data show just 1% of firms account for 80% of spending at OpenAI and Anthropic.

Baker says much of that heavy spending comes from other AI companies developing AI, and that these companies lack profitable business models and depend on venture capital. He warns that venture firms will not keep funding them indefinitely, so some heavy spenders may not survive. He also notes that some investors are backing away and that some data centers have been canceled, often blamed on local political opposition or difficulty arranging power. In his view, those explanations are more appealing than admitting weak demand, though he treats the cancellations as potentially promising for the industry's health. Baker is a senior economist at the Center for Economic and Policy Research and the author of Rigged, and the piece was reprinted from his Substack.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Has A Big Problem: Nobody Wants To Pay

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Powered Tutoring Bots Market Insights Report Analyzing Demand TrendsCompetitive Positioning
stories.Summary:
This is a market research press release, not breaking news, and the article carries enough detail to support the required structure. The release, published October 27, 2026 by TBRC Business Research Pvt Ltd. via EINPresswire, presents a market report on AI-powered tutoring bots. It forecasts the market to surpass $12 billion by 2030 and cites a compound annual growth rate of 28% through that year. Asia-Pacific is projected to grow from $1.2 billion in 2025 to $4.3 billion, while the USA is expected to expand from $1.0 billion to $3.4 billion over the same period.

Growth is attributed to several drivers, each with an estimated contribution to annual growth. Personalized learning technology is expected to add about 2.0 percent, remote and digital education demand about 1.5 percent, and improved efficiency and learning outcomes about 1.0 percent. Machine learning and predictive analytics is forecast to be the largest technology segment in 2030, making up roughly 51 percent of the market or about $6 billion. Natural language processing is expected to add around $3 billion between 2025 and 2030, and machine learning and predictive analytics about $5 billion over the same span. The release also describes segmentation by deployment type, application and end user, including K-12 education, higher education and corporate training.

The market is described as moderately fragmented, with the top 10 companies holding 18 percent of revenue in 2025. The release lists OpenAI LLC at 5 percent, Pearson PLC and BYJU'S at 3 percent each, Duolingo Inc. at 3 percent, Sana Labs AB at 2 percent and Khan Academy Inc. at 1 percent, with smaller players each holding under 1 percent. The release credits The Business Research Company as the source for these share figures. It also notes that leading firms are pursuing multi-avatar tutoring systems, generative AI integration, partnerships and multilingual support. As a promotional document, the release encourages readers to request a free sample or access the full report, and its projections are the publisher's own estimates rather than independently verified results.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Powered Tutoring Bots Market Insights Report Analyzing Demand TrendsCompetitive Positioning

stories.Headline: AI Disclosure Proposal Targets How Models Help Build Their Successors
stories.Summary:
Major AI developers would have to disclose whether and how extensively they use their own technology to build new models, under a policy proposal reported on October 27, 2026. The framework comes from Americans for Responsible Innovation, a nonprofit made up of academics, former congressional staffers and government officials, and was first reported by Nextgov/FCW. Under the proposal, companies would file quarterly reports with a new office in the Commerce Department, and significant changes in research practices would trigger notice within four business days. The group's concern is that AI could increasingly do the research needed to build more capable successors, shortening development timelines and leaving officials and safety researchers less time to assess emerging risks.

The proposal would extend government visibility beyond incident reporting. Companies would disclose how much research AI performs and how closely humans supervise that work, even when nothing has gone wrong. The Commerce Department would gain authority to seek more information and require more frequent reporting, and knowingly false or incomplete filings could be referred to the Justice Department. The group also proposed a whistleblower program. Its suggested safety standards would cover hacking capabilities, large-scale influence operations, and chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear and explosive threats, with technical analysis drawn from the existing Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence at the National Institute of Standards and Technology.

The group argues that Washington's visibility into this shift should not depend on what companies choose to announce, according to a blog post describing the framework. The proposal arrives as a Trump administration task force engages industry and outside groups on AI risks. President Donald Trump tapped Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton this month to lead the "Super Intelligence Force," established by an executive order signed in September. The task force has assigned Pentagon technology official Emil Michael to develop protocols for laboratories to report breaches and cybersecurity problems, and has commissioned a study covering cybersecurity, biological threats and control over AI systems.

The proposal leaves open whether oversight would stay within Commerce or be divided among agencies. The administration has emphasized company-led safeguards and resisted a broad new regulatory regime, and a September industry accord calls for internal controls, outside audits and independent oversight committees. The framework would move toward mandatory reporting about the development process itself, which would require companies to document AI's research role, human supervision and significant changes as development proceeds. Whether the administration embraces that approach will determine how much federal oversight depends on voluntary industry cooperation.

Articles.Title: AI Disclosure Proposal Targets How Models Help Build Their Successors

stories.Headline: World's Best Employer Combines Artificial Intelligence and Research to Evaluate America's Employers
stories.Summary:
The World's Best Employer initiative, conducted by the United States Institute for Quality (USIQ), has announced its evaluation of American employers as part of its 2026 study. The research was published on October 27, 2026, through a press release distributed by Quality Standardization and Certification LLC. The initiative combines scientific research, publicly available information, employer evaluations, and AI-supported analysis to assess workplace attractiveness. Its methodology draws on 36 different sources and goes beyond conventional employee ratings and workplace awards.

According to the release, the evaluation uses a multistage process that includes research collection, data coding, analysis, and the determination of recognized employers. The framework allows a maximum assessment score of 500 points, distributed across defined core areas. The study considered a market containing more than 250,000 employers in the United States. Nominated companies for 2026 may use the digital seal graphic permanently without charge, and optional marketing packages are also available for additional promotional materials.

The release attributes the initiative to the USIQ, described as a partner in the international Quality Standard Network, and names Mr. Ged Abadies as the contact person for the company. The organization says it emphasizes neutrality, independence, and comprehensive evaluation as central objectives of its research. It also states that publishing its methodology and research sources allows employers and professionals to examine how recognition decisions are developed. The release presents the initiative as a way to highlight attractive workplaces while helping organizations communicate their strengths to prospective employees.

The announcement reflects a broader interest in independent employer recognition as companies compete for skilled professionals. The article is a paid press release, and the publication notes that inquiries should go directly to the distributor. The source does not provide independent verification of the methodology or the claims made about the study's results. The article does not say how the 2026 recognitions will be publicly listed beyond the availability of the seal for participating organizations.

Articles.Title: World's Best Employer Combines Artificial Intelligence and Research to Evaluate America's Employers

stories.Headline: How To Govern Artificial Intelligence Without Government
stories.Summary:
Major charitable foundations, along with philanthropies from across the political spectrum and the technology sector, are being urged to create and fund an independent nonprofit to oversee frontier artificial intelligence. The proposal, published on October 27, 2026 by Reed Hundt and Blair Levin of the Benton Institute, would keep the nonprofit separate from both government taxation and the AI firms it supervises. The founders would select a governing board of experts with no economic stake in any AI company, and those members would serve paid, staggered five-year terms and choose their own successors. Sectors that buy AI services, such as health care, finance, education, energy, and state and local government, would hold a formal advisory role.

The institution would pursue three main tasks. First, it would evaluate the models of every major AI firm and rate them on safety, transparency, data protection, and related factors, drawing a comparison to the movie industry's ratings system created in 1968. Second, it would protect competition by keeping each firm's data confidential and walled off from rivals, so companies compete for high ratings rather than coordinating in ways that could invite antitrust scrutiny. Third, it would issue advisory opinions on where the industry should cooperate to deliver public goods, pointing to Biohub's Virtual Biology Initiative, which has grown to $1.8 billion and draws on support from the National Institutes of Health, the Energy Department, Meta, and Google DeepMind. The authors argue that firms would have strong reasons to comply, since poor ratings could make insurance and government contracts harder to obtain.

The authors say the proposal responds to a gap they see in current policy. They note that Congress has introduced nearly 600 AI-related bills in the 119th Congress, but they doubt most will pass soon given the executive branch's opposition to regulation. They also describe a federal task force, the Super Intelligence Force, led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, which has 120 days to recommend the government's role but lacks an ongoing structure to address concerns. The authors cite warnings from AI executives and researchers, including Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, and Demis Hassabis, who have called for some form of governance, and they point to American nonprofits such as Underwriters Laboratories and the American Law Institute as precedents for building institutions that governments later adopt. They acknowledge that the nonprofit would not resolve every risk, and that a successful AI future would still raise questions about human purpose and control that will need institutions able to change over time.

Articles.Title: How To Govern Artificial Intelligence Without Government
