On the wider region, Singapore will chair ASEAN in 2027 and plans to work with Germany to push toward an ASEAN-EU free trade agreement, which the two regions' 50 years of relations in 2026 make timely.

Wong said that pursuing that trade pact would be challenging and complex, but he expressed some optimism because the EU has already signed bilateral trade pacts with Singapore and Vietnam and is negotiating with Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand. He also cited ASEAN's Digital Economy Framework Agreement as a step toward bringing the two regions' digital systems together. Merz said Germany was ready to support the ASEAN Power Grid initiative, which aims to connect electricity networks across the region, and that he favoured linking existing free trade structures with German regional partners. Wong welcomed Germany's endorsement of the GUIDE initiative, a voluntary effort to protect subsea cables and pipelines, of which Singapore is one of 17 founding members. Defence cooperation will also expand into areas such as defence technology, cybersecurity, space and supply chain resilience, Wong said.

The leaders' meeting followed a series of earlier engagements, including a lunch hosted by Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong and a meeting with President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, at which the two sides discussed mutual investment and reform of the multilateral system. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs described the renewed declaration as a forward-looking and ambitious guide for relations between the two countries. Wong said the partnership rests on six decades of friendship and that closer ties matter more as the world becomes more uncertain and fragmented. Merz said both countries were committed to developing the partnership over the long term. The articles do not say when the new AI institutions were set up or when specific joint projects will begin.

Articles.Title: Singapore, Germany to collaborate on AI use in industries, step up research on new tech

stories.Headline: Your AI Stack Is Exposed. Make It Unreachable.
stories.Summary:
Dark Reading published a sponsored piece on October 27, 2026, arguing that organizations running AI infrastructure face the same exposure problem that has long plagued internet-facing services such as VPN concentrators, firewalls, and remote access gateways. The article, written by Galeal Zino, founder and CEO of NetFoundry, says attackers increasingly exploit unauthenticated network-facing flaws, a category marked in CVSS as network attack vector with no privileges required. It notes that the 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report already ranked vulnerability exploitation as attackers' top breach vector. The core concern is that AI stacks, including MCP and LLM gateways, are often missing from asset inventories even though they are well connected and attractive targets.

The article describes how fast these exploits now move. It says automated scanning began within 20 hours of the March disclosure of Langflow's CVE-2026-33017, with attackers harvesting .env files within a day and no public proof of concept needed. Sysdig reportedly saw exploitation of an SSRF flaw in the LMDeploy inference engine 12 hours after disclosure. The piece also cites a campaign against more than 460 targets, in which an AI-driven agent, after failing against the Langflow flaw, independently found and pursued a CVSS 10.0 flaw in n8n.

Against this, the author argues that patching alone is insufficient because attackers begin acting 12 to 20 hours after disclosure. The article's recommendation is to apply Zero Trust to workloads so that services are unreachable from the network. It proposes giving every human, agent, or workload a unique cryptographic identity, requiring mutual authentication and service-specific authorization before any connection opens, and closing all inbound ports so services connect outbound only. The author says NetFoundry's Zero Trust Workload Connectivity product makes this practical, citing 3,000 customer companies delivering more than 1 billion sessions per month.

The piece also says this approach requires no firewall changes and lets teams revoke agent access quickly, while noting that it is written by a company executive promoting its own product. The article places the issue within a longer pattern, describing AI as having multiplied and accelerated a decades-old problem rather than creating it. It concludes that reachability is the variable organizations can control, and that doing so lets a critical flaw listed in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog be handled as a scheduled ticket instead of an emergency. It does not describe any specific new regulatory requirement or deadline, and it offers no independent confirmation of the timelines it reports.

Articles.Title: Your AI Stack Is Exposed. Make It Unreachable. - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: Beware the Slasher: AI Could Kill Off Cybersecurity Pros' Skills
stories.Summary:
Nathan Hamiel, senior director of research at Kudelski Security, warned at Black Hat India in Bengaluru that AI used in cybersecurity operations could erode the very technical skills that professionals need to use it well. Speaking to Dark Reading, he said the concern is growing louder, though he first noticed the problem around 2005 and 2006. He is giving a keynote at the conference titled "The Death of Skills and the Persistence of Problems," and the reporting was published on October 27, 2026. The article frames his point as a double-edged risk for security staff.

Hamiel said that automation can simplify complex tasks, but it can also separate practitioners from the underlying problems they are trying to solve. Without a firm grasp of fundamentals, staff may fail to notice when a tool gives an incorrect result or when its findings need deeper investigation. He argued that these skills must be kept so that tools can be used as effectively as possible. He also said a domain expert using AI gains benefits that a novice without experience cannot, which makes the distinction increasingly important as AI becomes more deeply built into security workflows.

Hamiel also cautioned against extremes in the debate about AI, saying the truth lies between doomers and those who dismiss the technology. He said that recent incidents described as "rogue" AI activity, including OpenAI models reportedly hacking the Hugging Face framework, may reflect a familiar problem in which organizations failed to address basic security weaknesses. In his view, such incidents could prompt a "cybersecurity correction" rather than an apocalypse. He added that many people had not been doing the right thing for a long time.

Hamiel placed the erosion of skills within a longer trend in which technology increasingly stands between professionals and their work, moving them from hands-on operators toward monitors of dashboards. He warned that automating lower-level tasks removes the practice through which junior professionals learn, creating a long-term problem for employers who still need experienced staff. His advice was to apply AI to suitable activities such as threat hunting, threat intelligence and AI-powered penetration testing, while keeping human expertise central. He concluded that skilled professionals using AI will make better use of it than those with less knowledge of the task.

Articles.Title: Beware the Slasher: AI Could Kill Off Cybersecurity Pros' Skills - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: Cognizant restructures software engineering business as clients seek AI returns
stories.Summary:
Cognizant Technology Solutions Corp. is undertaking what the article calls its largest restructuring in nearly four years, merging its application development, digital engineering and software testing practices into one group. The company started reorganizing effective 26 October, according to internal memos that Mint accessed. Under the new setup, the business is split into three units: Industry Delivery Units, Frontier Capability Units and Application Services Units. Employees began being tagged to newly formed departments from 1 October, and the company has spent the last four months preparing them for the change.

The new Software Engineering Group will serve clients across industries including financial institutions, healthcare and life sciences, product and resources companies, and communications, media and technology firms. The Frontier Capability Units will build AI-native software products using models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google's Gemini. Employees assigned to the Application Services Unit will specialize in mainframes, application management and software testing tools. The company said the model is meant to protect current client delivery while building the talent and partnerships needed for AI-native work.

Cognizant attributed the restructuring to clients demanding better returns on their artificial intelligence investments, as stated in an internal memo that Mint also reviewed. The memo described the gap between AI spending and returns as the defining challenge enterprises face today. Chief executive Ravi Kumar, who took charge in January 2023, leads the company, which reported 2025 revenue of $21.1 billion, up 7% from a year earlier. Mint could not independently confirm the leadership structure of the new units, and questions sent to the company on Sunday went unanswered.

The change follows earlier steps, including a "Bridge Program" introduced in June to help employees move into future-ready roles. The article notes that rivals have also reorganized, with Accenture consolidating its businesses under "Reinvention Services" in September 2025 and Tata Consultancy Services undertaking a similar exercise in July 2026. Cognizant also announced Project Leap in April, a transformation program with investments in AI and workforce upskilling that it expected to cost $230 million to $320 million and save as much as $300 million this year. The article does not say what further changes may follow.

Articles.Title: Cognizant restructures software engineering business as clients seek AI returns

stories.Headline: Infostealer riding the AI Train
stories.Summary:
The Aokigahara infostealer, a newly observed piece of malware that Check Point Research described on October 23, 2026, combines traditional data theft with dedicated routines for AI applications and developer tools. Its operators may have previously used the names Kamidere or Stygian for an earlier version. Beyond the usual targets such as browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, VPN clients, FTP clients, password managers and email applications, the malware is built to collect authentication files and session data tied to Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot and Gemini CLI. It also gathers AWS, Azure and Google Cloud credentials, Git credential files and SSH private keys from development environments.

The researchers say the expanded targeting reflects a shift in what attackers may value, namely access to AI services and the environments developers use to build software, not only personal accounts and money. Valid credentials or session tokens could expose private conversations and development data, enable unauthorized use of paid services, or be resold as access to compromised accounts. Such secrets could also let an attacker reach cloud resources and source code repositories without a password. The analysis, however, does not confirm how the operators actually monetize what they steal.

The report describes the malware's capabilities in detail, including screenshot capture, clipboard collection, browser credential and cookie theft, and file grabbing from the Desktop, Documents and Downloads folders. It also includes a clipper component dropped beneath a Microsoft Vault directory for clipboard manipulation, along with anti-analysis checks. The language check stops execution on systems set to a list of eleven languages tied to countries of the former Soviet Union, including Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian. Other checks look for debuggers, virtual machines and sandboxes.

Check Point's research is the only source for these findings, and the articles provided do not describe any confirmed victims, attribution to a specific group, or a timeline for further activity. The report is a technical analysis of the malware itself. The research does not state what the company plans to publish next or what defenses it recommends beyond the detail provided. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Infostealer riding the AI Train

stories.Headline: AI in drug development is only as reliable as the evidence behind it
stories.Summary:
AI tools used in drug development are only as dependable as the scientific evidence they draw on, according to a Wolters Kluwer article published on October 27, 2026. The piece argues that AI-enabled workflows in life sciences should keep track of where evidence comes from, what its limits are, what clinical context applies, and what it is meant to convey. It frames these concerns as part of patient safety, since decisions made early in a drug's development shape how it is later studied, communicated, and used. The article stresses that trust in an AI output should rest on the transparency of its underlying evidence rather than on how quickly or confidently the answer appears.

The article sets out what it says life sciences organizations should require from AI systems. Companies should extend the same accountability and governance they apply to research and commercialization to the AI workflows that now feed those processes. Provenance and validation should be the first priorities when selecting an AI tool, meaning users should know the source of the information, the content it is built on, and who stands behind it. The article cites a survey finding that 91% of providers consider it important for AI systems and sources of generated clinical content to be validated by a human expert. It also recommends expert-reviewed, structured medication intelligence so that teams across research, medical, access, commercial, and lifecycle functions work from consistent information.

The article is written by Wolters Kluwer, which sells the products it describes, including UpToDate Expert AI and Medi-Span Expert AI. It presents these tools as examples of evidence-grounded systems that show their sources and keep a link to supporting research. Dr. Kristen Eckler, Director of Clinical Content for UpToDate at Wolters Kluwer Health, is quoted saying that the principle of "do no harm" should guide how new technologies are evaluated and adopted. The article itself makes the broader point that AI does not replace medical expertise and should be designed to work under clinical judgment.

The article supplies several figures to explain the stakes. It says medication-related harm affects 1 in 30 patients and accounts for about half of all avoidable harm in healthcare, and that 41% of physicians and 37% of nurses report using AI to check diagnoses or drug interactions. It also notes that industry leaders see AI output reliability as weak in edge cases, rare diseases, and atypical dosing, and that generic large language models have shown limits in dosing calculations. Looking ahead, it forecasts the global medicine market to grow at a 5 to 8% compound annual rate through 2030, with aging populations adding to medication complexity. The article does not describe any specific incident or regulatory action, and it does not say what will happen next beyond calling for broader governance.

Articles.Title: AI in drug development is only as reliable as the evidence behind it

stories.Headline: Chinese AI models underpin nearly half of S.Korean developers' new releases as open-weight adoption grows
stories.Summary:
A recent study by the South Korean think tank Rockbridge Network Korea found that nearly half of the AI models published by local developers on Hugging Face this year were built on Chinese foundation models. Of the 1,845 models posted by South Korea-based accounts between January and August, 49.3 percent were based on Chinese models, compared with 35.9 percent on US models and 14.9 percent on domestic ones. The Chinese share has climbed quickly, rising from 1.2 percent of new releases in 2023 to 22 percent in 2025, before nearly doubling this year. Alibaba's Qwen led the field with 864 models, or 46.8 percent of the total, well ahead of Google's Gemma and Meta's Llama.

The shift matters because open-weight models, unlike closed systems such as those from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google's Gemini, make their underlying weights publicly available. Developers can download, modify and fine-tune them, including with Korean-language data, without depending on cloud-based AI services. The report said low costs and a broad range of model sizes drew Korean developers to Chinese options, with output costs about one-34th those of comparable top-tier models in one measure, a gap that narrowed to roughly fourfold across a full benchmark run. Industry voices also raised concerns about technological dependence, noting that Alibaba offers both models and cloud infrastructure, which could make it harder for developers to switch away from its ecosystem.

The report's survey of 102 small and medium-sized companies found that 80.2 percent worried about potential data leaks from Chinese AI models, and 67.7 percent pointed to a lack of transparency in how personal data is handled. An industry official quoted by The Korea Times warned that the biggest risk is less about information leaks than about technological dependence and supply-chain vulnerability, especially if US-China tensions led to sanctions or sudden licensing changes. The official also said opaque training-data origins could make it hard for companies to meet strict safety, reliability and compliance requirements. The official argued that Korea should pursue a two-track strategy, building its own secure foundation models while protecting technological sovereignty, rather than deepening reliance on outside models for short-term savings.

Chen Jing, a vice president at the Technology and Strategy Research Institute, offered a contrasting view to the Global Times, arguing that developers choose models based on engineering trade-offs such as cost, performance, licensing and update speed rather than national origin. Chen said the strength of Chinese models increasingly lies in the surrounding ecosystem of documentation, tools and community support, which lowers barriers for smaller teams. China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology reported that Chinese open-source models had recorded more than 10 billion cumulative downloads globally as of July. Chen suggested that wider overseas adoption could give China a larger role in shaping global AI practices and technical standards, while a South Korean AI start-up official said the company used Qwen and DeepSeek mainly for high-traffic services where operating costs were central.

Articles.Title: Chinese AI models underpin nearly half of S.Korean developers' new releases as open-weight adoption grows - Global Times

stories.Headline: AI boom, high-tech prowess fuel China's industrial profit growth, with momentum set to continue: experts
stories.Summary:
Profits at China's major industrial firms rose 15.5 percent year on year in the first nine months of 2026, according to data the National Bureau of Statistics released on Tuesday, October 27, 2026. Firms with annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan (about $2.8 million) earned combined profits of 6.03 trillion yuan from January to September. Growth accelerated to 14.4 percent in September, up from 4.2 percent in August. The Global Times reported the figures, which it tied to strong earnings in artificial intelligence-related industries and high-tech manufacturing.

The electronics sector was the biggest contributor, with profits there doubling and adding 9.6 percentage points to the overall gain. Profits in electronic specialty materials jumped 220 percent, while semiconductor discrete devices rose 51.7 percent. High-tech manufacturing profits climbed 52 percent and made up 25.5 percent of total industrial profits, up 6.2 percentage points from a year earlier. Optical fiber manufacturing profits surged 570 percent as data center construction expanded. The article also cites customs data showing integrated circuit exports up 99.1 percent, electric vehicle exports up 72.3 percent and lithium-ion battery exports up 36.4 percent over the same nine months.

Yu Weining, chief statistician of the bureau's Industrial Statistics Department, described steady industrial production and double-digit cumulative profit growth as evidence of continued progress in high-quality development. Economists quoted in the piece, including Tian Yun in Beijing and Hu Qimu of Huaqiao University, argued that the earnings point to a more self-sustaining model in which technology generates profits that fund further investment. Guidelines issued on October 21 by the Communist Party's Central Committee General Office and the State Council call for closer ties between technological and industrial innovation and for upgrading traditional manufacturing. The bureau said it will expand domestic demand and speed the shift toward new growth drivers, and experts expect momentum to carry into the fourth quarter.

Articles.Title: AI boom, high-tech prowess fuel China's industrial profit growth, with momentum set to continue: experts - Global Times

stories.Headline: In pics: AI-powered restaurant in China's Nanjing
stories.Summary:
The AI Mirror World Restaurant in Nanjing, in east China's Jiangsu Province, drew customers and attention in late October 2026, according to photographs distributed by Xinhua on October 26. Images show diners eating at the restaurant and a customer taking a bowl of soup from a machine. The restaurant is described as operating on a human-machine collaborative model. Photographs of the kitchen show a robotic arm moving ingredients and a staff member working nearby. The restaurant prepares some of its meals and drinks through standardized production, using an AI-powered kitchen.

That kitchen is equipped with smart noodle-making and beverage-making machines. Human staff still take part in the operation alongside the equipment. The photo captions do not give figures on the number of machines, the menu items made this way, or the share of orders they account for. The photographs were taken and released by Xinhua, with photographer Ji Chunpeng credited for the images. The captions describe the restaurant's setup but do not name an owner, operator, or company behind the venture.

The articles give no statements from the restaurant's management or from any official. The articles offer no wider context about how common such restaurants are, nor do they say whether the restaurant plans to expand, change its menu, or face any regulatory review. Because the material consists only of photo captions, there is no further reporting on how the concept has been received so far. More to follow.

Articles.Title: In pics: AI-powered restaurant in China's Nanjing - Global Times

stories.Headline: Chinese investment in Vietnam expands into AI, other high-tech sectors, as businesses eye deeper cooperation
stories.Summary:
Chinese investment in Vietnam is expanding beyond traditional manufacturing into artificial intelligence, the digital economy and semiconductors, according to attendees at an investment forum in Beijing on Tuesday. The growing interest was highlighted at the China-Vietnam Economic, Trade and Investment Cooperation Exchange Meeting, jointly hosted by the Vietnamese Embassy in China and the China Overseas Development Association. Businesses there explored investment opportunities and possible partnerships in emerging industries. Vietnamese companies are also seeking closer cooperation with Chinese firms in advanced technologies.

Do Quang Tung, counselor at the Vietnamese Embassy in Beijing, described bilateral economic ties as marked by expanding trade, diversified investment and a clear move toward high-quality, technology-intensive sectors. He said China remains Vietnam's largest trading partner, with bilateral trade reaching about $256.5 billion in 2025 and exceeding $253 billion in the first nine months of 2026. Chinese investors registered $2.27 billion in newly licensed capital in the first nine months of 2026. China also ranked first by number of new projects, with about 850 in the first seven months of the year. Do said this investment is shifting from traditional processing toward railway links, clean energy, the digital economy, AI and semiconductors.

The presence of Chinese investors is already visible in Vietnam's industrial parks, where manufacturers are bringing businesses that sit along their supply chains. Bui The Long, general manager of Green i-Park Corp, said his park hosts 36 Chinese investors, mainly in electronics and electrical appliances, agricultural equipment and lighting products. He said upstream and downstream suppliers have followed these companies into the park. Earlier, Chinese investors were generally smaller in scale, while South Korean and Japanese firms made up a larger share of foreign investment, but Bui said large Chinese companies are now arriving. He also said Vietnam's AI sector is still at an early stage, and he hopes Chinese companies will develop AI projects there.

He Zhenwei, president of the China Overseas Development Association, argued that the next phase of cooperation should improve quality as well as trade volume, particularly in AI and the digital economy. He suggested AI cooperation could focus on localizing large-language models and big data applications in Vietnam. He said the aim should be local application of Chinese technologies rather than simple introduction, helping Vietnam advance industrialization and modernization. Do said the forum helped both sides better understand each other's policies and needs, which he called a crucial foundation for long-term partnerships. He called for more frequent exchanges and welcomed Chinese enterprises investing in high-quality, technology-intensive and environmentally sustainable projects in Vietnam.

Articles.Title: Chinese investment in Vietnam expands into AI, other high-tech sectors, as businesses eye deeper cooperation - Global Times

stories.Headline: Decoding the Bark: The Promise and Limits of AI in Animal Communication
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Kaunas University of Technology in Lithuania and other scientists have been using artificial intelligence to analyze pet vocalizations, according to an article published on vocal.media on October 27, 2026. The systems can sort recurring barks, whines and meows by pitch, duration, rhythm and frequency, and link them to behaviors or surroundings. Research published this year in Frontiers in Veterinary Science described a deep-learning system trained on thousands of dog and cat sounds that classified distress, playfulness and anticipation with high accuracy. The article describes this as a useful advance, though it does not claim the systems understand what animals mean. Scientists draw a sharp line between spotting a sound pattern and grasping a message.

The article says that recognizing a pattern does not show that an animal is sending a discrete message comparable to a human sentence. A bark is often an involuntary or semi-voluntary expression of an inner state rather than a word. Separate research tested advanced models on toddler sounds, where human meaning is already known, and the models sometimes grouped sounds with different meanings together while separating others with similar intent. The researchers concluded that sound alone is not enough and that context, body language and the listener's response matter too. The article notes that this challenge is even greater with animals, since the same bark can mean very different things depending on posture and surroundings.

Because of this, the researchers quoted in the article favor a multimodal approach that combines sound with facial expression, posture, tail movement, activity level and the immediate environment. Studies of dogs using pre-recorded communication buttons have likewise warned against reading a single press without the behavior that came just before and after it. The article predicts that a future animal "translator" will look less like the science-fiction devices of popular imagination and more like an analytical system estimating an animal's emotional state or likely intention. It suggests practical uses, such as helping owners spot early signs of stress, fear or discomfort, and giving veterinarians and shelter workers an objective additional clue when monitoring wellbeing and recovery.

The article also reports that scientists urge caution about claims that AI will let people talk with animals. Researchers told The Guardian that public excitement can outpace the evidence, especially when commercial apps promise more than current science supports. The article states that no validated system yet translates a dog's or cat's thoughts into human language, and that true semantic translation remains a distant, perhaps unattainable, goal. For now, the article concludes, AI works better as a tireless listener that detects subtle patterns humans might miss than as a universal pet translator.

Articles.Title: Decoding the Bark: The Promise and Limits of AI in Animal Communication

stories.Headline: Fitch affirms Broadcom at ’A-’ with positive outlook despite AI backstop risks
stories.Summary:
Fitch Ratings on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, affirmed Broadcom Inc.'s Long-Term Issuer Default Rating at 'A-' and kept its outlook at Positive. The agency said surging demand for artificial intelligence continues to strengthen the chipmaker's balance sheet, even as Broadcom takes on more off-balance-sheet financing. Fitch's view is that strong cash generation should keep core EBITDA leverage below its 1.5x upgrade threshold. It also said complex customer backstops add some credit risk.

The main concern is Broadcom's role in more than $70 billion of lease-financing transactions across two customer structures. These include a recent $43.5 billion residual value support pact, under which Broadcom guarantees lease shortfalls for custom tensor processing unit pods used by a frontier artificial intelligence laboratory. Broadcom has also made commitments tied to a $42 billion convertible note facility and a $1.5 billion delayed draw term loan. Fitch plans to add roughly $4 billion to Broadcom's adjusted debt by the end of fiscal 2027, rising to about $15 billion by fiscal 2029 under an accelerated depreciation model. The agency noted that Broadcom's liquidity gives it ample cushion and projected post-dividend free cash flow above $30 billion in fiscal 2026.

Fitch's analysis rests on Broadcom's own operations and on the wider industry. Its custom accelerator and Ethernet networking businesses are expected to grow faster than its legacy silicon and software operations, which temporarily concentrates revenue among hyperscalers and frontier labs. Predictable recurring revenue from VMware and legacy software is expected to keep operating EBITDA margins above 60% through cyclical swings. Fitch also warned that the broader AI buildout increasingly depends on circular commercial and financing ties among suppliers, labs and third-party capital providers. A sharp pullback in hyperscaler spending or frontier lab liquidity could reduce infrastructure orders and strain industry-wide conditions.

For credit investors, an upgrade would depend on Broadcom keeping leverage below 1.5x while reducing its reliance on vendor financing. Fitch said a change of the outlook to Stable would be tied to backstop-adjusted net debt rising above $150 billion. It set $185 billion as the level that could trigger a downgrade if hardware values fall sharply. The articles do not describe any further rating actions beyond these thresholds.

Articles.Title: Fitch affirms Broadcom at ’A-’ with positive outlook despite AI backstop risks

stories.Headline: People Who Absolutely Refuse To Use AI Usually Say 6 Things When Someone Brings It Up
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion-and-lifestyle piece rather than a breaking news story, so the full structure applies. A YourTango article by writer Sophie Bagheri, published October 27, 2026, lists six arguments that people who refuse to use AI commonly make when the subject comes up. The piece presents these as the typical positions of people opposed to AI, and it includes the author's own stated stance as someone who is against using it. The article frames the debate as one where some people see AI as a way to save the world while others fear it will be a downfall.

The first argument is that using AI amounts to plagiarism, since AI systems draw on existing sources and reproduce that material without credit. The article notes that legal experts are still working out how far AI infringes on the copyrights of the works it learns from, and that this will take time. Meanwhile, the author says, people who object feel a moral duty not to use the tools at the potential expense of the writers and researchers whose work is passed along unacknowledged. The second argument is that AI will take jobs, a debate the article calls complicated, since supporters point to a productivity boom while others expect unemployment to rise within the next decade. Opponents are most worried about entry-level and lower-paid workers already being replaced in settings such as grocery stores and customer service centers.

Other objections concern learning and the environment. The article argues that because AI lets people finish tasks without understanding the steps, younger generations may lose the ability to do the work themselves, and some say AI is making people less capable. It also cites studies showing AI uses large amounts of water and energy, and quotes Mike Weinstein, director of sustainability at Southern New Hampshire University, saying that AI data centers are often located in areas powered mainly by fossil fuels, which release greenhouse gases. Researchers also point to concerning water depletion in certain areas, including the Great Lakes. The article adds that New York City Public Schools have banned AI in elementary schools to protect students' critical thinking and their relationships with teachers, a policy many want applied elsewhere.

The final argument concerns art, with the article noting that AI can write poems and books, generate paintings, and even create actors. It quotes author Eric Reinhart saying that the essence of art is lost in machine invention and that democratic society is put at risk as a result. The author adds that art challenges society's norms, so handing that role to AI raises the question of what would be left to question. The article is part of a wider YourTango lifestyle series, and it offers no set timeline for how these debates will be resolved.

Articles.Title: People Who Absolutely Refuse To Use AI Usually Say 6 Things When Someone Brings It Up

stories.Headline: Lao Gan Ma faces backlash over AI automation claims, company denies mass layoffs
stories.Summary:
Lao Gan Ma, one of China's best-known chili sauce brands, has faced public criticism after comments from one of its executives about artificial intelligence were read as evidence of large-scale job cuts. The controversy started when Li Xin, the company's executive vice-president and chief quality officer, spoke at the 2026 Guizhou provincial quality development conference about the firm's AI-powered visual inspection system. Li said the technology had significantly lowered product defect rates and helped the Guiyang-based company reach record revenue of 5.4 billion yuan in 2025. According to China Business Herald, Li also said that more than 600 workers had sorted chili peppers on the production line before the system was introduced, compared with just 48 afterward. Social media quickly amplified the remarks, with some posts claiming that more than 500 workers had been laid off, and some consumers threatened to boycott the brand.

Commentary cited in the reporting focused on the human side of the debate. Jason Yu, general manager of CTR Market Research, said the backlash reflects growing public concern about how AI affects people, not a rejection of the technology itself. He argued that China's AI strategy has consistently stressed balancing technological progress with employment, and that companies should explain how workers are supported through a transition. Yu also said that for consumer brands, empathy matters as much as efficiency.

The company, for its part, has rejected the reports of mass layoffs. On October 26, a staff member from its human resources department told local media that such claims were false, and according to Phoenix News the firm confirmed it uses AI inspection technology but said it had never employed that many workers on the production line. Public records have nonetheless added fuel to the debate. Jimu News reported, citing data from the corporate information platforms Tianyancha and Qichacha, that the number of employees covered by social insurance at Guiyang Nanming Laoganma Flavor Food Co fell from 2,912 in 2022 to 1,783 in 2023, then to 941 in 2024 and 740 in 2025.

The same reporting notes that changes in insured headcount do not by themselves prove layoffs, since retirements, staff turnover, outsourcing arrangements, or changes in the legal entity responsible for social insurance can also shift the figures. Meanwhile, the company's financial performance has stayed steady. According to the 2025 Guizhou Top 100 Enterprises ranking, its revenue was 5.26 billion yuan in 2022, 5.38 billion yuan in 2023, and 5.39 billion yuan in 2024. The articles do not report any further official response or regulatory action.

Articles.Title: Lao Gan Ma faces backlash over AI automation claims, company denies mass layoffs - China Daily

stories.Headline: Cadence Raises Annual Revenue Forecast as AI Boosts Chip Design Productivity
stories.Summary:
Cadence Design Systems said on October 26, 2026, local time, during its third-quarter earnings call that artificial intelligence could make chip design up to 1,000 times more productive than in the past. CEO Anirudh Devgan compared the effort of designing a single central processing unit two decades ago, which required 500 engineers working for five years at IBM and Intel, with today's 50 engineers working for six months. He said chip design has already become roughly 100 times easier, and AI could add another five- to tenfold efficiency gain. The company also outlined plans to fold its own chip-design AI models into its design tools alongside general-purpose models.

Cadence unveiled Maestro, a family of AI models built for semiconductor and system design, based on open-weight models post-trained with the company's tools and data. A router inside the system chooses between proprietary models and outside frontier models depending on the task. Cadence said early results showed up to a 30% gain in design quality and up to a fivefold gain in token efficiency compared with general-purpose foundation models. The company plans to link Maestro to its AI design agents, ChipStack, InnoStack and AuraStack, which are already in use at major chipmakers. Devgan argued that controlling the models, agents and design tools together is essential for strong results and for protecting customer data confidentiality.

The agents have produced measurable gains for customers named in the report. Samsung Foundry adopted InnoStack in the third quarter to improve process migration and design technology co-optimization. Renesas Electronics reported a 34-fold productivity gain in its microcontroller development team after applying InnoStack to multiple tasks, and plans to extend it to layout automation. MediaTek put ChipStack into its digital verification flow, raising verification coverage by 50% to 70% while cutting engineering workloads by 1.4 to 2 times. Devgan also said about 45% of Cadence's business now comes from non-semiconductor companies, including hyperscalers, automotive, aerospace and financial firms designing their own chips.

Financially, Cadence reported third-quarter revenue of $1.63331 billion, up 22% from a year earlier, with a non-GAAP operating margin of 44.1% and non-GAAP earnings per share up 9% to $2.11. Backlog reached a record $8.2 billion at quarter end. Chief Financial Officer John Wall said AI agents can run far more design iterations than engineers working manually, which could sharply increase use of EDA tools. Cadence raised its full-year revenue forecast to between $6.387 billion and $6.417 billion, implying 21% growth, up from the 19% it forecast after its second quarter. The article does not describe further steps beyond these announced plans.

Articles.Title: Cadence Raises Annual Revenue Forecast as AI Boosts Chip Design Productivity - THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media

stories.Headline: AI research on online customer experience shifts from automation to emotion, ethics and trust
stories.Summary:
A bibliometric study of a decade of research has mapped how artificial intelligence has reshaped the study of online customer experience, and the field is in the middle of a shift. Researchers Yarramsetti Sumanth and G Somasekhar reviewed 257 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2015 and 2024, using the Biblioshiny interface of the R-based Bibliometrix package and the VOSviewer mapping tool. Their review appeared in Discover Artificial Intelligence. Output rose sharply after 2018, and the research topics moved from efficiency and automation toward chatbots, personalization, emotional AI, trust and ethics.

The authors built their corpus by searching Scopus for English-language journal articles that paired artificial intelligence or AI with customer experience in the title, abstract or keywords. That query returned 1,122 records, and screening by year, subject area, document type, source type and language narrowed it to the final 257. The authors warn that requiring the explicit phrase customer experience may have left out related studies on personalization, service quality or AI-enabled services, so their findings describe the narrower AI-CX literature. Publications grew by 53.75 percent across the period, which the authors link to greater industry involvement in the digital economy and the rising strategic weight of customer experience as a topic.

India led in output with 56 articles and the United States followed with 52, but citation impact told a different story. The United States gathered 2,318 citations from its papers, while the United Kingdom drew 2,993 citations from only 23. The authors attribute this to earlier publication dates, wider international collaboration and placement in prominent journals. The Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services contributed the most articles and held the highest h-index in the set. Jochen Wirtz and Anuj Kumar were the most productive individual authors, each with four papers, and Tat-Huei Cham and Eugene Cheng-Xi Aw recorded the highest total citations at 122.

The analysis of 906 author keywords identified four thematic clusters: a technology group covering chatbots, deep learning, generative AI and machine learning; an outcomes group covering satisfaction, service quality and support; a strategy group covering digital transformation and engagement; and an emerging group on anthropomorphism. Between 2015 and 2018 the research centered on personalization and big data for e-commerce, from 2019 to 2021 it turned to chatbots and real-time analytics, and from 2021 to 2024 the fastest-growing topics were omnichannel personalization, generative AI and affective AI. The authors describe this as a move from treating AI mainly as an efficiency tool toward examining it as a customer experience issue. They also note that their theoretical frameworks are interpretive and not empirically validated, and they call for future work combining bibliometrics with qualitative review, comparison across databases, and study of ethics and consumer vulnerability.

Articles.Title: AI research on online customer experience shifts from automation to emotion, ethics and trust

stories.Headline: AI slows growth for Infosys and keeps it afloat at the same time
stories.Summary:
Indian IT services firm Infosys reported mixed quarterly results late last week, revealing that its AI revenue rose 29 percent sequentially and now accounts for 10.5 percent of its incoming cash. Those gains came against a much weaker picture overall, with year-on-year revenue growth of just 1.5 percent in its second quarter. Chief financial officer Jayesh Sanghrajka told investors that growth fell below expectations, with lower volumes and smaller price increases than the company had anticipated. Infosys has said that customers now expect it to charge less when it uses AI, and those savings are already built into its multi-year deals. The company's full-year outlook has also been trimmed.

Sanghrajka said that Infosys will not cut prices to win deals and intends to keep its margins at around 21 percent. To support that goal, the company is running a program called Project Maximus to find efficiencies in its own operations, and it is also using AI-powered tools to win more sales. CEO and managing director Salil Parekh said that pricing pressure across the industry is linked to the wider environment and to discussion of AI productivity. He noted that large client programs now carry a three or five-year outlook. Sanghrajka also pointed to a large deal the company walked away from because it did not meet return expectations.

The company cited $8.8 billion of new deals won in the first half of its financial year, 68 percent of which came from net new customers, as evidence that its fundamentals remain sound. Even so, Infosys lowered its full-year revenue growth forecast from 1.5 to 3.0 percent in its first-quarter results to 1.0 to 2.0 percent in the second. Sanghrajka acknowledged that retail and high-tech clients have slowed their services spending and that the second half of the financial year is usually slow. Infosys's shares are down more than 25 percent over the past twelve months, though they did not fall sharply after the latest update. Bloomberg reports that investment analysts have downgraded the company, suggesting they see weak prospects ahead.

Articles.Title: AI slows growth for Infosys and keeps it afloat at the same time

stories.Headline: Singapore launches AI initiatives to help companies adopt technology - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
Singapore launched a suite of initiatives on Tuesday to help companies adopt artificial intelligence, according to a statement from Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG). The package includes programs aimed at industry leaders, small businesses and whole sectors. Separately, the Agency for Science, Technology and Research unveiled a new effort in materials research. The articles describe these as government-led steps and do not say whether they are ongoing or one-time.

Under the Champions of AI program, EnterpriseSG and other government agencies will help participating companies build long-term AI transformation roadmaps, gain access to expertise and solutions, and strengthen workforce skills. The program is open to Singapore-based companies that are committed to making AI a core driver of growth and to enterprise-wide transformation. It will begin with 24 companies across various industries, and more will join gradually over time. For small and medium-sized enterprises, a series of workshops on agentic AI has been introduced, following a pilot in which more than 280 small businesses applied such tools in marketing, sales and customer service.

The statement said more workshops will be rolled out next month and scaled further in 2027. A separate Catalytic AI Solutions initiative aims to speed AI adoption across entire sectors, starting with advanced manufacturing, trade and logistics. The Agency for Science, Technology and Research launched the Materials Accelerator for Research, Venture and Enterprise Launchpad, backed by about 150 million Singapore dollars, or 117 million U.S. dollars. The initiative is meant to close the gap between research and commercial use by combining AI models with automated laboratories. The articles give no further detail on how the funds will be divided among the programs.

EnterpriseSG said in its statement that AI is helping researchers identify promising new materials more quickly. It added that turning those materials into products that can be synthesized, validated and manufactured at scale remains a challenge. That challenge is the reason for the materials launchpad, which aims to speed the path from discovery to commercialization. The articles do not describe any reaction from outside experts or companies, nor do they set out a timeline for the materials program beyond its launch.

Articles.Title: Singapore launches AI initiatives to help companies adopt technology - Xinhua

stories.Headline: China Focus: China's booming embodied AI industry creates new professions - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
China's embodied artificial intelligence industry is creating new jobs, and Xinhua reported from Chongqing on October 27, 2026, describing several of them. In September, China's Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security and other government departments announced 11 new professions, including embodied AI robot application technicians and digital twin engineers. Tang Zixiang, an embodied AI robot application technician at Sevnce Robotics in Liangjiang New Area, trains robots to perform tasks. He adjusts knobs to simulate working conditions, uses the resulting data to train AI models, and then tests those models on robotic arms.

The work moves robots from laboratory settings toward real use, and the article describes what that demands. Sevnce Robotics makes specialized robots for the petroleum, chemical and power industries, where machines can replace or assist human inspectors in hazardous places. Technicians must set speed and accuracy requirements, test whether robots recover from failed operations, and decide when a robot should stop or call for human intervention. Robots in these settings must run reliably for long periods. Tang said the aim is to make machines that can operate safely over the long term.

Digital twin engineering is the other profession highlighted. Jiang Lei builds virtual factories through 3D reconstruction so inspection robots can rehearse routes and check whether their cameras capture instrument readings before deployment. Jiang said that traditional on-site commissioning might take two or three weeks, while rehearsal in simulation could cut that to two or three days. Simulation also generates data for algorithm testing and training, which reduces the time and cost of collecting data in real environments. Jiang studied vehicle engineering at university and moved from autonomous driving research into robot development, and Tang, who graduated this year in computer science, applies reinforcement learning and imitation learning.

The article places these roles within broader growth. According to figures from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, China had more than 400 humanoid robot models and produced over 40,000 units in the first half of 2026. The industry's expansion is also creating demand for workers in data collection, model training, system commissioning, and operations and maintenance. Earlier this month, Beijing City University launched a high-skilled training program in embodied AI applications that gives industry workers five days of intensive study combining classroom instruction with hands-on work on real robots. Tang said he hopes robots will take over dangerous, tedious and repetitive work and complement human workers rather than replace them.

Articles.Title: China Focus: China's booming embodied AI industry creates new professions - Xinhua

stories.Headline: More people are running their health concerns by AI before their physicians: What to know
stories.Summary:
Many patients now consult AI chatbots about their health before they ever see a doctor, and the trend is growing. An Aflac survey released in August found that three-quarters of Gen Z adults and nearly two-thirds of millennials turn to AI for health support before seeking professional care. The survey of 2,000 adults also found that 18% of Gen Z and 14% of millennials schedule doctor's appointments only after exhausting AI or online tools. Clinicians say patients increasingly arrive with conclusions already formed from their searches.

A Pew Research Center survey found that 34% of U.S. adults have asked AI chatbots about their health. Nearly half of those who did said the information was extremely or very helpful. Physicians interviewed for the coverage described patients who wanted to stop cholesterol medication or question vaccines based on chatbot conversations. Mental health has drawn particular attention, because some patients use chatbots in place of licensed professionals, which can delay real care.

Liability is an open question. Meghan O'Connor, a health law partner at Quarles & Brady, said the answer is still emerging and may take years of litigation to settle. She noted that AI companies' disclaimers that their outputs are not medical advice may not hold up if a tool was marketed as diagnostic. She also said a clinician's failure to correct inaccurate AI advice could become a malpractice issue.

Medical malpractice attorney Rick Groffsky of Sommers Schwartz told Healthcare IT News that health systems should expect AI-related lawsuits. He advised them to document how they evaluated AI products, who oversees them, and how performance is monitored after rollout. Groffsky said future suits could arise from both overreliance and underreliance on AI. Reporters following the story are urged to talk with clinicians, patients, health system informatics officers, and to track legal cases, such as a Florida man's lawsuit against ChatGPT.

Articles.Title: More people are running their health concerns by AI before their physicians: What to know

stories.Headline: These Dividend-Paying Stocks Offer Notable AI Exposure: AVGO VRT
stories.Summary:
Zacks Investment Research published an article on October 27, 2026, arguing that two dividend-paying technology stocks, Broadcom and Vertiv, offer exposure to artificial intelligence trends. The piece, written by Derek Lewis, says income-focused investors often overlook tech stocks because those companies tend to reinvest spare cash into growth. It singles out the two companies as examples of firms that combine AI tailwinds with regular payouts to shareholders. The article frames the idea as a way for investors to earn dividends while holding AI-linked shares.

Vertiv provides power, cooling, and IT infrastructure products and services for data centers, communication networks, and commercial and industrial facilities. The article says its shares currently yield about 0.1% annually, and it is rated Zacks Rank #2 (Buy). Analysts' consensus expectations, according to the piece, point to 46% earnings growth on 40% higher sales when the company reports its upcoming quarterly results. The article presents Vertiv as a play on data center buildout that offers a mix of growth and modest yield.

Broadcom is described as having moved quickly into the AI race, building a broad portfolio of technologies for next-generation AI infrastructure. The article says its shares yield about 0.8% annually and that the company has a five-year annualized dividend growth rate of 13.3%. It credits the company's strong cash generation with allowing it to reward shareholders consistently over its history. The piece also notes that Broadcom has long been a favorite among investors seeking tech exposure together with regular payouts.

The article was originally published on Zacks Investment Research and is one of many similar pieces on the platform. Its related-links list includes older articles on AI-linked dividend stocks, which suggests the theme recurs in Zacks coverage. The page also displays market data, including a 30-year mortgage rate of 7.41 and a Fed funds target rate of 3.88, with a Federal Open Market Committee decision scheduled for October 28, 2026. The articles provided do not describe any specific policy or market action tied to the two stocks beyond these figures.

Articles.Title: These Dividend-Paying Stocks Offer Notable AI Exposure: AVGO VRT

stories.Headline: ‘Black October’ exposes how criminals use AI to cause real-world chaos — but you can protect yourself
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a wave of cyber incidents that they call "Black October," which they say exposed how vulnerable much of the world's online infrastructure is. Among the examples given are serious flaws in PHP, the programming code on which about 70% of the world's internet sites are built, which could have let hackers break into servers and take control without a password. Malicious software was also distributed through LiteLLM, a tool used by AI developers, and many companies were rushing to fix flaws in their code. The article's sources do not give a single named perpetrator for the wider wave, though they describe criminals and an Iran-linked group called CyberAv3ngers.

The threats to the physical world are highlighted as especially serious. Seven states have confirmed attempts to sabotage water plants: New Jersey, Oregon, Minnesota, Michigan, South Dakota, Alabama and Georgia. More than 30 Minnesota water systems were attacked in July, and a Georgia attack led to a boil-water advisory in one county, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies. The article notes that the Colonial Pipeline shutdown in May 2021, after a ransomware attack, disrupted fuel supply to the East Coast and that the company paid $4.4 million to Russian hackers. On the defensive side, Anthropic said in an October 8 statement that six months of AI scanning had flagged more than 29,000 potential vulnerabilities, but humans had manually reviewed and fixed only about 6,000.

Scott Schober, CEO of New Jersey-based Berkeley Varitronics Systems, is the main voice in the article. He warned that AI is dramatically speeding up the discovery of software weaknesses, that criminals can exploit them before governments or companies can respond, and that AI lets people without programming skills write attack scripts. He called for stronger oversight and international coordination, and he advised individuals to keep passwords, Social Security numbers, bank details and sensitive family information out of chatbot conversations, and to use long, unique passwords with multifactor authentication. European authorities, the article says, advised businesses using PHP to coordinate with hosting providers, install updates and isolate exposed applications when repairs are not immediately possible.

The article places this in a broader context in which most of the biggest US companies have been hacked at some point, including UnitedHealth, Facebook, Microsoft, Ticketmaster, Yahoo and National Public Data, which had 2.7 billion records stolen in 2024. Schober said AI also helps criminals sort stolen records and link details about potential victims, making fraud and extortion more targeted, and that people's private chats with AI have been stolen on a large scale. Experts describe the risk of a "vulnpocalypse," a backlog of weaknesses growing faster than defenders can assess and fix them. Schober's view, as the article reports it, is that AI can strengthen defenses as well as attacks, but criminals are moving faster.

Articles.Title: ‘Black October’ exposes how criminals use AI to cause real-world chaos — but you can protect yourself

stories.Headline: AI and Technology-Related Securities Litigation Surge in 2026
stories.Summary:
According to Cornerstone Research, securities class actions rose sharply in the first half of 2026, climbing about 30 percent from 93 filings to 121. The sharpest growth came in AI-related cases, which reached 15 in the first half, nearly matching the full-year total for 2025. The article frames this as a trend driven by several core factors rather than a single event. Those factors are the focus of the analysis that follows.

One major driver is what the article calls AI washing, a deceptive practice in which companies exaggerate or fabricate their use of artificial intelligence in products, services, or operations. The article compares it to greenwashing and says the aim is to attract investors and lift stock prices. When real-world performance falls short of such claims, firms can face lawsuits, and financial regulators such as the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission can penalize misleading AI statements. Exaggerated financial benefits are a related problem, since promised growth or productivity gains may not materialize. Investors may then reassess the outlook, see share prices fall, and allege that earlier statements concealed the risks.

The article also points to high costs as a factor, noting that AI systems require heavy spending on computer chips, data centers, electricity, and skilled engineers. It gives the example of a company spending $5 billion on AI infrastructure based on forecasts of strong demand that customers do not meet. Securities lawyers often examine companies after large stock drops, and because major AI-linked firms carry huge market values, even small percentage declines can wipe out billions. The Cornerstone mid-year assessment found that AI-related cases made up about 13 percent of core filings but accounted for 73 percent of the disclosure dollar loss index. The article concludes that AI-related filings remain the most significant trend in federal filings and show no sign of slowing.

Articles.Title: AI and Technology-Related Securities Litigation Surge in 2026

stories.Headline: The Best Ways To Tell If Someone Is Using AI Glasses
stories.Summary:
The article is a how-to guide rather than a news report, so it does not describe a specific event with a date, a perpetrator, or a new rule. Instead, it explains how people can spot smart glasses that might be used to record them without consent. Its concern is that these glasses can enable stalking or other covert activity, especially as public recording draws more scrutiny. The piece was published on October 27, 2026, by Jack Peachey on Engadget.

The first set of signs is physical, since smart glasses often need thick frames, particularly around the temples and outer edges of the lenses where camera lenses usually sit. Most smart glasses also show a small LED indicator light when filming, so a person can look for that light. The article warns, however, that low-cost copies sold on sites like TikTok Shop and Temu may lack that light, and that audio-only glasses have no camera at all. Behavior can also offer clues, such as someone repeatedly pressing the temples of their glasses, pausing as if reading something, or murmuring voice commands. The article notes that these behaviors could also have harmless explanations.

The article also points to apps that scan for nearby Bluetooth devices and identifiers linked to AI glasses. It names Nearby Glasses and ZuckOff as examples and says neither is fully reliable, because a wearer may have Bluetooth turned off and false positives can occur. The article advises against confronting someone just because of a suspicion. It recommends moving away, contacting authorities if someone is following you, and, at a private meeting or event, making a neutral statement that smart glasses are not permitted. If you do approach a stranger, the article says to do so calmly in a public place.

Articles.Title: The Best Ways To Tell If Someone Is Using AI Glasses

stories.Headline: The Global AI Buildout in 122 Deals
stories.Summary:
This is a monthly roundup rather than a single breaking event, so the three-to-four-paragraph format applies. Writing it in my own words from the article, the headline's "122 deals" is a count of verified data center transactions tracked worldwide in September 2026, and the author picks out ten recurring patterns and a top-ten ranking. The biggest buyer named is Anthropic, which signed seven-year project plans with Akamai committing about $11.6 billion, leased capacity at Zerra DC's Western Downs Digital Park in Australia subject to foreign investment review, and anchored a $35 billion cloud deal with Lambda for roughly 350MW at Hut 8's Beacon Point campus in Nueces County, Texas. Other large moves included Google's 22-year nuclear power agreement with Fortum for the Loviisa plant in Finland, Google's pledge of at least €13 billion to Finnish digital infrastructure for 2027 and 2028, and the completion of CPP Investments, Equinix and Partners Group's $4.0 billion acquisition of atNorth alongside a separate $4.1 billion financing package. Financing was large as well: VIRTUS closed £2.45 billion of bank debt from 13 lenders, ZanKore signed a senior term loan of up to $3.1 billion to fund an initial 100MW of NVIDIA AI infrastructure in Indonesia, and Mistral closed a €3 billion Series D at a valuation above €21 billion.

The article describes a shift toward on-site gas generation and very long contracts. Aligned broke ground on its 2GW Project Phoenix in Pennsylvania with onsite gas power planned, INNIO booked a firm 450MW order for gas-engine prime power, and Woodway signed for a 22-mile pipeline feeding behind-the-meter generation. Commitments are also lengthening, with a 15-year anchor lease between Blockfusion and CoreWeave at Niagara Falls and a ten-year agreement for 65.1MW in Malaysia from Bitdeer AI. The top-ranked deals split four in Europe, three in North America, two in Asia-Pacific and one in the Middle East and Africa. Among them, PPC and AWS signed a binding memorandum for a 15-year lease at Agios Dimitrios in Western Macedonia, with a first phase planned at 240MW of IT load within 300MW of total power demand at an estimated cost of about €1.2 billion, and Cerebras signed a seven-year capacity agreement with Compute Nordic for 165MW in Mikkeli, Finland.

Governments were changing the rules during the same month. The article reports that Scotland now requires a full environmental impact assessment for new data centers above 50MW, Virginia restricted nondisclosure agreements with state agencies, California signed seven data center bills covering electricity, water and land use, and Thailand paused sector development across 166 projects while it drafts national standards. Brazil enacted REDATA, a nationwide tax-incentive law for data centers, and during LEAP 2026 in Saudi Arabia, MIS announced a $1.2 billion expansion to 192MW while AWS and HUMAIN committed up to 50MW at the country's first AI Zone by 2028. The author's closing question is whether state capital flowing into developed markets, or private debt flowing into emerging ones, will build the next gigawatt faster.

Articles.Title: The Global AI Buildout in 122 Deals

stories.Headline: Hong Kong privacy watchdog issues guidance on AI ‘smart glasses’ to curb covert surveillance
stories.Summary:
Hong Kong's privacy watchdog has published guidance on AI-powered smart glasses, aimed at preventing the covert collection of personal data. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data released the "Smart Glasses: Tips on Protecting Personal Data Privacy" note on Tuesday, warning that camera-equipped eyewear could pose heightened privacy risks. The guidance comes as the devices can take photos and record video or audio without drawing attention. Officials framed it as a way to encourage users to handle such technology in a way that respects others' privacy.

Privacy Commissioner Ada Chung said in a statement that smart glasses can record photos, videos or audio discreetly, which may increase the risk of excessive or covert collection of personal data. She added that the material captured by the glasses may be analysed and processed by AI systems, creating additional privacy risks. The watchdog singled out hospitals, clinics and changing rooms as places where the use of smart glasses raises the risk of improper collection of sensitive personal information. It noted that people reasonably expect a higher degree of privacy in those settings.

The articles do not say whether the guidance is legally binding or what penalties, if any, would apply to misuse. They also do not describe any specific incident that prompted the release. What the note sets out are practical tips for users and a call for privacy-respecting use of the devices. Further details on enforcement or follow-up measures were not provided in the reporting.

Articles.Title: Hong Kong privacy watchdog issues guidance on AI ‘smart glasses’ to curb covert surveillance - Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

stories.Headline: For the Sake of Our Retirement, Let’s Hope AI Is for Real
stories.Summary:
Public pension funds may be exposed to a possible AI investment bubble, according to a report from the New York Times cited by Gizmodo's AJ Dellinger on October 27, 2026. The Times estimated that as much as $700 billion in public pension money, held for city, county, and state employees, could be tied to AI-related investments. The article notes that more than 37 million people took part in state and local pension plans in 2025, based on US Census Bureau data. Those participants would be at risk if the companies propping up the economy suffered sharp losses.

The bets on AI still look strong in the short term, the article says, because spending continues on frontier AI model makers and on data center projects. A Brookings Institution study is cited as projecting $10.3 trillion in infrastructure spending from 2025 to 2032, which would equal nearly 4% of US gross domestic product per year. The article also describes how the SpaceX public listing led to rule changes that let the company enter index funds sooner than usual. As a result, millions of Americans with retirement savings in index funds, 401(k)s, and similar accounts now hold a stake in SpaceX and its subsidiaries, including xAI.

The Open Markets Institute and Americans for Financial Reform warned in a report that an AI downturn would hit pension funds hard, since AI-linked assets dominate stock and corporate bond markets. The Times drew comparisons to the 2008 financial crisis, which the article says cost many Americans as much as a quarter of their retirement savings. Dellinger's piece is an opinion column, and its headline suggests that readers should hope the AI boom proves sound. The article does not describe any formal action by regulators or fund managers in response.

Articles.Title: For the Sake of Our Retirement, Let’s Hope AI Is for Real

stories.Headline: Citadel, Bridgewater, and Man Group are using AI to perfect their processes, but fear bad bots and 'cognitive surrender'
stories.Summary:
Citadel, Bridgewater, and Man Group, three large investment firms, used a New York conference hosted by Bloomberg on Tuesday to describe how they are using artificial intelligence. Executives from the firms said they have built AI processes and found time-saving uses for them. Citadel has built AI agent clones of some of its investing teams that can conduct independent research. Bridgewater's AIA Labs is spreading research and processes it has perfected across the rest of the organization.

None of the executives said they were ready to hand their organizations over to machines, and none expected to do so soon. Aaron Linksy, a partner at Bridgewater who was part of its founding AIA team, said it remains an unsolved problem that agents cannot be trusted not to put the firm at risk. Citadel, according to the report, spends considerable effort keeping its agents inside a sandbox so they cannot leave it. Andrew Janian, who rejoined Citadel this year as interim chief technology officer, said fundamental investing teams should use AI to prepare for meetings or challenge their ideas rather than to write their investment theses. The speakers also said AI alone is not an edge in investing.

Greg Bond, chief investment officer of Man Group, warned against what he called "cognitive surrender," the habit of people who hand their entire work to the technology and go on autopilot. He said he wished PowerPoint presentations would fade away and that meetings would focus more on bringing people together to talk. Bond, who once headed one of Man Group's quant units, said humans design these systems and that markets remain driven by humans. Man Group, he added, is trying to let its staff spend more time on the enjoyable parts of their jobs and less on routine grunt work.

Articles.Title: Citadel, Bridgewater, and Man Group are using AI to perfect their processes, but fear bad bots and 'cognitive surrender'

stories.Headline: China’s AI race needs data fuel. Can a new state-owned giant deliver?
stories.Summary:
China's state planners have launched a centrally managed state-owned enterprise to turn the country's large pool of data into fuel for artificial intelligence and economic growth. The company was established on October 20 and is headquartered in Xiongan New Area, Hebei province. At its inauguration, Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang called the move a major strategic decision meant to strengthen China's competitiveness in AI and the digital economy. The launch signals that Beijing wants to convert its digital holdings into a competitive advantage, though the articles give few operational details beyond the company's founding and location.

Experts quoted in the reporting warn that the group's success will depend on removing entrenched barriers that keep data from being shared across institutions. The entity is backed by major state enterprises, including the country's large telecoms carriers and power grid operators. Responsibility for the project rests with the central government, and Ding Xuexiang framed it as a strategic priority at the ceremony. The reporting attributes the warning about data-sharing barriers to experts rather than to officials.

The article was written by Ben Jiang in Beijing and published on October 26, 2026, by the South China Morning Post. The creation of the group reflects a broader push to make data a productive input for China's AI sector, which the articles present as a race with other countries. Whether the company can overcome the barriers that experts describe will determine how far that push goes. The articles do not say what the group's specific targets, budget, or timetable are.

Articles.Title: China’s AI race needs data fuel. Can a new state-owned giant deliver? - South China Morning Post

stories.Headline: AI Power Stocks Fell 7% to 13% in a Week While Exxon and Chevron Just Hit Record Highs. Here's Which Side I'd Rather Own.
stories.Summary:
Over the past five days, shares of several AI-linked power companies fell sharply, according to a Motley Fool article published October 27, 2026. Bloom Energy dropped about 13% from its high in that span, while Oklo, NuScale Power and Constellation Energy each slipped roughly 7% from their highs. Over the same period, ExxonMobil and Chevron were trading at or near all-time highs. The article's author, Reuben Gregg Brewer, framed the pullback against fears that the AI boom could be following a path similar to the dot-com bubble that burst around the turn of the century.

The article's central argument is that AI power stocks carry risks that are harder to measure, because their prices are driven by a fast-changing AI theme, while the risks facing the oil giants are better understood. Brewer describes Oklo and NuScale as the most speculative of the group, since both are trying to build businesses around small modular nuclear reactors and are still losing money without proven financial viability. He points out that Bloom Energy, which sells hydrogen fuel cells for off-grid power to AI data centers, trades at a price-to-earnings ratio above 100 even after its pullback. Constellation Energy, an independent power producer that sells power to technology companies, is described as better positioned to weather a slowdown because of its long-term contracts. Exxon and Chevron are highlighted for their long dividend-increase streaks of 43 and 38 years, low debt-to-equity ratios of 0.16 and 0.2, and yields of about 2.2% and 3%.

Brewer attributes the oil giants' recent strength to a geopolitical conflict in the Middle East, which he says has pushed oil prices higher. He acknowledges that oil prices will eventually fall and that the two companies' stock prices will fall with them, but he argues they have weathered full energy cycles before. The article is an opinion piece, and it does not report any statement from the companies themselves. It does not describe any scheduled event or next step for the AI power stocks, and it ends with the author's stated preference for risks he says he can understand.

Articles.Title: AI Power Stocks Fell 7% to 13% in a Week While Exxon and Chevron Just Hit Record Highs. Here's Which Side I'd Rather Own.

stories.Headline: People are using AI to make expensive computer programs free. This could change everything
stories.Summary:
Software engineers are now using generative AI tools to reverse engineer expensive commercial programs and build free replicas of them. In recent weeks one engineer produced what are essentially free versions of Microsoft Office and Adobe programs, including a tool that mimics Photoshop. A freely available AI tool called Reverse Engineer Anything has also gone viral in coding circles. The approach works best on large, complex programs, where the AI breaks the software into component parts and then writes code that reproduces those parts.

Reverse engineering differs from vibe coding, in which a user describes what they want and the AI attempts to build it from scratch. The method may also sidestep the United States Digital Millennium Copyright Act, which made it illegal to break the locks that prevent tinkering, because reverse engineering does not appear to break any locks, though the article notes this may face legal challenges. Some observers see the trend as a return to the early internet, when much software was free and open source and users could adapt it. The article suggests it could also raise questions about how for-profit software will be sold in the future. Some of the AI-built software already shows unexplained bugs, which are likely to be hard to trace when much of the code was generated by a machine.

The article warns of practical problems with these clones. Files created in a free replica may not stay compatible with official products, so a document opened in one version might fail in another. Even a successful copy would lack the underlying data that powers certain features, such as Adobe's proprietary AI tools or the behavioral data behind Facebook's advertising. The article also traces how the commercial software model became dominant after the 1990s, when Microsoft became the best-known seller of paid programs and the 1998 copyright law secured their position. It notes that companies such as Amazon, Google, Apple and Facebook then grew into the large technology firms that followed.

The article does not name a party responsible for the clones beyond the engineer who built the Office and Adobe replicas, and it does not report any statement from Microsoft or Adobe about them.
