stories.Headline: Election 2026 Roundtable: Legislation to watch, AI, and reasons for hope
stories.Summary:
Congress faces a set of healthcare bills that expire at the end of 2026, along with growing pressure to examine artificial intelligence in patient care. The article is a roundtable discussion published October 27, 2026, by Chief Healthcare Executive and written by Ron Southwick, and it is the final installment of its Election 2026 series. Three experts took part: Lisa Kidder Hrobsky of the American Hospital Association, Robert E. Andrews of the Health Transformation Alliance, and Danielle Turnipseed of the Association of American Medical Colleges. Andrews served 24 years in the U.S. House of Representatives representing part of New Jersey.

Several funding mechanisms important to hospitals are set to expire at the end of the calendar year unless Congress extends them. These include funding streams for the Medicare Dependent Hospital Program, which supports hospitals serving a higher share of Medicare patients, and a program for hospitals with low volumes of Medicare patients. Both programs provide vital support to rural hospitals. Kidder Hrobsky said Congress has usually extended these programs within broader spending packages, so she believes they are probably safe, but she would like lawmakers to consider longer-lasting fixes. Andrews, for his part, said he wants an objective, clinically qualified group to set appropriate guidelines for AI used in delivering patient care.

Turnipseed also called for a more thoughtful approach to AI in healthcare, noting that leaders in the field have warned it could have unintended consequences if adopted carelessly. The panelists said the next Congress should move beyond routine extensions and examine the programs themselves. The article does not say which lawmakers will lead these efforts or what specific AI standards would look like. Each panelist's position reflects their own organization's view.

The panelists also shared reasons for optimism about the coming session. Turnipseed pointed to people who are engaged in managing their own health and turning to credible institutions and providers for science-based answers. Kidder Hrobsky said she sees potential for agreement on price transparency legislation, which she believes would help people find the care that is best for them. Andrews noted advances in cancer research and treatment that are helping people live longer. The article presents these views as the panelists' own hopes rather than predictions of outcomes.

Articles.Title: Election 2026 Roundtable: Legislation to watch, AI, and reasons for hope - Chief Healthcare Executive

stories.Headline: Transport & logistics firms boost AI spend despite gaps
stories.Summary:
A new survey from Sparq, published on October 27, 2026, finds that transport and logistics firms are continuing to increase spending on AI and technology even though many still see gaps in their operational readiness. The poll of 313 senior decision-makers at freight, trucking, parcel and courier companies with annual revenue of at least USD $500 million found that 90% said returns on their technology investments had met or exceeded expectations. Some 87% expect technology and AI budgets to rise in the next fiscal year. Respondents still reported weak spots, especially in demand forecasting, where 53% ranked accuracy among their top three readiness gaps despite 61% saying they had already adopted forecasting technology. The findings point to tighter financial scrutiny alongside continued spending.

Some 62% said their organisations now want faster return on investment timelines from vendors, and 49% said they are consolidating vendor relationships. Adoption is broad, with load and route optimisation used by 70% of organisations and real-time visibility and tracking by 67%. The most commonly cited barrier to moving faster on AI or data investment was legacy systems and integration problems, named by 24% of respondents, followed by data quality concerns at 19%, unclear return on investment at 17% and budget constraints at 16%. Ingrid Curtis, chief executive of Sparq, said transport and logistics companies are not pulling back from technology investment but that their expectations are changing. She argued that by 2027 simply having deployed AI or saved some employee hours will not be enough, and that leaders will want proof that investments improved margins, capacity or resilience.

Curtis also said the next phase of adoption will be less about adding tools and more about getting the systems companies already have to work together, connecting data and modernising critical systems. The survey, conducted in the US by InnovateMR for Sparq, focused on larger operators, with 78% working at companies generating USD $1 billion or more in annual revenue and 90% holding director-level roles or above. It carries a margin of error of plus or minus 5.5 percentage points at a 95% confidence level. The results suggest that forecasting and integration problems remain difficult for the sector even as spending grows, a tension that matters because forecasting errors can affect staffing, route planning, equipment use and customer service at once.

Articles.Title: Transport & logistics firms boost AI spend despite gaps - TechDay US

stories.Headline: Australian woman says AI glasses could replace her guide dog
stories.Summary:
Heidi Biggin, a woman with vision impairment in Ballarat, Australia, has said that artificial intelligence-powered smart glasses have helped her carry out everyday tasks and shop more independently. According to her, after about six months of using the device, she may no longer need to take her guide dog with her. Biggin has been legally blind for 16 years and previously relied on her guide dog for tasks such as crossing the road and buying groceries. She has been using her current guide dog for about four years. The account was reported by ABC News Australia and carried by UA.NEWS on 27 October 2026.

Biggin uses voice commands to ask the glasses which section of a store she is in. The device relays information about the surrounding space through an earpiece, including the location of the checkout, the entrance and store sections. She said the glasses make her feel less conspicuous in public places. She is raising three children and planned to buy blue T-shirts independently for her nine-year-old twins before their school athletics competition.

Using the glasses also brings difficulties. Biggin said strangers have accused her of filming them at least three times a week because an indicator light comes on while the device is in use, and people automatically assume she is recording. She also raised concern about a planned ban on smart glasses in schools in the state of Victoria, due to take effect from the first school term next year. Biggin, who works as an inclusion specialist in schools, said the procedure for obtaining exemptions for such devices remains unclear.

Erin Goodhart, a partnerships coordinator at Guide Dogs Victoria who also has a vision impairment and has used both guide dogs and smart glasses, stressed that the glasses cannot currently replace primary mobility aids such as a white cane or a guide dog. The article places this against the cost and wait for guide dogs. In Victoria, training one guide dog takes nearly two years and costs more than 50,000 Australian dollars, and waiting for such a dog can take from three months to nearly two years. The articles do not report any further steps planned by the authorities or the glasses' makers.

Articles.Title: Australian woman says AI glasses could replace her guide dog — ABC News Australia - UA.NEWS

stories.Headline: When AI becomes your default adviser, what happens to your judgment? - Fast Company Middle East
stories.Summary:
Fast Company Middle East published an article by Suparna Dutt D'Cunha asking what happens to human judgment when AI becomes the default adviser for everyday decisions. The piece cites a range of recent cases in which people relied on AI advice with harmful results, including a farmer in China who lost 25 acres of seedlings, hikers stranded on a mountain after following AI-generated instructions, and people who fell ill after eating mushrooms that AI had misidentified. The author notes that these examples do not prove everyday AI use is inherently harmful, but they show why assistance in matters of safety, health, money, parenting, or emotional vulnerability must be treated differently from casual use. A plausible answer, the piece argues, is not the same as a reliable one.

Several experts interviewed for the article describe the risks of overreliance. Dr. Mohammad Ayish, a professor at the American University of Sharjah, warns that growing dependence on AI for emotional support and decision-making raises serious concerns about human agency and social relationships. Samira Cutts, a cognitive neuroscientist, says routinely outsourcing reasoning risks weakening critical thinking and independent judgment, and that AI cannot replicate the reciprocity and emotional complexity of human relationships. Prashant Malaviya of Georgetown University's McDonough School of Business gives three reasons people trust AI too readily: it is easier than thinking for oneself, its smooth language seems expert, and users may lack the knowledge to question it. The article also mentions that New York City banned generative AI in schools over concerns about children's development.

The article presents a range of proposed responses rather than a single prescription. Martin J. Kraemer of KnowBe4 argues that the central challenge is identifying and protecting core human skills, while noting that AI can assist decisions without replacing the underlying expertise. Kellie Blyth of Addleshaw Goddard says consumers often treat these tools as confidential advisers even though they lack the legal and professional protections that doctors or lawyers provide, and she calls for clear disclosure about data use and accountability for providers. Malaviya suggests safeguards should go beyond warnings and encourage users to pause and question recommendations, particularly where stakes are high. The article adds that Saudi Arabia and the UAE have built AI literacy into national strategies, while China is setting rules for AI apps and chatbots to limit overreliance.

The authors agree that the technology itself is not the problem, and Dr. Ayish concludes that AI should enhance human capabilities rather than gradually undermine them. Blyth observes that while it may be too late to stop people from using AI, it is not too late to build safeguards that protect users from the most serious harms. Malaviya notes that research is still needed to determine whether overreliance comes mainly from convenience, misplaced trust, or a lack of knowledge. The piece leaves these questions open and does not describe any specific regulatory decision pending in the region.

Articles.Title: When AI becomes your default adviser, what happens to your judgment? - Fast Company Middle East

stories.Headline: Screen-time report dives into how tweens and teens are using AI, social media and more
stories.Summary:
Common Sense Media released a survey-based report on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, examining how tweens and teens use screens, artificial intelligence chatbots and social media. The report found that a typical teenager logs more than eight hours a day of screen time for entertainment, while a typical tween spends about five hours. It is the organization's first broad survey of youth media and tech use in five years, and it covers kids aged 9 to 17. Most kids now have their own cellphone by age 11, with 57 percent owning a smartphone at that age.

Among teens, the report found that they spend over three hours on TV and videos, two hours gaming, two hours on social media and an hour using AI each day. Teens spend close to two hours daily on short-form video, and they named YouTube and TikTok as the social platforms they use most. Half of tweens said they use social media for nearly an hour and a half on a given day, and a similar share said they use AI even though the organization says those platforms are not meant for children that young. The report also found that heavy use does not necessarily bring enjoyment, since 86 percent of teens use social media but only 47 percent of those users say they enjoy it a lot.

Michael Robb, Common Sense Media's head of research, said that social media and AI companies are doing a poor job of keeping younger children off their apps. He said many kids are pushed toward social media by the wish to keep up with friends, even though algorithmic feeds can show content they do not want or that makes them feel worse about themselves. Robb also said that a child owning a phone does not mean the child needs access to every app, and that not every fourth or fifth grader needs one. He added that parents can use built-in parental controls and hold short, ongoing conversations about AI reliance.

Robb said that research suggests the time spent on devices matters less than what the devices replace, so parents should protect sleep, outdoor time, reading and family time. He suggested keeping phones out of bedrooms overnight, noting that reading drops sharply as kids get older. He also said that while strict screen-time limits can be hard to enforce, parents can still add friction that makes unsuitable content harder to reach. The report's findings show how central media and technology have become to daily life for young people, and the organization is positioning them as a guide for families navigating those choices.

Articles.Title: Screen-time report dives into how tweens and teens are using AI, social media and more

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike finds AI agents running autonomous cyberattacks
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike reported that it identified four previously unreported threat actors using agentic artificial intelligence to carry out cyber intrusions, covering reconnaissance, exploitation and data theft. The company observed the intrusions between May and August 2026, and the activity hit organisations in healthcare, government, software-as-a-service and other private-sector industries. The four groups took different approaches, from complex systems coordinating several AI agents to simpler frameworks that relied on predefined instructions and publicly available skills. The findings show attackers using AI coding assistants to make operational decisions and run commands with little human involvement.

The investigation found that all four operators got around safeguards meant to stop AI models from helping with malicious activity. Common methods included describing intrusions as authorised penetration tests, placing files in agents' working directories that told them to treat targets as authorised by default, and using a runtime modification called ClawGod on Claude Code to strip out instructions that refuse destructive activity. Operators also kept pushing through refusals with repeated prompts, reframing requests, claiming ownership of targets or starting new sessions. Structured workflows, such as saving progress to files and defining steps for continuing past obstacles, helped keep agents working over long periods.

Among the documented cases, one agent attacking an Argentine healthcare organisation tried another route after firewalls blocked its first move, then set up a reverse shell, reached a domain controller and harvested five password hashes in about 20 minutes. In a separate incident, an agent used one compromised Argentine healthcare organisation to reach a second victim's network in a 12.5-minute session, after a single human prompt. Another agent against a Russian organisation chained a web application flaw and cloud credentials into cluster administrator access in a Kubernetes environment, reaching 726 tenant databases. The report says that at least 15 Argentine healthcare organisations were compromised by one actor, which also took credentials and medical records from at least one victim. Other operators hit government entities in Brazil, Colombia and Indonesia, a Bangladeshi government domain, and a US customer relationship management vendor.

CrowdStrike's 2026 Global Threat Report found that AI-enabled adversary activity rose 89% in 2025, and its OverWatch team recorded three times as many agentic intrusions in the second half of 2026 to date as in the first half. The company said it expects agentic AI-supported intrusions to almost certainly grow in volume and sophistication over the next 12 months, citing rapid attacker adoption, better AI models and open-source offensive agent frameworks. It also found that one of the least technically skilled operators succeeded by relying on a large set of public skills, and it identified the cost of running AI models, measured in tokens, as a current limit on scale that falling inference costs and larger context windows could ease. CrowdStrike further assessed that less-skilled attackers could soon run campaigns at a scale once associated with organised criminal groups or state-linked actors.

Articles.Title: CrowdStrike finds AI agents running autonomous cyberattacks - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Workiva warns weak governance is slowing AI reporting
stories.Summary:
Workiva, a reporting software company, has published commentary in IT Brief Australia on October 28, 2026, arguing that weak data governance is slowing the use of AI in corporate reporting in Australia. The argument draws on survey findings from Australian finance, risk and sustainability leaders. The company's figures show that 95 per cent of respondents expect measurable return on investment from AI within a year, yet only 14 per cent believe their organisation's data quality is good enough for AI use in reporting. A further 21 per cent said data quality issues had significantly limited their use of AI in reporting workflows, and 44 per cent had worked around those issues anyway.

Workiva says the gap should not be read simply as a data problem. It describes the matter as a governance problem, arguing that AI does not fix inconsistency where the same figure sits across several spreadsheets, presentations and email chains, and can spread errors faster while making them harder to spot. The survey also found that 79 per cent of respondents were at least somewhat confident in AI outputs without human review, which the company says highlights the risk of relying on systems built on fragmented information. Workiva recommends three foundations: a single source of truth for each figure, control through ownership, permissions and version history, and built-in data lineage so figures can be traced to their source. It also says 39 per cent of Australian executives reported that their most recent AI audit found data lineage gaps or traceability issues.

The commentary is written by Kristen "KP" Pimpini, Vice President and General Manager, Asia Pacific and Japan at Workiva, who has argued that reliance on reconciliations, offline copies and individual staff knowledge may keep work moving in the short term but weakens traceability over time. She has also set out a practical test for finance teams: trace one AI-assisted figure from a recent board report back to its source, and if that takes days or depends on one person's spreadsheet or memory, the organisation is not ready. The article notes that this matters in reporting because companies must explain where figures in financial statements, board papers and sustainability disclosures come from, and that Australia is introducing mandatory climate reporting, which increases scrutiny of how such information is assembled and verified. The piece frames the issue as part of a wider debate in which pressure for quick AI returns collides with older weaknesses in financial reporting and internal controls. The article does not say what steps, if any, regulators or individual companies will take next.

Articles.Title: Workiva warns weak governance is slowing AI reporting - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Cloudera launches blueprints to move AI into production
stories.Summary:
Cloudera has launched Cloudera Blueprints, a new portfolio that includes NVIDIA AI Blueprints built with NVIDIA Agent Toolkit on Cloudera, according to a report published on 27 October 2026. The offering is aimed at companies trying to move artificial intelligence projects from the pilot stage into full production. It is particularly relevant where data is spread across cloud environments, on-premises data centres and edge locations. The portfolio builds on Cloudera's existing Accelerators for ML Projects and adds preconfigured deployments that run on Cloudera AI.

The deployments are designed to connect NVIDIA reference workflows with Cloudera's data management, security and governance tools. Initial uses highlighted by Cloudera include transaction foundation models for financial services, healthcare agents for clinical documentation, telecom network configuration planning and systems for detecting synthetic video. The software supports deployment across public cloud, company-run data centres and edge environments, so customers can build and run applications without moving sensitive or regulated data. The NVIDIA components include NIM microservices and Nemotron models through Cloudera AI Inference, along with cuDF for Apache Spark in Cloudera Data Engineering.

Leo Brunnick, Chief Product Officer at Cloudera, said that enterprises want to move past experimentation but find it hard to turn prototypes into production-ready applications when data is scattered across complex environments. He argued that the launch narrows that gap by pairing NVIDIA's AI workflows with Cloudera's data management, security and governance capabilities. Pat Lee, Vice President of Strategic Enterprise Partnerships at NVIDIA, said the two companies are working to make it easier for organisations to deploy AI wherever their data resides. Cloudera said the software is built on an open-source foundation intended to give customers flexibility across models, infrastructure and deployment settings.

The launch addresses a persistent problem in corporate AI programmes, the gap between a working prototype and a system that meets operational, governance and security requirements. The announcement pointed to Deloitte research showing that only 28% of enterprises have moved at least 40% of their AI pilots into production, a figure relevant to markets such as Australia. The collaboration extends an existing relationship between Cloudera and NVIDIA, both of which are seeking a larger role in enterprise AI deployments. The articles do not describe pricing, availability dates or customer adoption figures for the portfolio.

Articles.Title: Cloudera launches blueprints to move AI into production - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: SuperEvolution AI Unveils 36 In-House Developed AI Research Achievements: Full Public Access to Open-Source Codes, Verified Experiments & Complete Generation Trajectories | Xinglian Portfolio Latest Updates
stories.Summary:
The article reports that Chaoyan Intelligence, which goes by SuperEvolution AI in the headline, released 36 research outputs generated almost entirely by its own AI system on October 27, 2026. The outputs cover two areas, AI research and robotic embodied intelligence, and the company says the system handled the full research cycle with only minor human involvement. That cycle includes literature review, method design, code writing, experiments, chart creation, drafting a LaTeX paper, and self-review with iterative revision. The AI research work spans five kinds of questions, while the robotics work focuses on embodied control and Vision-Language-Action models.

The article highlights five outputs in detail. One studies how recursively generated AI text drifts statistically, using about 37,000 generated texts from 8 base models in 5 model families, and proposes a classifier that separates original text from one-round and multi-round generated text, reaching an F1 score of 0.694 in leave-one-generator-out tests. Another examines safety probes on reasoning models and finds that the choice of network layer, driven by the metric used, can systematically bias results, with some deep layers giving precision gains of about 20 to 22 percentage points over text probes in 7B to 8B models. A third compares three vision-language-action architectures, OpenVLA, TraceVLA and NORA, on LIBERO tasks and reports that action training changes representations near the output layers and that some instruction-attention patterns already exist in the base models.

The company presents these outputs as evidence that its system can independently raise scientific questions, design rigorous experiments and draw insightful conclusions. The article does not identify any outside reviewers or independent verification beyond the company's own statements. It also notes limits in the work itself: the safety-probe conclusions for a 32B model are constrained by small test samples, the text-versus-hidden-state advantage depends on the specific model and encoder setup, and the recursive-generation findings have so far been verified mainly on base pretrained models rather than instruction-tuned or more complex real-world settings. The article gives no timeline for follow-up work beyond the stated need for further research.

Articles.Title: SuperEvolution AI Unveils 36 In-House Developed AI Research Achievements: Full Public Access to Open-Source Codes, Verified Experiments & Complete Generation Trajectories | Xinglian Portfolio Latest Updates - 36Kr

stories.Headline: Anthropic's Official Prospectus Unveiled: Can AI Large Language Models Achieve Sustainable Profitability?
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, one of the leading AI companies, publicly filed its prospectus with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on October 26, 2026, planning to list on NASDAQ under the ticker ANT. The filing, which laid out the company's full financial performance for the first time, arrived as the AI sector had been shaky, and the NASDAQ Composite rose 0.82% and the PHLX Semiconductor Index climbed 2.82% on the day it was released. The prospectus follows a week in which the semiconductor index had dropped 6.72% in a single session, and other listings had been postponed this autumn. OpenAI has said it plans to go public in 2027.

The filing shows revenue of $162.86 billion in the first half of 2026, about 14 times the same period a year earlier, and a GAAP operating profit of $9.74 billion in the second quarter. By the end of June, the company had signed computing power commitments and unstarted leases totaling about $5.87 trillion, to be paid over nearly 20 years, and it added at least another $2.45 trillion in new or expanded contracts after that date. The net loss of $807.48 billion in the first half came mainly from an accounting revaluation of financing instruments and involved no cash outflow. Operating cash flow was positive at $3.929 billion in the first half, while cash and short-term investments stood at $1,316.51 billion at the end of June.

Anthropic's revenue is split across three layers, the underlying models, a developer platform and its own products such as Claude.ai and Claude Code. In the first half of 2026, 80% of revenue was usage-based and 20% came from subscriptions, and 48% was sold through the cloud marketplaces of Amazon, Google and Microsoft. Enterprise customers paying more than $100,000 over twelve months rose to more than 11,900 by September 30, 2026, from more than 950 a year earlier. The filing also says the company's customer concentration is falling, with only one customer above 10% of revenue in the first half of 2026, compared with two customers at 12% each in 2025.

The company's financial position depends heavily on the timing of its computing costs, which are booked under long-term contracts 12 to 18 months ahead of use. The prospectus warns that when new large batches of computing power come online, expenses will be recorded before the related revenue, which could sharply compress margins and possibly return the company to losses. Investors in the listing will help cover future payments, and their willingness to pay will depend on whether Anthropic's top models keep selling at a premium to rivals. The filing does not explain the slowdown in quarter-on-quarter growth in the third quarter, though the articles point to summer seasonality, the removal of non-compliant customers and a U.S. export restriction that temporarily disabled two models.

Articles.Title: Anthropic's Official Prospectus Unveiled: Can AI Large Language Models Achieve Sustainable Profitability? - 36Kr

stories.Headline: Wang's Conjecture Fully Cracked by AI Overnight: Breakthrough in Mathematical Research
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced that its AI model had delivered three results at once, and the reported details were released around October 27, 2026. The announced achievements include overturning the Exponential Time Hypothesis, a computer science assumption that researchers have widely relied on for nearly 30 years, proving the local smoothing conjecture in all dimensions, and constructing a rigorous existence proof for quantum chromodynamics and Yang-Mills theory. The company said the local smoothing result, traced back through the chain of mathematical deductions, also solves the Kakeya conjecture in all dimensions. The mathematical proof was produced on October 18 and formalized in the Lean system the next day, while the disproof of the hypothesis was generated on October 16 and formalized the day after.

The articles stress that these proofs still require checking. Lean formalization confirms that reasoning steps follow formal rules, but it cannot by itself guarantee that the mathematical content is free of loopholes, and it does not replace peer review. Both documents have been posted to a public GitHub repository so mathematicians around the world can examine them. The physics proof has not been published in full, because the expert team decided the AI-generated material was too large and would first be sorted, reviewed and written up by researchers. The results also change how the Kakeya problem stands: in 2025, Wang Hong and Joshua Zahl proved the three-dimensional case, and the new work extends the result to all dimensions.

OpenAI invited the original proposers of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi of the University of California, San Diego, together with Ryan Williams of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, to lead an external review of the disproof. The external team asked OpenAI to disclose all raw data and to fund academic conferences on the consequences for computational complexity theory, and the company accepted those conditions. For the physics work, a team led by 2004 Nobel laureate David Gross, with Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov and Nikita Nekrasov, is reviewing the material. Jaffe helped formulate the official statement of the Yang-Mills Millennium Prize Problem, which the Clay Mathematics Institute listed in 2000.

The announcement follows an earlier release on October 6, when OpenAI published 722 AI-generated mathematical manuscripts covering 372 unsolved problems. Some proofs in that batch were later found to contain errors, leading the company to withdraw three manuscripts and revise fourteen others. Twenty days later it announced these three results and said it would now treat AI-generated proofs as original research data, bringing in outside scientists to verify, interpret and organize them. The articles say that if the academic community accepts the results, researchers would need to revisit the many computer science papers built on the Exponential Time Hypothesis, and the mathematicians' next task will shift toward checking AI proofs. Whether the claims survive independent scrutiny remains to be seen.

Articles.Title: Wang's Conjecture Fully Cracked by AI Overnight: Breakthrough in Mathematical Research - 36Kr

stories.Headline: AI Predicts Death List from Single Face Analysis: 50% of Subjects Passed Away Within 90 Days
stories.Summary:
The study was run by researchers at Mass General Brigham in the United States, and it was published on October 19 in The Lancet Digital Health. The team had an AI assign a mortality risk score to 3,820 cancer patients, and the AI had never seen any of them before. Each score was based on a single facial photo, most of them taken routinely before the patients began radiotherapy. Of the 122 people with the highest scores, 64 died within 90 days, while only 20 of the 975 people with the lowest scores died in the same period.

The system is built in two steps. The researchers first showed the AI about 40 million facial photos without any medical instruction so it could learn general facial patterns. They then trained it to estimate biological age, meaning the age of the body rather than the age on a document, and to estimate mortality risk directly, using photos from more than 34,000 cancer patients and their survival outcomes. In a separate test on more than 38,000 radiotherapy patients, people the AI judged to look more than five years older than their actual age had a mortality risk 21 percent higher, even after accounting for chronological age, sex and cancer type. The researchers also noted that a human baseline from last year, in which 10 doctors and researchers judged short-term survival from photos, reached about 60 percent accuracy, rising to about 80 percent once they saw the AI's analysis.

Ray Mak, a radiation oncologist at Mass General Brigham and one of the study's lead researchers, said the approach mirrors how doctors already take a first look at patients. He said the tool is meant to give clinicians an extra reference rather than make decisions for them, and the team has begun hospital trials on early-stage lung cancer patients over 65 to see whether it can flag frail patients who may need nutritional support or rehabilitation. Matthew Liao, director of the Center for Bioethics at New York University, warned that a misjudged patient might not get the care they need, and he worried about insurers or employers using facial photos to make decisions about people. The team also launched a public website last March where anyone can upload selfies for an age estimate, and more than 10,000 people have signed up, though the researchers say it is for research only and not a medical diagnosis. The AI was trained mainly on patients from the Boston area, most of them white, so its accuracy for other groups remains unclear, and the team hopes uploaded photos will help it learn from more diverse faces.

Articles.Title: AI Predicts Death List from Single Face Analysis: 50% of Subjects Passed Away Within 90 Days - 36Kr

stories.Headline: Grayscale AI Computing ETF Invests in Infrastructure Companies Including CoreWeave, Nebius
stories.Summary:
On October 27, 2026, Grayscale, the crypto asset manager, said its artificial intelligence computing exchange-traded fund, trading under the ticker GCPU, offers investors exposure to AI infrastructure companies. The announcement was reported by Bloomingbit and published that day. The fund invests in stocks tied to AI infrastructure, and its main holdings include CoreWeave, Nebius and DigitalOcean. Grayscale described GCPU as a product designed to give investors exposure to this sector by holding shares of companies linked to AI computing infrastructure. The articles do not describe any new legal requirement or regulatory change.

They also do not give the fund's size, assets under management, expense ratio or the weighting of each holding. The source material is limited to the company's description of the product and its key holdings. Because the articles offer no further figures, dates or details beyond these, the story stays within what Grayscale stated. Grayscale is the party responsible for the fund and for the statements about its purpose and holdings. The company said the fund gives investors access to AI infrastructure companies, which the articles present as the fund's central aim.

The reporting carries no further comment from Grayscale or from the named companies. The articles also include a note that the analysis is for reference only and is not investment advice. The announcement comes as interest in AI computing infrastructure continues, though the articles do not connect it to any specific market event. The articles do not say whether Grayscale plans additional products or changes to GCPU. More to follow.

stories.Headline: From prototype to production: Kyndryl’s smarter path to AI business value
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl has set up AI Innovation Labs in Dallas, Liverpool and Luxembourg to give customers test environments where they can move AI projects from experiment to implementation. The labs offer one-stop-shop settings for testing along with expertise to help customers use the innovation. The article says the labs aim beyond simply adding more AI features, focusing instead on helping customers create business value and earn a return on their AI spending. The labs are described as a way for customers to change how they operate, moving from being curious about AI to being built around it.

The company says the right sequence matters most, starting with the organization's challenges and the results it wants. Customers are encouraged to look across whole value chains, such as hiring-to-retiring, claim-to-settlement or order-to-cash, instead of single tasks. Results should be described in business terms, for example a new hire ready to work on the first day or an invoice sent correctly and paid on time. Before a customer arrives, the lab team defines a use case based on real business and technology challenges and then spends weeks learning about the customer's business, technology estate, processes and key metrics. The article says this preparation lets the team start designing with the customer on actual needs rather than theoretical scenarios.

Ismail Amla, Kyndryl's Global Consult Lead, is the person quoted explaining this approach in a question-and-answer interview with the company. He says organizations must understand their operations to find where they need to modernize and where AI could deliver results the business and its regulators would accept. Amla describes AI as a toolkit that Kyndryl uses with cross-industry data from Kyndryl Bridge and with insights built over decades of designing, building and managing complex IT systems for global enterprises. He presents the labs as the place where this method is put into practice.

According to the article, the labs follow a four-phase process of customer immersion, co-design, building and roadmap development, beginning with rapid prototyping. The labs are described as working spaces rather than showcases, staffed by consultants including Forward-Deployed Engineers and Human Systems Architects. The article is a company publication, so its account of results and value comes from Kyndryl itself, and the piece does not report independent outcomes or customer figures. It does not say what comes next for the labs beyond the approach it describes.

Articles.Title: From prototype to production: Kyndryl’s smarter path to AI business value - Kyndryl

stories.Headline: 3 Frameworks to Protect CISOs & Orgs Against AI Liability
stories.Summary:
Dark Reading reported on a set of three frameworks that cybersecurity legal expert Daniel B. Garrie, CEO of Law and Forensics, presented at the ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026 in Denver. The frameworks are meant to help chief information security officers defend their AI deployment decisions when litigators, regulators, or customers seek someone to hold responsible after a compromise. Garrie's work builds on the JAMS AI Rules, established in June 2024 to give arbitrators a framework for settling AI disputes. Although those rules do not explain liability, Garrie, who helped write them, says they offer useful guidance on handling technical evidence. The article was published on October 27, 2026.

The first framework addresses contract negotiations with AI vendors, which Garrie says should happen early and with cybersecurity leaders involved. CISOs should seek provisions that secure access to logs, preservation requests, and a snapshot of the model at the time of an incident, and should ask how quickly that snapshot can be provided. Contracts should also clarify risk allocation, including vendor AI use permissions, data restrictions, warranties, insurance, liability caps, operational controls, and how disputes will be handled. Garrie warned that once a contract is signed, vendors will provide only what is specifically outlined, so gaps may not be fixable until renewal. The article presents this as the difference between having the evidence needed to show a company was not negligent and lacking it.

The second framework is a five-factor rubric that scores the risk of deploying an AI tool across "potential harm," "data and rights," "autonomy," "evidence gap," and "vendor dependence." The resulting score places a tool into one of four categories: "standard review," "conditional approval," "restricted pilot," or "hold release." The third framework concerns board decisions, which Garrie says should be documented in granular detail, including the scope and timeframe of the decision, the associated exposure and supporting evidence, deployment conditions, human approval requirements, accountable parties, challenges raised, the final decision, the tool's owner, and due dates. Garrie added that the goal is to create ongoing records rather than a static one.

A separate tool for preserving data after an incident covers system state, interaction records, data and access information, governance records, and chain of custody, and Garrie advised CISOs to involve legal counsel immediately. Garrie also offered a 30-day plan for CISOs: test one AI deployment against his frameworks, improve one board report, and run one AI tabletop exercise on vendor evidence preservation and notifications. He concluded that regulators, litigators, and customers will judge organizations by the evidence they can produce showing they considered risks and acted responsibly, not by whether they followed guidance such as NIST's. The article frames liability as likely to turn on what a CISO and organization can prove they did to protect systems against AI compromise.

Articles.Title: 3 Frameworks to Protect CISOs & Orgs Against AI Liability - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: AI Reveals Elon Musk's Predictions Are Unreliable: When AI Masters Accurate Forecasting
stories.Summary:
Henry, a 25-year-old investor, founded the AI prediction company ProphetLab in May 2026, after earlier building a large position in Nebius, a stock that rose more than tenfold in 2025. The company's first public product was a World Cup prediction tool, which ranked the outputs of mainstream models and later added its own framework. That framework calls large models through APIs, combines data such as historical matches, player injuries, referee styles and weather, and simulates each match minute by minute. Repeated simulations produce a probability distribution of scores, and the company reports an accuracy rate above 70 percent, with a correct call of the top four teams, the champion and a 1:0 final score. ProphetLab is also working with fund institutions on a benchmark for financial prediction, which asks models multi-step questions about things like corporate sales and revenue.

Financial experts help design the questions and evaluate the answers, and the feedback will be used to train later models. A separate project collected public statements by figures in the AI industry and checked whether their predictions came true. According to the company, Ilya Sutskever, former chief scientist of OpenAI, ranks first on prediction accuracy, while Elon Musk ranks last. Henry describes the work as analyzing the analysis of human experts, and says the company has raised tens of millions of yuan in angel funding from multiple investors, including Ivy Capital.

Henry's account explains the company's approach, though the articles give few independent checks on its claims. The accuracy figure and the ranking of public figures come from the company itself, and the article does not describe how the rankings were scored or how many predictions were included. Henry says that during a months-long period of independent study he concluded that large language models can bridge the gap between quantitative and subjective investment research. He also says that AI outperforms humans at gathering and processing information, and that predicting the future follows traceable rules.

He calls prediction a ten-year project and says he hopes to build a prophet. The articles raise open questions about whether such predictions can be verified in fields beyond sports, and whether people who trust a forecast might act in ways that change the outcome. The interview ends with those questions unresolved. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI Reveals Elon Musk's Predictions Are Unreliable: When AI Masters Accurate Forecasting - 36Kr

stories.Headline: Shanghai Normal University unveils AI platform to enhance mental health education
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, October 22, Shanghai Normal University launched an artificial intelligence training platform aimed at mental health education in Shanghai. The platform is designed to strengthen educators' ability to handle mental health problems and to help build students' psychological resilience. The university says the Yuxin AI Resilience Platform is believed to be the first of its kind in the country. The launch took place the same day the university also unveiled its Research Center for Psychology of Moral Education.

The platform was co-developed by the university's School of Psychology and Shanghai SunResi Intelligent Technology Co Ltd. It centers on 10 practical counseling techniques that address eight categories of common student psychological concerns and 10 common types of parents. It is built around two scenarios, student counseling and home-school communication, and offers professional micro-courses, specialized exercises and simulation training. Through immersive dialogues and training debriefings, teachers can practice identifying students' distress, listening empathetically, and giving emotional support. The university says the platform aims to address the gap between theory and practical skills, limited chances to simulate complex classroom situations, and weak training feedback.

The university said the platform is intended to help teachers spot signs of mental distress in students early and provide suitable psychological support. The reporting notes that mental health issues among elementary and secondary school students have become increasingly challenging. Since 2023, China has introduced a series of policies promoting mental health initiatives in schools. Under this approach, mental health education is no longer the sole responsibility of school counselors but is shared by all educators.

Li Ye, vice-president of Shanghai Normal University, said that normal universities have a core mission of training educators. In his view, such institutions must produce research suited to local educational settings and must close the gap between research and basic classroom practice. He said the university needs to step up coordinated work across theoretical research, technological innovation and social services. The aim, he said, is to meet the real needs of young people's mental health and moral development.

Articles.Title: Shanghai Normal University unveils AI platform to enhance mental health education - China Daily Global Edition

stories.Headline: Who Oversees Personal Growth When AI Manages Learning? Qiming Talent Presents New "AI + Moral Education" Dual-Engine Educational Solution
stories.Summary:
This is a promotional piece rather than news reporting, and the articles give little independent verification of the claims. Still, the core facts are these. On or about 27 October 2026, Qiming Talent (Qiming Daren) presented its "AI + Moral Education" dual-engine education system at the Tianli · Zhi Education "AI + Moral Education" Innovation Summit in Guangyuan, Sichuan, according to a 36Kr Europe article published that day. The company says the system is meant to address three problems it identifies in student learning: unfocused learning, unmotivated learning, and learning that is not sustained. Its AI engine is described as diagnosing each student's weak points, generating a personalized plan, and feeding practice results back into the system, while its moral education engine relies on educators to track learning state, motivate students, and intervene when engagement drops.

The article says the system is drawn from the operating experience of Tianli, which it describes as having nearly 60 schools across 18 provinces and municipalities, more than 145,000 students, and 24 years of school operation. It claims over 1 billion teaching and research data points, with each function tested first in Tianli's own regular classes. It also lists credentials: recognition as a national high-tech enterprise and a Sichuan "Specialized, Refined, Differential and Innovative" enterprise, a self-developed AI learning companion large model that has passed national filing, and more than 50 patents. The article reports that among more than 1,000 students using the AI product over the past year, most improved their performance and more students crossed key target lines, though it gives no methodology, baseline, or comparison group for these results.

Xia Chen'an, Global Director Partner of McKinsey and head of high-tech business in Greater China, is quoted as saying that most mainstream AI education products focus on single-point capabilities concentrated at the learning level. Luo Shi, chairman and president of the Tianli International Board of Directors, is quoted as saying that private education cannot escape its difficulties alone and that the industry's future depends on collective wisdom, mutual support, and win-win symbiosis. The article frames the summit as a step toward turning Tianli into a platform for innovation, practical implementation, and industry support for private basic education, with a planned national private "AI + Moral Education" cooperation platform. It does not report any independent evaluation, regulatory review, or specific timeline for rollout beyond the summit itself.

Articles.Title: Who Oversees Personal Growth When AI Manages Learning? Qiming Talent Presents New "AI + Moral Education" Dual-Engine Educational Solution - 36Kr

stories.Headline: AI-Generated Comic Dramas: Viral Traffic Secret with Cute Henan Dialect Baby & Northeast Dialect Stepmother
stories.Summary:
Dialect-speaking AI comic dramas have become a new way for shows to win viewers on Chinese short-drama platforms. Series such as The Little Junior Sister Who Is the Group Favorite of Our Sword Sect give a cute immortal-cultivation baby lines in Henan dialect, while Northeast Stepmother, Rectify the Whole Family gives a stepmother in a wealthy household a Northeast accent. The articles report that Hongguo Short Drama had 168 million daily active users as of July 2026, up 107 percent year on year. By October, four of the top five works on its overall popular list were AI comic dramas. The Sword Sect series has run five seasons with 1,809 episodes and has accumulated 23.7 million collections on Hongguo.

The articles note that Hongguo's algorithm weights collections above likes, which they read as a sign of viewer loyalty. A second Henan-dialect series, The Little Farming Junior Sister: Qinglian Farm Baby, has reached its seventh season, and the articles say its popularity is smaller than the Sword Sect series but its steady output shows a solid base of viewers. Northeast Stepmother ranked seventh on Hongguo's list in mid-October, with popularity values between 60.59 million and 62.12 million and collections and likes both above one million. The articles credit the producers' choices of dialect and character rather than any single company. They say dialect works best when it fits a character's habits, since a Henan accent does not by itself make a character simple or honest.

They also say AI production lowers the cost of trying different regional speech styles compared with live-action shooting, though creators still have to check whether accents and phrasing sound natural. The articles do not name any individual producer or give a formal statement from the platforms. The articles describe dialect as a way to make a fantasy or family story feel closer to everyday life, and they suggest that the trend is likely to grow as creators look for ways to make characters memorable. They also note that dialect in live-action short dramas has been used for years, so the newer part is its use in animated AI productions. Whether the trend lasts after novelty fades is not settled in the articles, which describe the current popularity but offer no forecast beyond that.

Articles.Title: AI-Generated Comic Dramas: Viral Traffic Secret with Cute Henan Dialect Baby & Northeast Dialect Stepmother - 36Kr

stories.Headline: Anthropic revenue driven by new models under six months old
stories.Summary:
Anthropic's S-1 filing, submitted ahead of its planned Nasdaq debut, shows that models released in the six months before September 30, 2026, generated more than 80 per cent of the company's third-quarter revenue. The filing was reported by TechGig on October 27, 2026. Anthropic released eight widely available Claude models and three restricted-access Mythos models between April and September 2026. Reuters, citing attendees at an investor meeting, reported that the company brought in $16.8 billion in third-quarter revenue.

The filing points to a tight link between when new models arrive and how much customers spend. According to the company, each new release, with its added capabilities, encourages existing users to use Claude more and draws in new customers. Anthropic describes this as a cycle in which each Claude generation helps fund the next. Its heaviest Claude Code enterprise users spend about 20 times more than other enterprise users. The figures show that a large share of the company's income comes from products that are only a few months old.

Anthropic is the company responsible for the filing, and it stated in the document that customer spending tracks the frequency and capabilities of its model launches. The company has not, based on these reports, separately detailed how the figures will change after the planned public listing. Reuters supplied the $16.8 billion figure from its own sourcing at the investor meeting, so that number has not appeared in the filing as reported here. The filing sets out the revenue relationship in plain terms, presenting new models as the main engine of growth. Further detail on the public offering and future revenue would come from later filings or coverage.

Articles.Title: Anthropic revenue driven by new models under six months old

stories.Headline: HolonIQ Latest Report: Tech Giants Deepen In-Depth University Partnerships, AI-Related Collaboration Proportion Surges from 2.1% to 12%
stories.Summary:
AI-related collaborations between universities and technology companies have grown sharply, according to a report from HolonIQ released on October 23, 2026. The "2026 Q3 Education AI Observatory Report" found that about 12 of every 100 global higher education cooperation initiatives now involve AI and data, up from around 2 five years earlier. The findings were covered by 36Kr, which published its article on October 27, 2026. The growth reflects rising demand from universities for AI services, courses and competence certifications.

In the third quarter of 2026, skill training and competence improvement made up 40 percent of global education AI initiatives. Degree and curriculum system construction accounted for 23 percent, bringing the two categories to 63 percent combined. National strategies and investments made up 10 percent, scientific research and computing power construction 9 percent, and other types 18 percent. The United States led with more than 100 projects in the quarter, while the United Kingdom had between 30 and 99, and China and India had between 10 and 29 each.

Governments are also setting rules for AI in schools. In the third quarter, the Commission on Higher Education of the Philippines issued Memorandum Order No. 21, which sets a national framework for AI use in teaching, research and operations. The state of Florida requires its 28 public colleges to prohibit students from using AI in graded assignments in principle, unless an instructor gives permission. HolonIQ counted fivefold growth in higher-education AI policy entries from July to September, and it cites QS research showing that 67 percent of scholars and 62 percent of students use generative AI every week.

AI companies are moving from selling tools to co-building programs with universities. INSEAD and the University of Sydney have given ChatGPT Edu to all students, faculty and staff, allowing schools to manage accounts, permissions and data centrally. In July, Western Governors University in the United States announced a strategic partnership with Anthropic to explore new learning systems and competence certification tied to changing job skills. Kean University launched a Bachelor of Science in Artificial Intelligence, the first such undergraduate program in New Jersey, and several South Korean universities are building AI semiconductor research institutions.

Enterprises are investing heavily in AI training as well. The report says Microsoft plans to invest about 2.5 billion US dollars in an AI deployment team, AWS is investing 1 billion US dollars in an AI engineer team, and Caterpillar has committed 100 million US dollars to talent in AI and robotics. On October 2, Anthropic announced a 100 million US dollar Claude Frontier Academy to train 10,000 frontier deployment engineers by the end of 2027, with Accenture, Bain, Deloitte, McKinsey and Morgan Stanley among the first participating firms. The article notes that these shifts are opening new opportunities for vocational colleges and training providers.

Articles.Title: HolonIQ Latest Report: Tech Giants Deepen In-Depth University Partnerships, AI-Related Collaboration Proportion Surges from 2.1% to 12% - 36Kr

stories.Headline: IT ministry to use AI for investor fraud detection
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology plans to deploy 12 AI services to detect fraud in investor claims for unclaimed shares, dividends, and matured deposits. The services will help the Investor Education and Protection Fund Authority, which currently examines around 2.9 lakh filed forms by hand. The plan was documented in a request for quotation issued by the National e-Governance Division, which the articles describe as the body that issued the document. The outlet reporting the story says the plan was published on October 27, 2026.

The request for quotation lists around 28 reported and anticipated fraud patterns that the system must address. These include forged identity documents, altered entitlement letters, and multiple claims filed against the same securities. It also names a newer behaviour, claim reasons generated in bulk by language models and submitted as templated text. The proposed system would pair document checks with analysis across claims and verify details against official records. The articles state that the AI will supply informative scores, while a government officer keeps the final decision to approve or reject each claim.

The articles identify the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology as the body behind the plan, with the National e-Governance Division handling the procurement document. The request for quotation sets out the fraud patterns and the design of the system, and it confirms that human officers remain responsible for outcomes. The articles do not include any statement from ministry officials beyond what the request for quotation says. The story gives no cost figures, vendor names, or timeline for deployment. Because the articles stop at the planning stage, they do not say when the services will go live or how the system will be evaluated once it does.

Articles.Title: IT ministry to use AI for investor fraud detection

stories.Headline: Google prioritises AI research over short-term Cloud revenue
stories.Summary:
Google CEO Sundar Pichai has confirmed that the company is allocating some of its limited computing resources to artificial intelligence research, putting that work ahead of serving paying Cloud customers. The decision means Google is giving up potential short-term revenue, according to Pichai. He described access to computing power for Google DeepMind as non-negotiable. The report was published on October 27, 2026, by TechGig.

Google faces a shortage of computing capacity, which Pichai said will affect future customer commitments for 2027. Infrastructure planning requires long lead times, and current capacity reflects investment decisions made in 2024. Even so, Google Cloud generated $24.8 billion in revenue in the second quarter, an 82 per cent increase year on year. Its contracted revenue backlog stood at about $514 billion at the end of June, which the article says points to substantial demand. Alphabet expects capital expenditure of $195 billion to $205 billion in 2026, with a large share going to AI and Cloud infrastructure.

Pichai said that access to advanced computing resources helps Google DeepMind build frontier AI models and identify capabilities for future products. He expects increasingly capable AI systems to help researchers develop later generations of models, a process he called recursive self-improvement. Demand from Google's own products adds further pressure on available capacity. Gemini 4 Argon processed nearly 25 trillion tokens in its first 72 hours, about three times the volume handled by Gemini 3.

Articles.Title: Google prioritises AI research over short-term Cloud revenue

stories.Headline: HCLTech opens two India centres for Rapidus chip engineering
stories.Summary:
HCL Technologies, the Indian IT services firm, and Japanese chipmaker Rapidus Corporation inaugurated two HCLTech development centres in India on Monday, according to a release. The centres are located in Bengaluru and Hubli. They are meant to support Rapidus's growing semiconductor engineering needs. HCLTech will offer several capabilities through the centres, including mask design, design infrastructure, process design kit development, design technology co-optimisation, and layout design. The firm will also work with Rapidus to build a pipeline of Indian engineering talent.

That pipeline is intended to meet Rapidus's changing talent requirements in Japan. The articles give no figures on headcount, investment, or timelines beyond the opening itself. Atsuyoshi Koike, Representative Director and CEO of Rapidus Corporation, said the company expects to tap India's growing pool of semiconductor engineers through the collaboration. C Vijayakumar, CEO and Managing Director of HCLTech, said advanced semiconductors will define technology over the next decade. He also said the partnership reflects a growing strategic collaboration between Japan and India.

Both statements were issued alongside the opening. The partnership comes as Japan and India deepen ties in semiconductors, a sector both countries are pursuing. The articles do not describe any further steps, next phases, or follow-on announcements. More to follow.

Articles.Title: HCLTech opens two India centres for Rapidus chip engineering

stories.Headline: Europe’s Rising Anxiety in the Global AI War: Key Challenges and Strategic Responses
stories.Summary:
Europe's growing unease over the global AI race has come into focus after German Chancellor Merz hosted NVIDIA founder Jensen Huang in Berlin, with executives from Siemens, Mercedes-Benz and Audi attending discussions on bringing AI into factories. The article, published on 27 October 2026 by 36Kr, describes this gathering as a sign that even Germany can no longer stay on the sidelines. It frames the event against a wider worry across the continent that Europe, once a leader in steam and combustion engines, has slipped behind the United States in chips and models. The piece argues that the centre of technological power has moved to a handful of players, leaving Europe with strong industrial assets but weak control over the systems that matter.

According to the article, the United States dominates through a closed chain running from NVIDIA's chips and its CUDA software ecosystem to TSMC's manufacturing and the large models built by OpenAI and Anthropic. Japan holds key positions in materials and equipment, including silicon wafers and chip testing systems, while South Korea's SK Hynix recovered from a 2023 memory downturn through its high-bandwidth memory products. China is described as cutting inference costs and applying AI to manufacturing, with the DeepSeek R1 model launched in early 2025 cited as an example. Europe, by contrast, is portrayed as holding valuable pieces such as ASML's lithography machines and France's Mistral, yet lacking the capital and integration needed to turn them into lasting advantage. The article says Mistral took a 15 million euro investment from Microsoft in 2024 and tied its distribution to Microsoft's Azure cloud.

The article notes that the European Commission and the OECD data show weak adoption, with about 8% of EU enterprises having deeply integrated AI into core business processes as of 2024, and fewer than 10% of European manufacturers applying AI to core production lines. It identifies fragmented data standards, costly compliance rules, a split market across 27 member states and scarce late-stage venture funding as the causes. NVIDIA, the article says, plans to invest nearly 10 billion US dollars in Europe, including tie-ups with Siemens and Audi on physical AI and industrial simulation. The article warns that if European industry builds its simulation, robotics and training systems on NVIDIA's platform, the company could become a foundational layer of European manufacturing, a dependence the piece treats as a serious question rather than a settled outcome. It concludes that Europe's best chance lies in its industrial data and engineering know-how, provided it can overcome the barriers that divide its markets.

Articles.Title: Europe’s Rising Anxiety in the Global AI War: Key Challenges and Strategic Responses - 36Kr

stories.Headline: How Walmart Develops AI to Power Its E-Commerce Business: Key Strategies & Implementation
stories.Summary:
Walmart has been expanding its use of artificial intelligence in e-commerce, and on October 21 it unveiled Agent Profiles, an Agent Gateway and shopping rules for external AI agents. Under this framework, customers can create separate profiles for different agents, set spending limits, approve each transaction individually and revoke authorization at any time. The Profiles program is scheduled to launch in November, while the Gateway is still in an early phase limited to invited testers. The move marks a shift from simply integrating AI shopping tools toward building open frameworks and rules for working with outside AI systems. Walmart has been more open to external AI than Amazon, which still restricts unauthorized outside agents from its ecosystem.

Walmart's in-house assistant, Sparky, launched in June 2025 and has grown from answering product questions to handling image-based shopping, assembling multi-product shopping plans, assisting checkout and resolving customer service issues. Walmart's CEO said on the August earnings call that customers who shop with Sparky spend 40% more per order than those who do not. Behind these features lies years of digital work, starting with a website in 1996, online ordering and in-store pickup in 2007, and the merging of grocery and general merchandise apps alongside the Walmart+ membership in 2020. In March 2025 Walmart also launched Wally, an internal AI tool for its merchandising team, after building a semantic layer to define the meaning and statistical basis of its operational data.

Walmart's connections to outside AI have grown steadily, beginning with a voice shopping partnership with Google in 2017. Last October it announced a cooperation with OpenAI that lets customers buy Walmart products inside ChatGPT, and in January it announced a deal with Google to bring Walmart and Sam's Club products, accounts and memberships into Gemini. Walmart also appears among the shopping partners Meta announced in September for its Muse assistant. Walmart's Daniel Danker said in March that customers already buy food and household goods there every week, so new AI channels could let it reach categories such as electronics, beauty, apparel and home goods. Retail partners such as Best Buy, Gap, Sephora and Wayfair appear on the same list, which suggests they are also seeking new traffic from AI.

Walmart's openness is conditional, because it wants to avoid being reduced to a fulfillment pipeline for outside AI. Danker observed earlier this year that products checked out directly through ChatGPT converted at about one-third the rate of products that sent shoppers to the Walmart website, which he attributed to breaking the habit of adding items to a cart before checking out. To address this, Walmart let Sparky enter external chat environments so shoppers can connect their Walmart accounts and carry over existing carts and membership benefits. In this model, external AI handles discovery while Walmart keeps control of accounts, transactions and fulfillment. The articles say this setup also lets Walmart keep building long-term service relationships using past purchase records.
